Hon. N. W. ROWELL (Minister of Health) moved the third reading of Bill No. 20, to amend the Opium and Drug Act.
Mr. D. D. MlAiCKENZIE (Cape Breton North and Victoria):	When this Bill
was in Committee, I asked the President of the Council (Mr. Rowell) for certain information as to the meaning of some of its terms and, in particular, what is mean by the term "import into Canada." I do not understand that any drugs which come into Canada which are not for consumption in the country are imports. I want to have a clear understanding of what is meant by the word "import," and whether there has been any finding by the Department of Justice on that point.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
In answer to my hon. friend I would draw his attention to the definition of the words "imports" or "imported" in the definition clause of the original Act of 1911. Paragraph (c) of that Act provides:
''Imports" or "imported" means and includes the bringing or conveying, or causing to be brought or conveyed, Into Canada of any drug.
The view of -the Department of Justice based upon this Act and the amendment of last session, which requires a license to import or to export, is that a license is required even though it is the intention to bring in the drugs in bond for trans-shipment. I beg to move that the title be "An Act to amend the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act."
Motion agreed to, Bill read the third time, and passed.
Hon. ARTHUR MEIGHEN (Minister of the Interior) moved the second reading of Bill No. 57 (from the Senate), to amend the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, 1907.
Will the minister explain the nature and significance of the proposed amendments?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The amendments are two or three in number. One of them provides for the settlement of disputes between classes of employers and classes of employees, making it compulsory upon either class to select an arbitrator instead of re-

quiring an arbitrator to be selected compulsorily only by one employer of each class.
There is no arbitrator under the Act. I presume the minister means a member of the Board of Investigation.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, I should have described him as a member of the board. There is an amendment to section 2 providing that application for the establishment of a board of conciliation must be authorized by a majority of the members of a union, in cases where the employees are organized, or by a majority of the employees concerned, in cases where some or all of those affected are not members of a union. As the Act now stands, a strike may be declared by a comparatively small proportion of those affected. The next amendment provides for merely clerical corrections. Section 4 provides for a uniform scale of fees for witnesses giving evidence before boards of conciliation. The next amendment forbids the declaration of a strike until a copy of the report of the board has been delivered through the registrar to both the parties affected. Section 6 of this Bill permits the establishment of a board by the Minister of Labour without application from the employers or the employees concerned in cases where a strike seems to the minister to be imminent.
There are some amendments that I should like to refer to perhaps a little in detail. I shall not take up the time of the House just now as that can be done in committee.

Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1-interpretation of "Employer" extended:
Will the minister please explain the purpose of this amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It is designed to permit the establishment of a single board to deal with a dispute in which a number of individual empoyers are concerned having interests in common. Cases occur in which demands presented on behalf of labour, and resultant disputes, affect several different firms or companies engaged in the same line of industry. In such cases, as the law now stand, it has not been found possible to establish a joint board without first obtaining the consent of the several employers concerned. It has sometimes happened 1211
that such consent has been withheld, and the inability of the Department of Labour to establish a joint board has been followed by a strike. As I explained on the second reading, if the strike threatened is on the part of the employees of various companies engaged in the same line of industry, and employing men of the same grades, all that is compulsory on the part of the employers as the law now stands is that each one shall select an arbitrator. The question to be settled in such a case is really one between the whole class of empoyees on the one hand, and the whole class of employees on the other, but there is no provision in the Act compelling employers to make such recognition of the essential unity of interest of the employees as would be entailed in the appointment of an arbitrator to represent the employers. The amendment provides that in such cases the minister may require the employers, all of whom are affected, to select an arbitrator. If they are to do that, of course they will do it, because otherwise the board would be created without them, and they would suffer accordingly.
As a consequence, one board will be able to act where formerly, construing the Act literally, it required half-a-dozen boards. Before this section is carried I have an amendment to suggest.	'

As all of us have not the original Act before us, and as this is a very important matter, I would ask the minister to read the section with the proposed amendment so that we may thoroughly understand its import.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have not the original Act before me. Possibly the leader of the Opposition will read it for the information of the hon. members.

Paragraph (c) of the original Act defines the term "Employer" as
-any person, company or corporation employing ten or more persons and owning and operating any mining property, agency of transportation or communication, or public service utility, including, except as hereinafter provided, railways, whether operated by steam, electricity or other motive power, steamships, telegraph and telephone lines, gas, electric light, water and power works.
The amendment proposed to add to that the words:
Or any number of such persons, companies or corporations acting together, or who in the opinion of the minister have interests in common.
1902'

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I have not discussed
this specific question with the Minister of Labour, but it would occur to me that if we were to amend the Act as my hon. friend suggests so as to make it applicable to the employees of municipalities the question would immediately arise whether we should not make it also applicable as well to the employees of provinces. If the hon. member purposes to press the amendment I would ask that we proceed to the consideration of the next clause, because I should not like to take the responsibility of answer-

ing definitely as to where the Government should stand on the amendment until I have had opportunity of consulting the Minister of Labour.

Of course, the industries mentioned in the Act are in the nature of public utilities, and it is necessary to keep that fact in mind with reference to the significance of the amendment I propose. I do not think my
4 p.m. hon. friend will find the Minister of Labour disposed to reject an amendment of this kind.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman's amendment be wide enough to include the telephone employees of the province of Manitoba?

It. might be
well to go a step further and make it clear that it is intended to take in provincial employees of this class. If my hon. friend is prepared to let the clause stand for further consideration I will not press the amendment at this stage.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I should like to have
it stand.
Section stands.
On section 2-signatures requisite for applications to refer disputes to boards and for statutory declarations accompanying them:

I do not want to take any advantage of the minister's unfamiliarity with the Act, but there are one or two. matters that it may be of advantage to make a little clearer. The minister spoke of the amendment as relating to a strike being declared. That, of course-

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No. It is a declaration.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think the hon. member is wrong as to that. As the Act now stands a strike may be declared-

-A strike
cannot be declared under the Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I know a strike cannot be declared. What I mean is that an application may be made and the strike that depends upon the issue of the application may follow, where the initiative has been taken not by a majority at all but by a very small minority o'f the employees con-. cerned. It is clear from the reading of the Act as it stands that it applies when the issue has been precipitated by a very small minority because the provision reads as follows:
If made by employees, members of a trade union, shall be signed by two -of its officers duly authorized by a majority vote of the members of the union, or by a vote taken by ballot of the members of the union present at a meeting.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
If there is only a small number present all they would require is a majority of those present to authorize two men to sign. Under the new reading the procedure would be quite different.
(d) by employees who are members of a trade union, by two of its officers duly authorized by a majority of the members of the union.
Then there comes a full stop. The majority of the members must authorize.

That 'being the case it does not matter very much what the special purpose of their being together is because the majority must act-not a majority of those who happen to be present at the meeting but a majority of all the members must act. That is the essential difference between the law as it will be, if this Bill passes, and the law as it was before; in fact the essence of the whole thing is the requiring of an absolute majority. Such being the case there does not seem any need for requiring that the meeting shall be called especially for a certain purpose, because no matter how called, if they actually decide by a majority of all the members- whether they are there or not-that they shall make this application, then they should be allowed to make it.

It is not perfectly cleat what is meant by "the meeting of a union." Take my own province of Nova Scotia, we have miners' unions extending all over the whole province. In particular we have them in Cumberland, Pietou, Inverness and Cape Breton. We have one miners' union extending all over these counties, and I would like to be quite clear whether the minister intendb that a vote of the whole union shall be taken before an application can be made. There may not be the same difficulty in the case of one of the mines of the Dominion Coal Company, or at Sydney Mines, because this is a body of men by themselves. But does the minister understand it would be necessary to take a vote of the miners at Springhill and Pietou because they are all of the one union? Or is it the intention that the vote shall be confined to the group which are immediately affected by the proposed action in applying for a board?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: As I would read the amendment I would say that the majority of the union would have to authorize an application.

Does not the minister think that is a very difficult way of getting at the matter?
. Mr. MEIGHEN: I do not know that 1 can say finally what the minister thinks. I do' not think my opinion on the subject ,is very valuable, really I am not familiar .enough with these matters to press a very intelligent opinion. But the meaning of the amendment clearly is that if the employees who ask for a 'board are members of a trade union they must first of all have their request, if they ask for it, come from a

.majority of the members of the whole union.	,

If the minister had not been so polite as to tell me that I .was wrong, I would not challenge his statement. However, I know this Act rather well, and I think I understand the significance of its provisions as well as of the amendments that are 'being suggested. I have the existing Act and a copy of the proposed Bill before me, and I will ask the minister-after listening to what I say- whether I was right or whether I was wrong. The original Act, subsection (3), reads that where the application is made by employees who are members of a trade union it shall be signed by two of its officers duly authorized by a majority vote of the members of the Union. That is the wording of the original Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, but go on.

That is where the majority of the men are members of the union. Now the amendment appears the same in that regard. "If the application is made by employees who are members of a trade union, it shall be signed by two of its officers duly authorized by a majority of the members of the union, etc." Both sections are identical.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Oh, no, my hon. friend is wrong.
Where is the difference?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The way the original Act readls it is the punctuation that to my mind makes the difference. The Act says this:
The application shall,
-if made by employees, members of a trade union, shall be signed by two of its officers duly authorized by a majority vote of the members of the union, or by a vote taken by ballot of the members of the union present at a meeting called-
All in the one sentence. So the vote is taken by the union, and a majority of the members present carry it. That must be the interpretation given by the Minister of Labour. The hon. member will see that under the amendment it is different altogether because in the amendment there is a period after the iword "union." "There must be a majortiy of the members of the union." There the sentence stops making it absolute. It does not make the word "present" which follows, at all affect the meaning of the word "union" or modify its

meaning in any way. That is, the word "present" does not modify -the word "union" .as it appears to-day in the present Act. I will read 'the explanation given me by the Minister of Labour on the subject. He says:
2. The amendment proposed in section 2 of the Bill provides that an application for the establishment of a Board of Conciliation and Investigation must be authorized by a majority of the members of a union, in cases where the employees are organized, or by the majority of the employees concerned, in cases where some or all of those affected are not members of a trade union. As the Act now stands it is possible for a relatively small minority of workers in an industry to make application for a Board. Experience in the administration of the Act has proven the desirability of the proposed amendment.
He is taking his opinion from the actual interpretation given to it, and it coincides with what I give as my opinion from the reading of the law. The way it reads now is:
The majority of the members present at a meeting.
He wants to change that and compel the majority of the whole union to agree before they shall take such action.

If I read the rest of the section I think my hon. friend will see the significance of what I have been pointing out. The original Act continued in this form:
Or by a vote taken by ballot of the members of the union present at a meeting called on not less than three days' notice for the purpose of discussing the question.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

That would
leave an opportunity for a minority to take that particular action. But that is not the significance of the amendment now suggested. In the latter the words "for the purpose of discussing the question" are left out, and as I read the amendment it simply enables a ballot of the members of the union present at any meeting, whether it is called particularly in relation to the consideration of a strike or of an application for a board concerning a strike, and it makes possible what I said a moment ago- a hole-and-corner meeting for the purpose of making application for a board. When this Act was drafted-and il remember it quite well, because I had a good deal to do with the drafting- the endeavour all the way through was to have its provisions apply to both organized and unorganized labour. Where men are not organized in a union, or have not met together specifically
to consider an application for a board, they are required to call the meeting by notice with specific reference to the dispute, and at that meeting the ballot shall be taken and the majority decide on the application. The amendment leaves the part relating to organized labour exactly as it was before, but in regard to men who are not organized, and are not considering a question specifically relating to the dispute, this amendment provides that such men may at any meeting convened without reference to the dispute at all send in an application for a board.
An application, if made by employees who are members of a trade union, shall be signed by two of its officers duly authorized by a majority of the members of the union.
That is all right, But the second part reads:
If such authorization is obtained by a vote taken in whole or in part at a meeting, such meeting shall be called on not less than three days' notice and the vote shall be by ballot.
That does not say anything about the meeting being in reference to the particular question in dispute. It leaves it open to any body of men whether belonging to a labour organization or not to take a vote at any meeting in the absence of other members and to send in an application for a board that other members might not wish. I think that will be the effect of the amendment if it goes through.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: This is purely a matter of interpretation, but with all deference I must press the point once again. The hon. member argues that the difference between this legislation, if it passes, and the old law is merely that under this the Act does not require the meeting to be called for the express purpose of deciding this question.
That is what I said.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I think the hon. member entirely misapprehends the effect both of the old law and of this amendment, but especially of the latter. We do not need to distinguish between the case of men contemplating a strike and the members of a union who are not; the one argument applies to both classes. Let us take the old law as to the case of men who contemplate striking and who are members of a union.
The application for a board, if made by employees members of a tradte union, shall be signed by two of its officers duly authorized by a majority vote of the members of the union, or by a vote taken by ballot of the members of the union present at a meeting called on not less than three days' notice for the purpose of discussing the question.

Now "union" ends with a comma, and consequently the words following are an alternative; that is to say, or the two men may get their authority by a vote taken by ballot of the members of the union present *at a meeting called on not less than three days' notice for the purpose. 80 it is clear, is it not, that they can get their authority by the vote of the majority of the members present at such meeting. So if there are 500 members of the union, and a meeting is called on three days' notice, and only 60 are present, 31 of those 60 can authorize the making of the application. I will ask the hon. member if that reasoning is right? In that case we would get an application for a board from 31 members.
Under the new law.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, under the old law. Is that not the case?
With this [DOT]qualification, that the vote could only be taken at a meeting called for the purpose of discussing the question of the strike.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I thoroughly agree with that.

That is the
point.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Providing notice is sent out, it is for the purpose of making this application.

That is
right.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Then, under the circumstances I set out, providing the notice was properly sent, 31 men could make application for the board. Is that clear?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Now the question comes: Could 31 men do so under the new law?
The application and declaration accompanying it shall be signed, if made,-
(d) by employees who are members of a trade union, by two of its officers duly authorized by a majority of the members of the union.
If we stop there for good, they certainly could not. Suppose we call that the end of the sentence? So far undoubtedly 31 members could not. If there are 500 members it takes 251 to authorize those two officers to act. Let us go on and see if that is modified.
If such authorization is obtained by a vote taken in whole or in part at a meeting,-
UMr. Meighen.]
It must toe authorization provided in the preceding sentence, that is the authorization of 251 men.
-such meeting shall be called on not less than three days' notice and the vote shall be by ballot.
I hope it is clear to the hon. member that such authorization must be endorsed by at least 251 members; it has to be that now. If it is taken at a meeting, then the meeting must be called on three days' notice, and the object of the meeting need not be stated, but it requires 251 members to give the authorization. What I am arguing is that so long as you have to have a majority authorizing action to be taken, it is not necessary to require that the object of the meeting shall be discussed, because if a majority present actually authorize an application, and vote by ballot for that specific purpose, they should not be denied a board. Doubtless the reason the purpose of the meeting was required to be stated in the old law was because the members might not all attend, and there might be a requisition by a fraction of the members of the union; but under the amendment that is impossible. Consequently it has not been thought worth while to say that the meeting shall require to be called by such specific notice.
Now, I am sure I have established that under the old law 31 men out of 500 members could ask for a board and bring about a strike in that way; whereas under the new law no less than 251 out of the 500 could possibly do so. That must he abundantly clear.

They cannot bring about a strike by asking' for a board; the purpose of asking for the board is to avoid a strike. If the intention of the amendment is as the minister now describes it I think the amendment changes a very significant feature of the Act. My own idea is that it is much more in the interest of labour, and more calculated to avoid a dispute, to permit a majority of the men attending a meeting specifically for the purpose of considering an application to the Government for a board to make such application than to place on the section the interpretation that the minister is apparently placing on it.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If the majority had to ask for it, is it worth while to say that they must call a meeting for that purpose? I do not think it is very objectionable at all.

Most industrial disputes have grown out of a group of men,

not the whole body, having a grievance and very often the grievance is something which affects only a handful of men. Where opportunity is denied of having a grievance investigated, it leads often to a very serious situation. The purpose of the Act is to avoid strikes and for that reason it enables any group of men who have a grievance and are sufficiently interested to have it investigated to call a meeting of all the men to consider whether or not they should apply to the Government for a board. They have a right under the Act as it stands, that they will not have under the law as the minister proposes to amend it. As I see the amendment of the minister, he is going to place it in the hands of one or two labour leaders, or one or two employers to decide as to whether or not there is to be an investigation of the dispute. It goes to the otljer extreme. If a group of men have a grievance and they want to have it investigated no such amendment as the minister proposes could give them that right. He says that they should call a mass meeting and if the men turn out to that meeting a board will be granted. He will not allow them the privilege of taking action unless then can rally enough men to make a demand on the Government by a majority vote. It practically puts the control of the situation in the hands of the leaders of either party, and I do not think it is going to work advantageously.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I know the hon. member sees that his reasoning was wrong before and I think I can show him that he is wrong again. It will take a majority, if the law passes, to make application for a board. But, he says that places the whole power in the hands of two or three leaders. How does it? That is just exactly what the object of the amendment is to avoid. If a majority of the 500 members of a union must ask for a board, how is the power of one or two men enhanced? Previously the one or two men could call a meeting at three days' notice. If only a very few attended or were interested and the balance were not interested all they had to do was to convert 31 men in the case I have described, and they had their board. Now they have to get 251 instead of 31. The burden put upon the men who want to make trouble is heavier than it was before. It is giving control to the majority and not a few and that is the express purpose to be served by the Act. It is democratising the power of invoking boards and calling strikes. It is placing in the hands of the majority a power that formerly might be exercised by a few.

I will just put on record my own view of the matter and leave the responsibility with the minister. Take the case of a coal mine. You have a group of men working say, the pumps, and they have nothing whatever to do with the other parts of the mining operations. These men have a real grievance and they want to get it investigated. Under the law they can do it where other men are sufficiently interested in the dispute to come to a meeting. Under the law as the minister proposes to change it, if these men in the pump house were not prominent in the organization and the leaders who were in control wished to avoid any investigation because it might bring up some other matter affecting relations between one group of men and another, they would see to it that a sufficient number of men did not attend the meeting, the application would not be made and it would be impossible to have the grievance of this group of men investigated.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That is another point
altogether. That has been raised by the hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie).
It is occasioned by this clause as now interpreted.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
It is affected by the
Act but it is very different from what the hon. gentleman is talking about. It will be affected by the Act to the extent that members of the union will require to have a majority in their favour before they can apply even although the dispute might directly affect only a small portion such as the leader of the Opposition describes. I presume that employees belonging to a definite union will feel that their interests are interests in common. I am rather of the opinion, although I do not want to speak positively, that this amendment has the approval of organized labour. If it is an objection that the majority of the members of the union must support the application, then, the amendment is subject to that objection. But it would not appear to me that it was an objection. However, I do not claim that my opinion is worth much on that point. If hon. members feel that this is a very important matter I have no objection to this clause standing as there is already one clause standing and we can discuss it again when the committee resumes.

The widespread import of this amendment is highly objectionable. I feel that it is particularly open to objection taken in connection with con-

ditions in our own province. We have a union extending over four important and largely separated counties. I think the practice was that it was not necessary to have a vote in the different counties but all they had to do was to get the opinion of a majority of the group of employees immediately affected by the difficulty. We have a little coal company in 'Cape Breton called the Bras d'Or Cbal Company. It is a comparatively small concern but these men belong to the provincial union. Suppose we had a difficulty at the Bras d'Or Coal Company, that would only affect 300 or 400 men, is it rather not a ludicrous and clumsy method of settling that difficulty by means of a board to make it necessary to get the vote of the men at Springhill, and Pictou, and the men employed by the Dominion Coal Company and the Nova Scotia Steel Company? They are not concerned except in a sympathetic way. I have never heard of a provincial vote being taken for the purpose of getting a board and if that is the effect of the proposed amendment I do not think it is desirable at all. It should be localized to the place where the difficulty is and where the board is required. If it has not been submitted to the organizations in my own province I would strongly urge upon the minister the desirability of submitting all these changes to them and securing their opinion upon them.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. member must keep this in mind, that the object of a board of conciliation is to effect a settlement without a strike. If a strike occurs then all the members of the union who are affected will go on strike and not merely the section that may possibly have the immediate grievance. If all the members of the union are to be affected by this board of arbitration, surely it is only right that they should have a say as to whether a board of arbitration should be appointed. I do not see how you are going to restrict it, and I do not apprehend it has been restricted where there has been a union and within it a unit smaller than the union itself. I think it is necessary in practice that all the members of the union should have a say and in fact as the law stood every member of this union was entitled to notice of the meeting, and he could go there and vote the proposition down.
If they did not have a meeting, then, under the old law there had to be a majority of the members of the union, just the same as now. Therefore, the cumbersomeness of which the hon. member speaks was just the same under the old law as it could pos-

sibly be under this. The only difference is that under the old law, if there was a small meeting,-a very small cabal might precipitate the whole proceedings leading to a strike. Under the new law, a majority of those who are affected and expect to go on strike must be consulted before they launch the machinery that leads to that end.

I still do not see how the minister makes out the point he has been endeavouring to make that a majority of the members of the union is necessary in view of the change that has been suggested under this proposed amendment. There are two sentences in the clause, the first being:
By employees who are members of a trade union, by two of its officers duly authorized by a majority of the members of the union.
That is perfectly clear. The next sentence is a perfectly independent one which has nothing to do with the first. It reads:
If such authorization is obtained by a vote taken in whole or in part at a meeting-
It does not say "at a meeting of the union." It may be at any meeting.
-such meeting shall be called on not less than three days* notice and the vote shall be by ballot.
The whole effect of that is, as I said at the outset, simply to do away with the necessity of it being designated that a meeting is to consider a particular subject, and to give to the men present at any meeting that may be called the right to vote by ballot and a majority of them to put in an application.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: What is the effect of the word ".such"? The word "such" refers to the preceding sentence, "duly authorized by a majority of the members of the union."
Such authorization means authorization to apply for a board.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: But of the character previously described. That is what the word "such" is used for.
Will the minister agree to making that all one sentence, taking out the period at the end of the first sentence?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No, because the period is of great effect; it has the effect that I have contended for all along. The first sentence describes what the character of the authorization must be; it must be an authorization

by a majority of the members of the union. The second sentence says that such authorization, if secured at a meeting, must be secured so and so. This must be a majority authorization of the members of the union, or the word "such" has no meaning at all.

It seems to me that the amendment as it reads would preclude the possibility of men on a given property being able to make application for a board, provided that they belonged to the same organization as the men employed, for instance, in the entire camp, such as we have in the riding from which I come. We know there are grievances in individual properties, which grievances do not embrace all the properties in a mining camp, and this amendment would preclude the possibility of two or three hundred men in a given mine making application for a board when the men employed in the other mines in a given camp might have no inclination to apply for a board. Yet there is an injustice perpetrated on the men in this property, and the amendment states clearly that they cannot make application for a board because a majority of the rank and file of the membership who have no grievance whatever have to vote for the board. This amendment has a joker in it; it is taking away from the -workingman one of bis prerogatives.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: What the hon. member says as to the effect of this arises evidently out of a little apprehension as to what it means. That is just what the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) has been arguing it does not mean.

My hon.
friend, (Mr. McDonald) has expressed exactly the view I expressed a minute ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext: Then, as I understand the matter, there is nothing in this that precludes the possibility of a walk-out through the mere fact that there is no way of redress on a given property.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, there is.
There' is, under this amendment, no way of getting redress on a given property without involving all the members of a union in a given camp.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Everybody in the same union, yes.
Then, according to the minister's explanation, it seems to me that this amendment, instead of being beneficial to labour organizations, is aiming at their destruction.
Collective bargaining.

It is taking away the men's right to make application for a board if you insist that the application must be approved by 100 per cent of the employees. The effect is to preclude from being law-abiding citizens men who wish to abide by the constitution. Either that, or they have to submit to tyranny.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They submit themselves to the majority of the members of their union, and I would be very loth to say that that was submitting to tyranny. They submit only to a majority of the members of their union, for the reason that that majority, indeed, their whole union, is affected by the proceedings, and are expected to answer for the proceedings should they result in a strike.

I want to emphasize very strongly what my hon. friend (Mr. McDonald) has said. Speaking as one who has a practical knowledge of the difficulties which arise in mining camps, perhaps the minister will be prepared to listen to him if he will not listen to anything I may say. My hon. friend (Mr. McDonald) has said exactly what I said when making objection to this clause as interpreted by the minister. The minister does not know the Act or appreciate the purpose for which it was introduced. All through the discussion he has talked about a strike, and of the action of a few men involving the rest in a strike. That shows a complete ignorance of the purpose of the legislation. It is for the purpose of investigating disputes, not for the purpose of saving a whole group of men from being brought out on strike. It is to make possible at the public expense an investigation of difficulties that may lead to a strike. A group of men may have their grievance investigated under this Act and have it satisfactorily settled without bringing others into the matter at all. Allow a handful of men to suffer under a real grievance for a time, and very soon you will bring a whole district into a state of unrest and discontent. The primary purpose of the Act is to begin investigation as speedily as possible where there is a real grievance. Men are not going to ask for Government investigation of a difficulty if they have not a substantial grievance. If they give public notice that they desire a certain matter should be investigated, and a majority interested ask for a board, I think they should have it. The only way to solve these problems is to have just as much publicity as we possibly can have, when there is any question of unfair treatment to be investigated.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have no desire to recriminate with the hon. member at all, but what he argued for a long time was that there was no difference between this amendment and the previous law, except that the previous law required calling the meeting to say what the object was. Otherwise, he "said, there was no difference at all.

I said, where
the meeting was called for the purpose in question those attending the meeting should have a board granted if the majority present were in favour of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. member said precisely, and argued strenuously, and answered my question categorically when I asked if that was not his contention, that there was no difference at all except the one I have stated. He argued that a majority was required, and it was still required. Now he says he is wrong, and he wants to get in line with somebody else. I know the hon. member knows more as to the wisdom of this legislation than I do, because he had more to do with it, but as to interpretation, there is no question that the interpretation given on behalf of the Government at the opening of the committee was the right interpretation. That is the intention of this law, whether it be right or wrong. It may be that possibly I have not in mind exactly the correct comprehension of union. Trade union is defined in paragraph (1) as follows:
"trade union" or "union" means any organization of employees formed for the purpose of regulating relations between employers and employees.
I do not know but what that may be wide enough to cover what is ordinarily known as a local union. If so, all that would be required is a majority of the local union. It would occur to me that local union would come within the terms of this definition, so there would be no need of going outside of that. If that is the case, I think it would meet the point raised by the hon. member (Mr. McDonald).

The United Mine Workers of America have about 30,000 men in Alberta. Under the amendment what number of men would be required to petition for a board in the case of a grievance concerning only one mine where say 300 men were employed?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I presume that would
be a local union.

Then the number
required would be a majority of the local

union because a union is defined as' "any organization of employees formed for the purpose of regulating relations between employers and employees." A local unim certainly is such an organization, so all that would be required would be a majority of the local union. My hon. friend (Mr. McDonald) is therefore wrong in saying that a whole camp would be tied up.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
He may have been misled (by my using the word "organization" instead of "union." Union is the right word, and a majority of the local union would be all that was required.
Mr. MeDONALD: I have not said that we would go on strike for this, because I want to impress on the committee that every workingman with an ounce of sense wants to avoid strikes as much as possible. It seems to me, however, that this amendment would tend to bring on strikes rather than to prevent them. I want to make any point clear. We have at least one property in the camp where I have lived for thirteen years, and where men have been fired because they had the temerity to vote for me at the last election. That, in my estimation is a grievance in a free country. This legislation would prevent the men employed on that property having recourse to constitutional methods for remedying their grievance. All the other employees at the different camps would have to be consulted. They would have to canvass the entire camp to get a majority of the organization to get out and vote, and if the men went on strike without doing that, they would be infringing on the laws of this country.
Mr. H. A. iMACKIE:	Does the entire
camp belong to the same union?.
Mr. MeDONALD:	Undoubtedly. Our
International Union embraces all crafts in our camp.

Is there just one
local union or several locals combined into one head union?

We have one local
union in our camp embracing all crafts. I contend that this legislation takes away from the people the incentive to be law-abiding citizens.
Mr. H. A. MAiOKIE:	How many men
employed in the camp belong to the same union?
Mr. McDonald : 2,500.
Mr. McKENZI'E: I think the minister should leave the law as it was, as regards
meetings and the decision that must be reached before employees can apply to the board. The old Act has been interpreted repeatedly through practice, and throughout labour camps, mines, and unions it is well understood what steps are necessary in order to get a board, and I have never heard of any particular difficulty having arisen because any board was obtained improperly or with too much facility. After all, representations have to be made to the minister and it is entirely in his discretion whether he will grant a board or not. It is absolutely discretionary on his part, and I therefore think that, with that ultimate safeguard in view, it should be made as easy as possible for the workingmen of this country to make their application in this matter. I want to warn the minister that the moment he passes legislation making an absolute majority necessary he at once starts a powerful faction among those companies and employees who may not desire to have any investigation made and who for that reason would keep men from attending meetings. And it is well known that the influence that can be exercised in this respect is considerable. Take a big company like the Dominion Coal Company, of Cape Breton, which has twenty-four different mines under its control. I presume that every one of those mines has its lodge; they do not call their unions "local branches" but "lodges." There is a lodge at Caledonia, and possibly one at every other mine, and if there were any difficulty between the management and the men, that lodge would call a meeting of its members to discuss the questions involved. Any number of men might attend that meeting, and under the old law a majority vote would entitle them to make application for the board. We should leave the matter as simple as possible, and leave no opportunity for the exercise of influence that would have the effect of rendering any meeting unconstitutional. We have in the town of Sydney Mines five or six different mines under one management, and I understand that any one of these hitherto had the right to issue a notice calling together those who were interested in .that particular mine and if there was a majority of those present favourable they had the right to make application. I think it would be well at all events to have the opinion of these lodges, and I have no doubt that the men in my own province would be opposed to any law that would put obstacles in the way of their getting a board when necessary. I rather think that the workingmen

in the province of Nova Scotia 5 p.m. will regard this new legislation as taking away the power which they now possess and conferring on employers a power which at present they have not and which they might use in preventing the labouring men from holding constitutionally called meetings. I agree entirely with the member for Timiskaming (Mr. McDonald), a workingman himself, that the obtaining of relief by constitutional means should be made as easy as possible, and that everything in the nature of arbitrary power should be removed.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I move that the clause stand.
Section stands.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
This sectiop also will have to stand; it depends on the passing of section 2.
Section stands.
On section 4-allowance to witnesses.

In speaking on this section in the Senate-if I may refer to what the Minister of Labour said in that Chamber in regard to the measure - it was intimated that the purpose of the amendment was to allow a fee of two dollars as the sum that was desirable. The Minister gave the figures that were paid!. In some provinces witnesses were allowed 75 cents and in others $3, and he suggested that in order to make for uniformity there should be an allowance of $2 as a fee. The amendment now suggests a minimum of $4.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The $2 to which the Minister of Labour referred was, I think, for attendance alone. In some provinces it is 75 cents and in others it is as high as $2, but this allowance will cover not only attendance but expenses. This is intended to make uniform, so far as possible, the fee taxable in all provinces. The allowance of $4 is the minimum for attendance and expenses.	.
That is not what the Minister of Labour said in putting through the measure in the Senate. If I might read his words I should be glad to call them to the attention of my hon. friend.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have no objection; it is of course against the rules.

I do not wish to take a course that is not proper, but I

have the Senate debates in my hand and the words of the Minister of Labour in regard to section 34 are perfectly clear if my hon. friend looks at Hansard.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I read the speech of the Minister of Labour as it appeared in Hansard and as a result I consulted him on the subject. I know he intends $4 to be the minimum for both attendance and expenses.

I do not think that this is a good amendment; it is an unwise departure. The law as it stands at present recognizes the fees paid witnesses in the courts in the different provinces and this legislation as drafted makes a change which I consider entirely unnecessary. The minister will find that in some provinces $4 would not be adequate as an allowance for attendance as well as expenses.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Four dollars as a minimum might he unjust in a city where the expense of maintenance was very high. Four dollars is the minimum, tout the idea of the Minister of Labour is this: That to provide that a witness in one province shall, in these times, only get seventy-five cents for his time will press upon that man unduly severely because the witnesses are very often workingmen themselves. The minister's idea is that it iis not fair in a province to pay a man at the present time only seventy-five cents for his day, so he declares there shall be a minimum always paid in respect otf attendance and expenses of $4. That is the only modification of the present law.

In our province in addition to witness fees, a. mileage payment is made. I certainly think that seventy-five cents for the attendance of a witness is ridiculously low. A -man cannot get his dinner now at Sydney, where the courts sit, for seventy-five -cents. I have not been able to re-ad the section, and I would therefore ask if it provides anything by way of travelling expenses in the shape of mileage?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
At present the law on this subject reads as follows:
Every person who is summoned and duly attends as a witness shall be entitled to an allowance for expenses according to the scale for the time being in force with respect to witnesses in civil suits in the superior courts in the province where the inquiry is being conducted.
The amendment adds:
with a minimum allowance of four dollars per day.

Thus the allowance of a witness shall not be less than $4 per day. He is entitled to an allowance for expenses according to the scale for the time being in force respecting winesses in civil suits in the civil courts in the provinoe where the inquiry is being conducted. Now he gets a minimum' allowance of .altogether $4 a day. He may get .more tout he cannot get less.

Why should witnesses toe allowed more when appearing before these boards than they are when appearing before the courts? The effect of this amendment -may simply be that forty or fifty men may be called in as witnesses for a minute or two, and thereby obtain the minimum allowance of $4. I think there is an advantage in keeping the cost of administering this Act as low as possible. Everyone would wish to see that, witnesses were properly compensated, but I think the allowance granted under the rules laid down for the superior courts of the different provinces is a fair allowance.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The idea of the Minister of Labour, I think, is this: It is not fair to take a man from his work-and the working man is usually the type of man who is called- and pay him, to meet all his expenses, a less sum than $4. Where a board is meeting it is thought there is very little chance of such a witness being away from his work less than a day. That is the minister's only idea in making this provision. It does seem to me that the time of a workingman is just as valuable in Prince Edward Island or Nova Scotia as it is in Ontario or Manitoba where the rates are higher. There does not seem to be any reason why we should distinguish, because the provinces for their own purposes distinguish in the cases referred to- that is the minister's only idea.

Section agreed to.
On section five-relation of parties to remain unaltered pending proceedings before a board, and delivery of report.
Will the minister explain this change?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The purpose is to prevent the declaration of a strike until the report of the Board of Conciliation is delivered to the parties concerned through the registrar.
That has always been the law. I think there was some technical objection taken, was there not?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think a technical ruling was given.

I think some employer in Toronto refused to wait until he got a copy of the report in the ordinary way.
On section 6-Minister may, on or without application, order a board or recommend inquiry.
Will the minister kindly explain this amendment?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The purpose of this amendment is to permit the establishment of a board by the Minister of Labour without application from the employers or employees concerned in cases where a strike seems, to the minister, to be imminent. Apparently the minister cannot call for a board as the law stands, unless there is a strike.
Unless there is an application.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes. Anyway the effect of the amendment is to enable him to establish a Board of Conciliation. In any case where a strike seems to him to toe imminent he can establish the board himself.

I do not want to appear unduly critical, but some of the points I am bringing up were very carefully considered when this law was being drafted, and this happens to be one of them. I think it would be a great mistake to adopt the amendment which is suggested here, giving the minister the right to establish a board wherever he thinks a strike is imminent, for the simple reason that the Whole purpose underlying the Act is to allow either of the parties to a dispute to request a board when they feel that their interests demand it, but otherwise to render the chance of Government interference as remote as possible. This amendment means that the minister may, when he takes it into his head, start an inquiry and establish one of these boards without w'aiting for either of the parties to the dispute to ask for it. I can only think of one consequence of this amendment so far as the ministry is concerned. It is that where no action is taken under it the government of the day will be blamed for not having intervened, inasmuch as the minister is given power to intervene without the parties requesting any action; and, on the other hand, if the government does take action under this amendment, if it goes into the dispute on its own initiative, and trouble arises, the gov-

ernment will be told it had no business to interfere, and that it should have left it to the parties themselves to ask for a board. I think the amendment is a thoroughly mischievous one, and that if the minister Should take advantage of it and start in to investigate disputes, without either of the parties asking for an investigation, it will only get the Government and everybody else into trouble. I do not see how the minister himself could establish a board under this clause because the Act requires that the parties to the dispute shall be asked to name their representatives on a board. If neither of them has asked for a board I am inclined to think that neither will respond to the minister's request to get the board established. True, if they refuse to accede to the minister's request to name such members, then the minister himself may appoint them. That simply means giving the minister arbitrary power to frame a board of his own choice.if he thinks a difficulty is arising between an employer and his employees. I think the amendment may be well intended, but I am perfectly sure it will be construed as being in the nature of giving to the 'Government power to dabble in any industrial question when it suits it so to do, and to refuse to intervene of its own initiative when it may .seem unwise to do so, and therefore I doubt if it will be helpful. The law as it stands gives the minister the power to establish a board even where the parties have not requested it, once a strike or lockout arises. The minister has power at any time without application of an interested party to appoint an investigator or a commissioner under the provisions of the Inquiries Act. It is open to him at all times-in the event of a dispute occurring which is likely to affect the public interest-to appoint an officer of the department, or any two or three men, to investigate. The minister has that power under the Inquiries Act, but in exercising the power under that Act, other members of the Government would have a voice as to the wisdom or otherwise of instituting such an inquiry. I think that is a wise precaution. I do not think it is desirable to put in the hands of a minister the right of his own motion to institute an investigation into an industrial dispute without a request from any quarter, and that is the effect of this amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not happen to have the amendment of 1918 before me, but I think the objections the hon. member now raises to this amendment would be applicable to the amendment of 1918.

I -have that
amendment before me. It gave a minister the right to intervene if a strike or lock-out occurred without one of the parties making application. I think that was a good amendment, but the amendment suggested now goes much further, and proposes that before any application for a board has been made the minister himself may appoint a board of investigation if he thinks a strike is imminent. That puts a minister in a very arbitrary position.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I find the amendment of 1918 has the effect stated by the hon. member. That is, by the law as it stood in 1918, where a dispute reaches such a stage that a strike is imminent the minister may appoint a board, and that board becomes as effective as a board called for by the parties. But such a power vested in a minister is subject to practically all the objections the hon. member urges against this amendment. The minister in that case has to take the responsibility of deciding whether the appointment of such a board will be in the public interest; that is one of the objections the hon. member raises. Another objection is that the minister does not have to confer with his colleagues; but that objection is equally applicable to the amenndment of 1918. It is true that this amendment pushes that power a little further and gives the minister power to appoint a board even although no dispute has actually reached the stage of a strike. It does seem to me that if the minister has power to appoint a board after it is too late to avoid all the consequences of a strike, he ought to have power to appoint a board before the crisis is reached. Matters have got to a stage where both parties are fighting each other with all their might, and it is clear * that neither of them is going to apply for a board; but the strike is not yet called, it is only fixed for some time ahead. Now, if the minister comes to the conclusion that this is the state of affairs, surely it is desirable that he should then have porwer to appoint a board rather than wait until the strike is on, with all its disastrous consequences. It is true that this amendment goes a little further than the amendment of 1918, but there is no objection fundamental to the one which does not apply to the other. It is true there is * power to appoint a commissioner under the Inquiries Act which can be done by Order in Council at any time, llrat a commissioner under that Act has different functions and stands in a different relation to the two

parties to the controversy that a board does. A board, immediately it is appointed, is clothed *with the power vested in it by this Act, namely, to settle the industrial dispute, but a commissioner under the Inquiries Act has not that power. So it was thought advisable by the Government, on the advice of the Minister of Labour, to extend the power of the minister to enable him to appoint a board when, in his judgment, the dispute between the parties had brought them to the verge of a strike or a lockout, as the case might be, and thereby seek to work out a solution.of the difficulty before it was too late.

I submit that the really fundamental point is the public interest. When a strike is in progress it is obviously desirable that a board should investigate, and I think the minister should have poweT, if there is any hesitation on the part of the disputants, to go ahead and appoint a board. But in the absence of' any strike or lockout it does not seem to me desirable to give the minister power at bis own caprice to establish a board to investigate a dispute tha;, has not yet taken a form that affects the public interest one way or the other. When I was Minister of Labour the department repeatedly received requests by one or the other of the parties to an industrial dispute to start an investigation in order that the party applying might thereby secure some advantage. If I had listened to those requests it is difficult to say what consequences might have followed. But I rwas in the position of being able to say that it was for the parties themselves to apply to the Government; it was not for the Government on the action of one of the parties to take any steps. Usually I found that where pressure was being exerted it was to serve some end which was really not in the public interest. While I have every confidence in the present Minister of Labour in a matter of this kind, I can conceive of eases in which under another minister a very unfair advantage might be taken under such a clause, an advantage that might work very much to the injury oif the employers on the one hand or of the employees on the other. The fundamental idea underlying this legislation is non-interference by the Government until the public interest is adversely affected, leaving to the parties themselves to decide whether or not they will ask for the appointment of a board of conciliation.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think this amendment is all right and I would like to see it carried.

I move that it be struck out.

The House resumed, from April 29, consideration in committee of Bill No. 12 (Hon. Mr. Guthrie) respecting the election of members of the House of Commons, and the electoral franchise, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 40 (reconsidered) nomination of candidates:

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The clause is drawn the same as the old clause but we are making a change by this Act in the time that intervenes between nomination and polling day. Officers who are expert in matters appertaining to elections say that they fear that unless we state particularly in the section the date for polling as well as for nomination there may be some difficulty of mix-up in regard to these dates.
It has been suggested that clause 40 may be made more explicit by making certain amendments. I, therefore, move to amend subclause (1) of clause 40 by adding, after the word "candidates" in the second line thereof, the words "and the day for polling"; by substituting for the word "it" in the second line, the words "the days so fixed"; by adding after the word "election," where it appears the second time in the third line, the words "the same days shall be fixed for the nomination of candidates and for polling respectively in all electoral districts", and by striking the balance of the subclause from the Bill. The result of that will be that both nomination day and polling day will be fixed in the writ of election.
Amendment agreed to.
Was any amendment made to subclause 4?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: No. Under the old law the number was twenty-dive; under the proposed legislation it is ten.

I was not here when this subclause was under consideration before, but I desire to draw the attention of the minister to this subclause which reads:
Any ten or more electors of an electoral district	may nominate a candidate.
By paragraph (g) of clause 2, the word "elector" is defined:
"Elector" means any person qualified to vote at a Dominion election, whether his name is or is not on any list of voters.
We are in this position that we do not know whether at the moment of the election these ten men will be bona fide electors. Yet

we call them electors. Subclause (6) of clause 40 provides that the person who presents this nomination paper shall swear that those who have signed it are duly qualified electors; but at the time the nomination paper is handed in, it is impossible for any person to state whether or not these people are duly qualified electors, the lists not having at that time been made up.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: We have considered that matter before. I do not know that I would insist on the present wording; I do not think it would matter much whether we described the man as an elector or as a voter. This legislation is so general in its application that under it there are very few who will not be voters and who will not be electors. A voter is defined in clause 2 as a man whose name appears on the voters' list; but the objection to using the word "voter" here is that all the voters' lists may not be completed on nomination day. After nomination day, certain revisions take place. The list is not complete on nomination day; a man's name may be on the list on nomination day and may be struck off afterwards by the judge. I think little difficulty can arise if the man is described as an elector. In my riding I think I could get a man who would swear that the ten men are electors.
I was about to suggest to the minister that one way to get over the difficulty would be to have all the lists completed before nomination day.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The suggiestiom may
seem very simple on its face, but it will involve changing about sixty clauses and subclauses of this measure. These clauses are dovetailed as to a number of things, such as date of notice, date of completion!, and so forth, and it is difficult to make a change and know where you are going to land. I would rather the word was left as it is.

Under subclause (6) a man must swear that these ten men are duly qualified electors, and he cannot know that they are duly qualified electors; he may commit perjury. If there is no amendment to this, it is the easiest thing in the world for a man who desires to be a candidate to get ten names.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: He will take the consequences for so doing.

What is the object of putting in any names if as likely as not they will not be electors anyway?
122J	'

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I like the system in the province of a nominee and a seconder; but Parliament in its wisdom made the provision that twenty-five electors should make the nomination, and we thought it well to reduce the number to ten, as in some remote constituencies it is hard to get twenty-five names. I think a candidate will take enough interest in his nomination paper to see that ten of those who nominate him are electors.
Mr. LEVI THOMSON':	We have heard
something about crookedness of election officers, and provided the registrar, as it would be in this case, is crooked, it would be very easy to prevent the nomination of a candidate. This amendment would allow the registrar to keep off the list the electors who might join in nominating a certain candidate, and in that way they could prevent the nomination of the candidate very easily. I think the section is very much safer as it is, and my hon. friend would be well advised not to accept the suggested amendment.

If I caught my hon.
friend's remarks correctly he contends that a candidate may be nominated by, say, ten or more electors and then the returning officer or some official who is crooked may strike the names of those ten men off the list and the candidate may thereby be defeated, because a bogus nomination paper was handed in.

That would be
the effect were the amendment carried. As the Act stands now, I am an elector whether I am on the list or not, but the amendment could shut me out entirely. In the election of 1896 I know that sixteen electors in my polling district were deliberately left off the list by the enumerator. I would have no hesitation in swearing that they were all bona fide voters. I repeat, that if this amendment is agreed to, a crooked enumerator might easily prevent a candidate from being nominated.
My suggestion was that the lists should be completed before nomination day, so that those who swear these men are duly qualified electors might be absolutely certain of it.

It was after the completion of the lists that these sixteen were struck off. As the Act now stands, these men oan swear on election day that they are entitled to vote, but as the Act was then, owing to an amendment that had been made by the 'Senate, they could not do that.

This last minute registration, so to speak, by swearing in at the polls only exists so far as the rural districts are concerned. In the cities there is some finality to the lists some time before election day. 1 am suggesting that we obtain this finality with regard to all the lists, and have them completely closed before nomination day.
Would you prevent the rural voters who were left off the list from voting?
Yes.

Well I, hope
your suggestion will not be carried out, because otherwise the Government would be placed in a most powerful position, just as in 1896. It has never occurred since, because my hon. friend's leader at that time took strenuous objection and had the Act amended at once, and wisely so, I think. If ipy hon. friend's suggestion were adopted, the Government would be in entire control.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 44-granting of poll

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
This is really the counterpart of clause 37 in some respects. It provides for notice of the poll being given by proclamation. I Ibeg to move that in line 46 after the words "form P" the following words be inserted:
in the English and French languages in every electoral district in the provinces of Quebec and Manitoba, and in the English language only in other electoral districts.
Has clause 37 passed?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: No, it stands.

Has consideration been
given to the question whether the two languages will be extended to other provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
This will not affect
clause 37 anyway. If we are going to print in Quebec and Manitoba the first proclamation in English and French, certainly we should print the proclamation in regard to the polling divisions in the same way. The amendment is simply to make this clause correspond with clause 37 as drawn, in accordance with what we believe to be statutory authority. But perhaps it would be as well to let this clause stand.
Clause stands.
On section 53-certain officers and agents may vote at polling stations where employed:
fMr. Thomson.]

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I beg to move that the word "revising" which has been substituted by a previous amendment for the word "receiving" at the end of line 25 be struck out, and the word "returning" 'be substituted therefor.
Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I beg to move that after the word "certificate" in line 22 the words "to any candidate" be inserted.
Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I beg to move that paragraph (a) of subsection (2) be struck out in its entirety. This is already covered by subsection (5).
It might very well occur that he would issue more than two; but it is provided that not more than two shall be used. Does the minister understand me?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: We ought to limit the issue too.
If you intend to strike out one of the subclauses I think you should strike out 5 and retain the one which gives the number of certificates that may be issued.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I have the wrong amendment. I put the words "to any candidate" in line 22 after the word "certificate". That should read: "such certificate in form T1 of this Act". I move that the section be 'amended accordingly.
Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: In the first line of subsection 2 the words "revising officer" should be "returning officer". I move that the subsection be thus amended.
Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: With regard to paragraph (a) which I have moved to be struck out, I think that subsection 5, which provides that no more than two agents of any candidate shall have the right to vote "in such manner" at any polling station, covers the whole question. I move that paragraph (a) be struck out.

Amendment agreed to.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess.
The committee resumed at Eight o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Since the adjournment we have again examined this clause 53

with some care, and it has been pointed out that the amendments which were suggested or made before six o'clock would hardly be appropriate. Under our former law the returning officers were the officers empowered to grant agents' certificates to enable agents to vote at polls other than the ones at which they resided. It has now been pointed out to me that under the scheme of the present Bill, the returning officer has not the final custody of the lists. He may be absent on election business in some riding, perhaps two or three hundred miles away, delivering polling books, establishing polls, or the like; whereas the lists, in the urban divisions, are in the hands of a judge or revising officer, and, in the rural electoral districts, in the hands of the registrar. Consequently it has been suggested that the proper persons to grant the agents' certificates in urban divisions would be the revising officer, and in the rural divisions the registrar. To accomplish that end I will again have to move that this clause be further revised and amended. It can be done by striking out the words "qr registrar of such division" where they occur at line 23, and by inserting the following words:
Where such other polling division is an urban polling division, and from the registrar, where such other division is a rural polling division.
If that amendment be made the section will read thus: 1
(1) Any candidate, deputy returning officer, agent or poll clerk who is an elector qualified in a polling division other than that whereat he is employed on polling day shall be permitted to vote at the polling station where he is so employed if he produces and files with the deputy returning officer at such polling station a certificate in form T1 to this Act from the revising officer where such other polling division is an urban polling division, and from the registrar where such other polling division is a rural polling division, that such candidate, officer, agent or clerk is a qualified elector in such other polling division which certificate the revising officer or registrar shall give gratis.
The section should stop at the word "gratis," and the words "qualified elector who is on polling day so employed" should be struck out. If these last words are allowed to remain, any elector could go up to the revising officer, or registrar, and demand a certificate.
