I therefore move, Mr. Chairman, that the words I have indicated should be struck out and the others inserted, and that in line 26 of subsection one the words "to any qualified elector who is on polling day so employed" be struck out. I think the section will be all right then.
Are we leaving in ^a)?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I understood (a) was struck out. That opens the door too wide.
Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Are there any other amendments to that section?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The word "receiving" on line 29 should be "revising." We changed it to "returning" but it should be "revising."
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 55-when poll shall be held: The CHAIRMAN: Shall clause 55 carry?
If the clauses were read, Mr. Chairman, it would give us time to gather their meaning.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am very sorry that I cannot grant the hon. member's request. The clauses have all been read once and I think it is unfair to ask the Chairman to read them a second time.
I have reference now to clause 55.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It .was read on a former occasion when it Iwas amended and allowed to stand over. If the committee desires the clause read it has the right to have it read, but such is not the right of an individual member.
We cannot at a moment's-notice let a clause pass without having a little time to consider it.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: If the hon. gentleman had been present when the clause was last considered he would have heard it read by the Chairman and would not now have occasion to make such an application. '

I do not want to criticize your ruling, Mr. Chairman, but even if I had been in the committee at that time, and it is quite possible I may have been, it would be impossible for me to remember what that clause contains.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the clause carry?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: An amendment to that clause was adopted.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: In line 43?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It was amended by adding after the word, "but" the words "at an election other than a general election."

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: That was the only amendment.	_

I think the reason this clause was allowed to stand on a former occasion was on account of the provision that the polls should open at six o'clock in the morning. If I remember correctly, the minister said he was prepaired to consider the wisdom of keeping the polls open from six o'clock in the morning until six at night, or changing the time to some other hour. Some members were of the opinion that the convenience of the public would be better suited if the polls were opened at seven o'clock in the morning rather than at six o'clock.

What have been the
hours in the past?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
From nine o'clock to
five.

I am strongly opposed to
opening the polls at six o'clock. I have acted as returning officer at several elections and I have found that during the first hour in the morning only a few votes were polled. It is impossible tb run an election before daylight, but if the polls must be opened even at seven o'clock, it seems to me it would be better to have one or two more polling stations and close the poll at six o'clock in the afternoon. In this way, I think, the convenience of the people generally would be better met.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
One object in making
the hour six o'clock was to meet the convenience of persons who had to take early morning trains, particularly suburbanites living in the neighbourhood of our large cities. Many of those trains leave before seven o'clock in the morning, and those men do not get back to their homes in the country until after seven at night. The early hour might also be a convenience to a good many workmen who have a long distance to go to their work, but they have two hours for voting during which time they can absent themselves from work without loss. It is true that in many places very few votes would be polled between six and seven o'clock in the morning, but the early hour of opening the poll would be a convenience to a number of people, and I am satisfied that it would work no very great hardship on any one in charge of the poll.

I know many cases
where the returning officer lives anywhere from a mile to two and a half miles from the polling station in rural constituencies, and it will be absolutely foolish, if I may

use that word, to open the poll at six o'clock in the morning. I think it is an unnecessary hardship that the returning officer and their assistants should have to be on hand at six o'clock in the morning, when, as we know, very few votes are polled for the first hour or two; and I would suggest to the minister that he Tefrain from making this applicable to the rural constituencies. On the other hand, in the cities, I doubt if any one would be out of bed at six o'clock. So I do not see any necessity for this early opening of the polls except for the convenience of suburbanites.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The trouble is that the suburbanites live in the rural constituencies, and it is largely for their convenience that the clause is inserted. In cities like Toronto and Montreal many of these suburbanites are engaged in their business until five or six o'clock at night and do not reach their homes in the country until an hour later. I cannot see any great hardship in asking the returning officers and others to be on duty at six o'clock instead of at eight.
Is it possible that one set of officers could carry on from six in the morning until six at night?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: That was done during the last election. Those are the hours all over the United States, and also in England, and I do not think they find that any great hardship results.
How does the minister reconcile Rule 20 of Schedule A and Rule 5 of Schedule B with paragraph 6 of section 56? The poll will be open at six o'clock, but under those two rules-

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: We have to change section 32, and in the meantime that is forbidden fruit. I may tell my hon. friend that I have that noted.

I support the objection made by the hon. member for Carle-ton (Mr. Caldwell). In the West if an election were held in November the returning officers and his staff would have to travel over the prairie two or three hours before daylight to get to the poll. I do not see any reason for such an early hour in the rural districts, especially as, on an average,
I suppose not more than fifty votes are polled in the first hour. I do not know whether it is possible to make arrangements to extend the hours for the suburbanite vote, but certainly this early hour would not work out well in the rural districts.

Mr. MARCIL; I agree with the hon. member that so tar as the rural constituencies are concerned there is no real reason why the polls should open at six in the morning, and I think the old practice of opening the polls at nine o'clock and closing them at five would meet the case fully. In cities and surrounding districts the opening of the polls early in the morning may be an advantage, but it is certainly a disadvantage in the country.
If our railroad men are to be given an opportunity to exercise the franchise it is absolutely necessary that the polls should be opened at six o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: They are looked after by another clause.

Yes, but the advance polls do not give all our railroad men an opportunity to vote, because local trains at all terminal points leave at six-thirty and seven o'clock in the morning and the majority of those trains do not return until nine at night. By having the polls open at six o'clock our men going out on early trains would get an opportunity to vote.

I agree that the early opening of the polls gives the train men an opportunity to vote, but in our rural constituencies seven o'clock would be quite early enough and would give the electors ample opportunity to record their votes during the day, the total poll in such districts not being very heavy. The people throughout the country are not up at that time here provided, although a few of them may be. Some of them may be going away early in the morning, and of course this provision will give them a chance to vote. That is all right; I do not want anybody to be deprived of his vote. But at the same time, with the 250 votes which have to be polled in each subdivision, it would not be right to expect the people to get up and get to the polling booth at six o'clock in the morning.

I am at a loss to understand why there should be any objection to extending the hours for voting. If we were restricting the hours there would be some reasonable cause for protest, but surely it cannot be considered an objectionable thing that the polls should be open long enough to give every class of people an opportunity to vote. Even if it is only a small class that would find it impossible to vote if the polls were not open until seven o'clock, we should consider that class no matter how small it may be. In the
city where I live it was a great advantage in the last election to have the polls opened at six o'clock. From six to seven o'clock was a very busy hour. It gives a large number of people an opportunity of putting their ballot before they go to business, and they are not worried during the rest of the day as to whether they would be able to get away in order to cast their ballots. There are men in business who find it difficult, if not impossible, to get away at the noon hour and equally difficult to get away before the time for closing the poll. With this provision these people will get up a little earlier than usual and put their ballots in before they go down to business.
I cannot imagine why any one should object. unless it is the deputy returning officers; but as the Government and the country are paying them for their time and as we are putting that clause there to give every person a chance to cast his ballot at that early hour I think it should commend itself to the good judgment of the committee.

I cannot answer the contention of the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Hocken) without introducing a very disagreeable subject. I know that in the last election a great many people polled their votes in both urban and rural polling subdivisions. They voted in the city and then went out into country places and voted again. I submitted a number oi affidavits when we were discussing the Franchise Act last year showing that that kind of thing was done. It is possible for people to get around all over the country when the time is unlimited. Gave them eight or ten hours in these days of automobiles and they can travel through three or four divisions

I personally have no objection to my hon. friend (Mr. Guthrie) giving consideration to the question of having the poll open for twelve hours if necessary. From my experience in carrying on elections I do not think it is necessary. If I understand my hon. friend aright an election would be void if the poll was not opened at six o'clock in the morning. If that is correct I can assure my hon. friend that there will be many places in the country where the election will be void for that reason. In many places the polls will not be opened at six o'clock in the morning. You cannot get men to go for long distances to man the polls in the rural districts at that hour of the morning. In cities, I quite agree, it is all right. In the last election in some of the sections of my constituency the

polls were opened at six o'clock in the morning; but when I visited a certain poll there was no person there; there was no returning officer to open the poll at six o'clock or for some time afterwards. That was true also of many other localities throughout the country. It would be an impossibility for men to open the polls and to get them ready for the reception of electors at six o'clock in the morning. If the election were held in October or November it would be dark and you would have to have the place supplied with half a dozen lamps in order to make it possible to carry on the work. Therefore, I submit that in rural sections it is an impossibility. If it is made optional and the election is not void if the poll is not open at six o'clock I have no objection, but if the election is to be declared void if the poll is not open at six o'clock there will be many elections voided in the rural constituencies.
I would like to ask the minister if the point he has raised is not covered by section 100 which advances the poll for railway employees and others.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Some are provided for.

As I read the clause it covers the point which has been raised by the hon. gentleman. In cities the lists are final. It is known before a man goes in to vote whether the man's name is on the list and he is not entitled to vote unless his name is on the list. But in the way this Act is drawn in so far as rural districts are concerned any man who is prepared to swear that he has a right to vote is permitted to cast his ballot. As I read these two sections together it does seem to me that they are going to open the door to very serious mischief in the way in which elections may be carried on in rural districts. If you open the poll at six o'clock in the morning when it is dark, if the election is held, as is customary in the fall or winter any man can go to the poll early in the morning, swear that he has a right to vote, take his ballot, put it in the ballot box and leave the poll. That is the effect of the law as drawn at the present time. If there is anything in what the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) says, that we should extend the time for voting, let us have it from eight in the morning to eight at night, if need be, rather from six in the morning until six at night. I do not think there is any necessity for keeping the polls open from eight in the morning until eight at night in the rural districts, but certainly as the lawr stands at the present time, all

a man has to do to cast a vote is to swear that he has a right to vote, put his vote in the ballot box and go away, consequently this is a thoroughly wrong provision and ought not to be adopted.

The first objection to
keeping the poll open from eight in the morning till eight at night is that the people expect to get the returns. Besides, in order to cast their ballot at night, a large number, especially in the city which I represent, would abstain from voting until after they had their dinners, and at the last hour there would be such a congestion at the polls that it would be impossible for the returning officers to take the vote. You can easily understand that this condition would arise in a constituency such as I represent, which is a mile square and has 25,000 voters. It would be very much better to take from six to six than from eight to eight.

I do not press the point of changing from six to six to eight to eight. I think that as far as the rural districts are concerned if the poll were opened from eight to six it would be satisfactory to the people. But this clause read with clause 100, which I think will cause a great deal of discussion, gives to any man the right to cast his ballot in a rural district before daybreak if he swears that he has the right to vote at any particular poll. With a provision like that and a provision that the polls in the rural districts are to open at six o'clock in the morning, it is only inviting a kind of fraud which will be very detrimental. Unless the minister can give some very substantial reasons why the polls are being opened at six o'clock in the morning, we are entitled to believe that these two sections have some relation to each other.

There is another reason that should not be forgotten. It is very important that scrutineers should attend the voting, and it is difficult to get a man in the country to turn out of his home at four o'clock in the morning and have him drive some miles down to the poll to supervise this work. I have been electioneering for a long time; I was a deputy returning officer in 1878, forty-two years ago, and I have never heard, a request from any rural part of Quebec that the polls should be opened earlier than nine o'clock in the morning or that they should be kept open later than five o'clock in the afternoon. At five o'clock in the afternoon in the rural

part of the country the votes are invariably all cast; in fact, by four o'clock in the afternoon, everybody has voted, and nobody thinks of going to the polls before nine o'clock in the morning; so that as regards the rural constituencies, I can see no reason why there should be any change in the old hours that have been in force ever since Confederation. In the cities, the case is different. Although you give the working man two hours in which to cast his vote, there is something to be said in favour of an early poll. But I would not extend the time in the evening. Our experience in the city of Montreal when we had early closing apply to all kinds of business was that people did their business in the daytime instead of doing it at night. The early closing rule is universal in Montreal for everything, and people do not want to wait until the last hour to go to vote. They will vote in the daytime if they know that the poll closes at five o'clock in the afternoon. You should open the city poll at six o'clock in the morning, but you should leave the hours for the rural poll as they are now, namely, nine o'clock in the morning and five o'clock in the afternoon.

Clause 56 reads:
At the hour fixed for opening the poll the deputy returning officer and the poll clerk shall, in the presence of their candidates, their agents, and such of the electors as are present, open the ballot box and ascertain that there are no ballot papers or other papers therein, after which the box shall be locked, and the deputy returning officer shall keep the key thereof.
If the poll were to open at six o'clock in the morning, nobody but the deputy returning officer and the poll clerk might be present; the candidates or their agents might not be present. Would the deputy returning officer go ahead and accept ballots without first showing the candidates or their agents that the ballot box was empty? If he were allowed to do so, would not that be giving an opportunity for wrong-doing? It is the right of the candidates to see that the ballot box is empty before ballots are put into it. If they do not see that it is empty and the deputy returning officer is allowed to accept ballots, would that be legal?-because the clause states that a deputy returning officer shall show the candidates or their agents that the ballot box is empty.
Mr. GUTHIRI'E: I do not think I need answer that very fully; but if the duty is cast on the deputy returning officer to show the candidates or their agents that the box is empty, and the candidates take so little
interest as not to be present themselves nor to have their agents present, in my judgment, the deputy returning officer would be justified by law in proceeding with the election. The other people might not turn up all day. The action of the deputy returning officer in that case would be quite legal.
What would the minister say in regard to the election being void?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: That is another question.

In the cities great good will be accomplished by having the polls open at six o'clock in the morning. At the last election in the city of Winnipeg, the hour from six to seven o'clock in the morning was the most active hour of the whole day in some of the city polls. Men polled their vote on their way to work. Men who were going away on the trains at seven o'clock in the morning polled their vote, went to the train and attended to their business. If it is essential to arrange matters so that the rural polls may be opened at a later hour, it would serve every purpose to do so.

My experience in the last election was that between six and seven thirty o'clock in the morning very few votes were polled; as a matter of fact, the returning officers and the clerks had an excellent opportunity to put in an hour's sleep which they had lost. It is rather refreshing for city dwellers to hear our bucolic friends insisting on a later opening of the polls. We have heard a great deal in the last few years about daylight saving, our friends telling us that the farmer gets up with the lark in November as well as at any other time. It is rather refreshing for us who come from the cities to know that they share in our bad habits and sometimes sleep in a little in the morning. If the polls in the rural constituencies are allowed not to open until eight o'clock, it is reasonable that the same rule should apply in the cities. In the cities, any complaints that I have' heard recently have been on the part of those whose duties, either political or semi-judicial, oblige them to be at the polls at six o'clock in the morning. Dozens of people, when they heard that a new Franchise Act was being framed, asked me to protest against opening the polls at such an early hour. As the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) has said, the spirit works least well in the early hours of the morning, and an unwary returning officer and innocent candidates and their agents are more likely to be trapped by

wily opponents than at any other hour. Besides that, it is really a nuisance to have to get up so early in the morning.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Perhaps I might suggest a compromise. I see the force of what has been said in regard to rural polls particularly. Not that I fear any wrongdoing such as the leader of the Opposition fears will take place, especially in the early hours of the morning, hut as a matter of general convenience, my suggestion would be that the clause should read that the poll shall be open from six o'clock in the morning until six o'clock in the afternoon as regards urban divisions and that the hours for rural divisions he eight o'clock in the morning until six o'clock in the afternoon.
Hear, hear.
The farmers win again.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: These late risers all applaud that. I therefore move to amend suibclause (6) of clause 55 by inserting after the word "day" in line 20 on page 39, the words "in urban polling divisions, and be opened at the hour of eight of the clock in the forenoon and kept open until six of the clock in the afternoon in rural polling divisions".

I think the minister is making a mistake in yielding to what appears to be a certain amount of sentiment in regard to rural polls. In large cities like Toronto and Hamilton, there are hundreds of people who live outside of the city limits, who are not in the municipality-there are thousands of such people throughout the country-and the bulk of those people of whom I speak, men and women, boys and girls, entitled to the franchise, work in the cities. Many men and women have to go several miles to their work and be there at seven or eight in the morning. They cannot vote before leaving home in the morning because the poll will not be open. They are engaged in the city all day, and if the poll closes at six o'clock they cannot get out home in time to vote. It will be a great inconvenience to that section of the public who live in rural divisions adjoining a city. While I quite agree that the minister's amendment is faiT and reasonable as regards purely rural polls,
I am certain that if the amendment is carried many thousands of voters will be absolutely disfranchised, and the law never did recognize that franchise Acts were made to disfranchise voters.
With regard to the statement of the leader of the Opposition about a man rushing in

at lamplight in the morning to commit perjury, I do not think that should be assumed. The crime of perjury is a very serious one, and if a man is so brazen as to commit perjury for the sake of voting he will do it as readily at nine or ten or eleven o'clock as at six in the morning. I think the vigilance with which the polls are manned is quite sufficient protection against evil practices of that kind. If the minister wishes to extend the franchise to the greatest number of people-and that ought to be the policy-I think he is making a mistake in yielding good-naturedly to pressure from those who live in purely rural municipalities. I think there should be some saving clause to protect those who otherwise are going to be absolutely cut off from their vote through living in rural municipalities and working in an adjoining city.

I wish to support the minister in changing the hours in the rural ridings to eight in the -morning. My hon. friend (Mr. Morphy) has argued that the Act should be framed to do the greatest good to the greatest number, and if that is the policy he supports he should support the minister's amendment, because there are only two or three of these urban divisions near to large cities that would be affected in the way he points out. In the province of Alberta there are two sets of polling hours, one for the urban and the other for the rural centres. The hours for the urban centres are fom six to six, and for the rural from nine to five. That has worked out very well, and there has been no trouble whatever. I remember, in the election of 1917, visiting a city poll somewhere around six in the morning, and I discovered that the returning officer had not provided a lamp. It was dark and there was a void of that poll, strictly speaking, because you could not see your hand in front of your face. There is a certain amount of red tape in connection with all these appointments, and before you could get a lamp you had to hunt up the returning officer and get the necessary authority. That poll was in total darkness for nearly two hours.
The hon. member's party has refused to shed any light on that election ever since.

As my hon._ friend (Mr. Copp) says, if a poll were void from the fact that the deputy returning officer and his clerk were not there, fifty per cent of the polls in every rural district would be voided. Now that patron-

age has been taken out of the hands of members of Parliament, it will be difficult to get even people who are paid to work at a poll from now on, and I think that the less obstacles we throw in the way of having the polls properly manned, the better. I support the minister's amendment.

I think there is a very direct and proper answer to the question raised by my hon. friend (Mr. Morphy), who contends that those who live in rural centres but who work in cities will be deprived of their votes by not being able to get back before the polls are closed. I think section 100 has been drafted to meet cases of that kind. It provides that all those who will be absent on polling day during polling hours, which means all those who are absent from their usual place of residence, may vote at an Advance Poll. Those who have reason to believe that "because of necessary absence from such place of residence in the pursuit of his employment or calling" they may not be able to vote on polling day, may so vote in advance. Therefore, I submit, that these people will not be prejudiced at all by the amendment, because they will have three days before polling day within which to vote.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The only difficulty is that there are not likely to be any Advance Polls in very small places, but only in large centres of population. People who work in Toronto and live at Oakville or Leaside would all be able to vote, because these are all urban divisions and under the terms of this Act, the polls would open at six in these places.
That is not the class I refer to, but the people outside in the township who have gone out there and built a little home.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I recognize that there
is a class who live in localities that are purely rural, to whom this provision would certainly be an inconvenience and perhaps a hardship; but on the other hand I believe that the balance of convenience is in favour of not opening the polls in the rural districts too early. I am inclined to think there would be very great difficulty in manning the polls in the more or less remote country districts at six in the morning. That was my reason for suggesting a change in this section. Howe\er, it is for the committee to say.

In the past, the hours from nine to five were entirely satisfactory in the rural constituencies, but now that
women are enfranchised there will be a larger number of voters and I approve of the minister's amendment to have the polls open from eight to six. That will give ample time for the rural vote to be polled.
I think eight o'clock is certainly early enough for the rural divisions.

I want to emphasize the point made by my hon. friend (Mt. Morphy). We have people working in the city of Toronto who live in the counties of Halton, Peel, North York, West York and East York. With' the exception, perhaps, of East York, I presume all these would be classed as rural constituencies, and yet we have a trainload of people coming in to work, from Oakville in the county of Halton, and others from the county of Peel. They have to catch an early train to go to their work and cannot get home to cast their vote, if the polls close at six o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: How did they do it in the last election when the polls were open from nine to five?

Well, I guess they did not vote, and my hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Charters) probably did not get as large a majority as he might have received. If you want every person to get an opportunity to vote you must class as urban some constituencies that might ordinarily be considered rural. The commuters' train runs from Oakville to Toronto, a distance of twenty miles, and the Streetsville train also runs into Toronto; and people from every direction in these rural constituencies would not have a chance to vote unless they took special time off for that purpose

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The proposal now is so much in advance of what it was before that we are conferring a great measure of convenience upon these very people described by the hon. gentleman. At the last election these people who lived in rural districts must have voted between the hours of nine and five, whereas this proposal, making the hours eight to six, gives them an advantage of two hours at any rate. A trainload of people from Oakville, under this proposal, can vote from six o'clock, and so can those people from Weston and Brampton. It is the voter who lives, not in the organized village but in the township that will be inconvenienced. There are not a great many of this class of electors, but there are some that I am aware of. This Act gives the people from Oakville and those places at least two hours more than any law hereto-

fore passed, and I honestly believe that the difficulty in the country would be serious if the polls were opened at six o'clock.

I wish to support the proposed amendment of the minister. In most rural districts you will not find very many voters at the polls before at least ten o'clock in the morning, because there are chores to do on the farm in the winter time and children to be got to school, besides various other household duties. You will not, therefore, give men a proper opportunity to vote in those constituencies if you open the polls at six o'clock in the morning. I think that eight o'clock is early enough.
Where does the minister draw the line between rural and urban constituencies? What population does he consider necessary to constitute an urban constituency?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
That is defined at pages 2 and 3 of the Bill. An urban or city poll is defined as a polling division which is wholly or partly contained within
9 p.m. places having a population of more than one thousand persons and which places are, under the provincial laws, cities, towns or incorporated villages. A rural polling division is one whereof no part is contained within a place having a population of more than one thousand persons and which place under the provincial law is a city, town or incorporated village.
Amendment agreed to.

Subsection 6 provides that the poll shall be opened at the hour of six in the forenoon. At present we have two standards of time, and when it is six o'clock in Montreal and Ottawa it may be only five o'clock in Casselman or Vars. The elections might take place in summer and there might be a confusion as to the opening of polls. Moreover, some counties embrace part of a city as well as the country. Does this clause mean that standard time shall apply in all cases, or daylight saying time wherever it is adopted?
Mr, .GUTHRIE:	The hours of the day
when mentioned in this Act shall be calculated upon standard time. That comes under section 2 of the Bill which we have not yet discussed.
Section, as amended, agreed to.
On section 63-name not on list:

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I have forgotten what
amendments were made to this section.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Section 63 was read
and discussed but not amended.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I have one or two verbal amendments to offer. In line 30 after the word1 " make," there should be inserted the word " and " so that it will read " as the deputy returning officer directs him to make, and as is required by any provision of this Act."
Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: In line 22 subsection (2) reads " set forth in Form Z to schedule I of this Act." It should read " set forth in forms Y or Z, or either of them," etc. I move that the subsection be so amended.
Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I move that subsection 3 be struck out. It is practically a repetition of subsection (1) of section 57 which reads:
Except as otherwise provided in this Act every person shall he entitled to vote whose name appears on a voters' list prepared under this Act. He may vote at the polling station ol the polling division upon the list of voters for which his name so appears and at no other. (Secs. 143, 65, and 148.)
Amendment agreed to.

With regard to the section itself may I direct the minister's attention to the fact that it is pretty closely related to the section in regard to the preparation of the lists which iwas allowed to stand? I think the present section, next to the other section referred to, is the most contentious of any in the Bill, and piobably the minister will be agreeable to not going on with it for the present.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I have no objection to it standing.
Section stands.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The next section is section 76.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: May I ask, Mr. Chairman, that you return to page 48 of the Bill? You have an amendment, have you not, to subsection 6 of section 66?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
No. Not to subsection
6.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: There is an important amendment suggested by the Auditor General.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Mr. Guthrie moves that by unanimous consent the committee return to consideration of clause 66.
Motion agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The Auditor General suggests that this section be inserted in subsection 6, on page 48, after the word, "ballot-box," in line 39:
-he shall also fill in the blank expense voucher furnished to him by the returning officer, cause it to be "signed by the various officials of his polling station entitled to fees, certify the same, and place it in a special envelope furnished for that purpose and deposit the same in the ballot-box.
The meaning of that is that at the close of the poll a statement shall be made out and signed by each official setting forth the fees which he claims or is entitled to, and that shall be enclosed in a special envelope and deposited in the ballot-box. It is for the purpose of auditing the account after the election. I told the Auditor General that I did not see any objection to the insertion of that clause and he asked that it be put in. If that amendment is adopted a consequential amendment will be necessary in the first line of subsection 7. That is that after the word "ballot-box" the following words shall (be inserted:
-together with the two envelopes mentioned in the next preceding subsection.
Another amendment is required in line 16 of subsection 9 after the word "'ballot-box," the addition of the following words:
-and in the proper envelopes provided for that purpose.
If the committee is agreeable I move that these amendments be made to that section to carry out the suggestion of the Auditor General in that respect.

I would point out that the result of the deputy returning officer not pdtting all the accounts in the box will be that officers on duty at the poll will lose their fees. The constable at the door may not turn in his account before leaving. Under subsection 9 he will lose his fees, through no fault of his own. In my opinion it is a very peculiar way of paying men who work for the deputy returning officer.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: If I caught my hon. friend's point correctly I would say in reply to it that this clause is inserted for the purpose of insisting, as far as possible, that the returning officer shall enclose the statement referred to in the box. If he does not do so he is liable to penalties under this Act, and in addition to the general penalties provided, he forfeits his fees. I do not think there is anything improper in the provision, and I do not think any hardship is imposed. If he complies with the Act, and deposits the envelope as required, no question of loss of his fees can arise.	.
Amendments agreed to.

What provision is made for the cost of returning the ballot boxes? The common practice is for the returning officer to direct that the ballot boxes shall be taken to the nearest express office and expressed to him. For that service no provision is made in this section, as this is a subsequent expense, and apparently it is only to be dealt with as an estimate.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The next clause provides for the custody of the ballot boxes after the election. If the boxes are not required by the courts in connection with a re-count of the votes, it is provided:
After the close of the election the returning officer shall cause to be deposited In the custody of the sheriff of the county or district, or of the registrar of deeds in the county, or registration division, or of the postmaster in the locality, in which the nomination was held, the ballot boxes used at the election ; and the sheriff, registrar or postmaster shall, at the next ensuing election, deliver such ballot boxes to the returning officer named for such election.
The duty of the returning officer is clear enough, although the section does not say whether he is to deliver or express the ballot boxes to the sheriff or other official. When we come to the fees of the returning officer I think a proper fee might be inserted.
The point was not how those ballot boxes are to be sent into the returning officer, but the absence of any fee for returning them. If no fee is provided those boxes will not be returned.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: There is an allowance for the return of boxes.

As a matter of fact that is always arranged between the returning officer and his deputies. Prior to the election he sends instructions to them as to the manner in which the ballot boxes are to be returned to him, and provision will be found in the schedule of fees to cover that work.

Then is it contemplated that two accounts will be sent in by each returning officer? Because that is what this would involve. His first account will cover his expenses down to the return of the ballot box, and he will have to put in a supplementary account for that additional expense. '	.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: He can put that expense in his first account.
He has not incurred it, and therefore can only make an estimate of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not think any difficulty will arise there.
Clause as amended agreed to.
On section 69-custody of ballot boxes after the election.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: It has been suggested by the parliamentary counsel that after the words "ballot boxes" in the sixteenth line we add the words "and padlocks." I move that the section be so amended.

Amendment agreed to, and section as amended agreed to.
On section 72-election return:

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Since the section was
carried it has been further examined by the parliamentary counsel, and certain suggestions have been made by him which I think are essential to the proper working of the section. In the first place, it is suggested that the words "election papers" be used in this section to include: The ballot box, the ballots, and all other papers that are returned to the Chief Electoral Officer and which may be called for in case of a re-count; and that instead of enumerating them the term "election papers" be defined under the interpretation clause. In the second place, it is suggested that subsection 1 be amended by adding a clause as paragraph (d) in the following words:
The lists of voters furnished to him by the different rural registrars in compliance with the provisions of rule 5 of schedule B to section 32 of this Act.
Otherwise, the parliamentary counsel points out, he would not have these official lists in his possession. Then, it is suggested that the following be added as subsection 6:
The Chief Electoral Officer shall immediately after each general election cause to be printed a report giving by polling subdivisions the number of votes polled for each candidate, the number of rejected ballots, the number of names on the list of voters, together with any other information that he may deem fit to include. He shall also at the end of each year cause to be printed a similar report on the by-elections held during the year.
In the past, I understand, it has been customary to compile such reports after general elections. There is nothing in this Act, as originally drawn, to cover this, and in the opinion of the parliamentary counsel

it will be of value to have such a report after each general election, and an annual report on all by-elections. I therefore move, Mr. Chairman, that the section be amended as suggested.
Amendments agreed to.
This provision in the new paragraph (d) seems to apply only to rural lists. I presume there is a clause that requires a- return of the urban lists?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, section 32 provides for it. I beg to move to amend subsection 4 by replacing the word "ballot" in line 31 with the word "election".
Amendment agreed to.
If, in connection with that section, in rural polling subdivisions, any person upon taking the oath may cast a ballot, is there any provision for a return of the persons voting in that way?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The vote has to be
marked in the poll book.
On section 75 (reconsidered)-Chief Electoral Officer to retain papers', etc.:

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I beg to move that in line 21 the word "papers" be struck out and the words "election papers" be inserted; that in line 26 the words "ballot papers" should be struck out and the words "election papers" inserted; that in line 33 the word "ballot" should be struck out and "election" put in; in line 35 the word "ballot" should be struck out and the word "election" inserted; and that in line 39 the word "ballot" should be struck out and the word "election" inserted.
Is there any definition of the term "election papers"? I think it is a very wide expression.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
We will have to provide a definition for it, but we have not reached the clause yet. The amendment I shall propose is:
" Election papers " means all ballot papers, including those unused, poll books, lists of voters, and such statements used at the polling station, and all other documents signed by any returning officer or Chief Electoral Officer in com-plianc yith this Act or under instructions issued by the said Chief Electoral Officer.

Section 75, subsection 2, says:
No person shall be allowed to inspect any election paper in the custody of the Chief Electoral Officer except under the rule or order of a Superior Court or judge.

And so on. "Election papers'' includes lists, does it not? Does that mean that anybody shall be allowed to inspect the lists?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
You would not be allowed to inspect any documents in the possession of the Chief Electoral Officer without the order of a judge. You will have your own lists to inspect in your own riding. These are the official lists sent down for the purpose of safe custody after the election and kept here at headquarters.
Section as amended agreed to.
On section 77-how disagreements as to taxation of expenses settled:

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The Acting Solicitor General has proposed an amendment to this clause, to strike out all the words after the words "Auditor General" in the first line and to replace them with the following:
-shall, in accordance with this Act, tax and pay all election expense accounts. Any disagreement between the Auditor General and any claimant shall be referred to the Chief Electoral Officer and he shall either confirm the action of the Auditor General or if he disagrees then, if the question involves only the legal right of the person claiming payment to be paid at all, it shall be referred to and be finally resolved by the Treasury Board ; or if the question involves only the fairness of the amount payable to any person with relation to services or materials supplied, it shall be referred to and shall be finally resolved by the Secretary of State. Notwithstanding anything in this section contained the rights, if any, of all claimants to compel payment, or further payment, by process of law shall remain unimpaired.

I suggested at an earlier stage of the discussion that this would seem to assign a class of duties to the Auditor General at variance with what the Audit Act contemplated. Has my hon. friend considered that point?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, to some extent.
Does he not propose to make any change in that respect?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I have given consideration to the matter and I find that the custom [DOT] for a great many years has been to permit the Auditor General to audit these accounts. I had thought that the matter was more properly one for the Department of the Secretary of State. The Auditor General, however, handed me copies of some corres-pondance which took place at the time my hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) was Minister of Finance; the question came pretty fairly up for decision then; the accounts were referred, at the suggestion of my hon. friend, to the Department of the Secretary of State; but that department would have nothing to
do with the accounts and said that they had no competent staff to audit them and that they should be referred back to the Auditor General. So the matter was settled and the Auditor General undertook to audit the accounts. The Auditor General has all the machinery in his Department for auditing; he has greater facilities for auditing the Recounts than any other department, and probably he can expedite matters more than any other department could. Moreover, he is, perhaps, a more independent officer than any we have in other departments. There is every good reason why the Auditor General should continue to audit the accounts in the future as he has done in the past.

My hon. friend has
misconceived the point, if there was a point, in my observations. I do not object to the Auditor General auditing the accounts. In a sence, all accounts are, at one stage or another, audited by the Auditor General. My idea was precisely that the Auditor General should deal with these accounts as he does with other accounts. It struck me that there was a mixing up with the authority of the Auditor General, that of the Chief Electoral Officer and that of the Secretary of State. It might be better if the Auditor General were to audit these accounts under the general terms of the Audit Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The amendment as drawn is one prepared jointly by the Chief Electoral Officer and the Auditor General, and I thought it met the case very well.

I think the amendment as drawn meets part of the objection raised by my hon. friend. It takes out the provision that the Chief Electoral Officer shall pass on the accounts. There is a reference to the Secretary of State's right to pass finally on some matters.

Amendment agreed to, and section as amended agreed to.
On section 78-election expenses:

Is there any change in
this clause from the corresponding clause of the old Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, we went over this subclause by subclause. None of the sections are new, that is, as having been drawn for the purpose of this Bill; everyone of them was either in our former Act or in English Act.

One of the
points under consideration in connection with this clause was in reference to para-

graph (b) of subclause 3. Subclause 3 provides that no payment is to be made except through the official agent. By paragraph (b) it is provided that this subclause shall not be deemed to apply to payment-
-by any person, out of his own money, for any small expense legally incurred by him, if no part of the sum so paid is repaid to him.
I think it was mentioned that the effect of that paragraph was practically to allow a candidate to make any payments he liked as long as he made them in small amounts, and that, the effect of the exception was to do away with the main object of the whole subclause, namely, that the agent should be a sort of accounting officer for the expenses of the candidate.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Personally, I cannot see any objection to this subclause; it is not new. It is from both the English Act and our Act-section 237 of our Act.

The other
point raised was whether $500 was enough for a candidate to be allowed to spend.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I remember that point. It was suggested that $500 was not enough for a candidate to be allowed to spend. The present clause is a limitation which does not appear to have been in the old Act.

If there is
any way of defining what is meant by "small expenses," there could possibly, be no objection to subclause 3 as it stands; but the purpose of subclause 3 is to prevent a candidate from making any payment of any considerable amount excepting through his agent, and the effect of paragraph (b) is that if a candidate makes the payments in small amounts out of his own pocket, that is all right.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: No, paragraph (b) does not refer to the candidate; it says "by any person"; paragraph (a) refers to the candidate. I can understand that somebody travelling with a candidate may pay out a small amount for livery hire or something of that kind, and as long as that money is not to be repaid to him, it need not be accounted for.

At present, we
have no provision for publicity if any funds supplied except for candidates. Is there to be no provision with respect to the publishing of campaign funds for parties or groups of candidates? I think every one will agree with me that ithe present provision does not cover over twenty-five per cent of the money raised from time to time for such purposes. During the elec-

tion campaign of 1911 I think millions of dollars were spent by the manufacturers and big interests of Canada in advertising in newspapers. I have seen full-page advertisements in paper after paper all over Canada. These expenses were not included in the election expenses of any candidate, although I dare say there was more money spent in that way in the election of 1911 than in the published election expenses of all candidates. Does the minister intend to provide against the real and great danger which he apparently is trying to meet in this section?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I think the Bill provides for it very well indeed.
(Mr. L. THOMSON: Where?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
All expenses have to be set out and all contributions have to be made public. This matter was discussed on clause 12 when my hon. friend (Mr. Mc-Master) moved an amendment. His amendment proposed, if I recollect aright, that the details of all election contributions should be made public, and I pointed out at the time that section 79 made express provision for that. It provides that all payments by the candidate shall be published, that all payments made by his official agent shall be published, as well as the amount of personal expenses, if any, paid by the candidate; all disputed claims, so far as the official agent is aware; all unpaid claims, 'if any; and all money, Jaeourities and equivalent of money received or promised, and the like. Then by subsection (5) :
The returning: officer, within ten days after he receives from the official agent any return or supplementary return respecting election expenses, shall publish at the expense of the candidate a summary thereof with the signature of the official agent thereto in one and the same newspaper published or circulated in the electoral district wherein the election was held.
The following subsection provides that all such returns shall be preserved, and that after siix months they may be destroyed or returned to the candidate. Then, a penalty is provided for any member who sits in contravention of this section without an authorized excuse. So, I think the provision is rather ample in that respect. I know it is customary to cry out-and I see it in the press from time to time: Why don't you compel the publication of moneys contributed for elections? Well, I do not know any way of compelling that except the way adopted in this Bill. The duty is imposed upon the candidate and upon the election officials actually to publish these things and heavy penalties are imposed for any one

who seeks to evade that duty. Now if there is any better means-I do not mean any means that simply suggest themselves to a man's imagination-let us know it. I certainly think this is better than the plan proposed by my hon. friend (Mr. McMas-ter) the other night. I know that in the United States, where they recognize political parties in their legislation they say that the Republican managers shall publish this, and the Democratic managers shall publish such-and-such a thing. Here we do not recognize in our legislation the Unionist party, the Liberal party, the Farmers' party, the National Democratic party, or any other party. How, then, could you compel such unofficial organizations or associations to make public the contributions they have received? It comes down to the individual, and the individual is the candidate. If the candidate makes that statement, and it is certified to and properly audited, what more publicity could any one want? I know you can satisfy a popular cry in this country by talking about the millions that this party and the other party gets. There is more or less of a joke to that when it comes down to election time. We know how every candidate is pretty hard pressed for his own election expenses, and my own experience is that the newspapers well reveal the cost of elections in this country. If in the West contributions are pouring in at election time, let my hon. friends make them public. They are bound to do so under this law. I have run in a good many elections for this House, and I have given my experience.
iMr. L. THOMSON: But this section only provides for publicity with regard to the monies that pass through the hands of the candidate and his agent. There are other election expenses which do not pass through their hands, and which my hon. friend know are not all right.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: What are they?

During the campaign of 1911, the Regina Leader, for instance, which was in favour of reciprocity, published, and said it was paid for publishing, page after page of advertisements against reciprocity. That did not appear in the election expenses of the candidate. The paper was circulated in my constituency, but this item of expense certainly did not appear in the election expenses of my opponent. These are the big expenses, and they are not covered at all by this section.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I remember cases of that kind, and I remember what damage 123
they did me. The Toronto Globe in the 1911 election accepted page advertisements from the Davies Company condemning reciprocity, which it was supporting, and which I was supporting in my riding. The Davies Company paid for these advertisements. Were they not entitled to give publicity to their views? I took issue with the Toronto Globe for publishing them, and they said "Cannot the Davies Company pay to circulate their views just as you go around the country circulating your views?" Where are you to draw the line? The Davies Company issued pamphlets and circulated them. They paid for this publicity. Should that be a breach of the law? I submit that it should not be. Anyone has the right to hire the press and - issue advertisements giving publicity to his own views. Do you call that the election expenses of a party, or of candidate, or of anybody? I do not. I may say that I objected to it very strongly at the time, and I would yet, but I do not see any principle upon which those contributions should be made public. They might just as well say to my hon. friend: If we cannot advertise at our expense in a newspaper, you cannot hire a hall at your expense and make a speech, or get others to do it for you. The advertisement itself is the publicity. We know it is being paid for, it carries that evidence on its face because we know that papers opposed politically to the advertiser would not publish his advertisement unless they were paid for it and paid, probably, good round sums.

Why should they not be made to show what was paid for these advertisements? I have to make public what I spend on advertisements. Why make an exception in the case of the big interests? The minister said we do not recognize parties here, therefore, we cannot deal with them. Why don't we recognize them? Why don't we give them recognition and bring them within this law? I am convinced that the public is right in thinking that the biggest injury is done by contributions made to party funds, and I believe that these amounts should be made public.
My hon. friend says we do not recognize political parties in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: In our legislation.

Does not this Act provide that any political party must be incorporated for political purposes before they can contribute or spend money at elections as a party? So they must be re-



cognized as parties. I do not see, therefore, why the minister could not hold them accountable for the money they spend as a party.
Is there anything in the Act which requires an advertisement in relation to an election to bear on its face the fact that it is an advertisement and also information as to who inserted it?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: There is none.
Suppose there is no newspaper published in the county in which a candidate runs, where will he publish a statement of his expenses?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
It is published in the
adjoining county if there is no paper pub- -lished in the electoral district.
In regard to the question of contributions to political funds, it seems to me that the minister has left the door wide open to the big interests.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member is not in order in discussing under section 78 the question of contributions to political parties. That question was discussed the other evening under section 12, and it is also involved in section 79 which has been passed by this committee; and only with the unanimous consent of the committee to reopen clause 79 would the hon. member he in order in continuing that discussion.

If I am out of order, Mr. Chairman, I desire of course to be so informed. But if my hearing was accurate,
I was under the impression that we were discussing campaign funds a few minutes ago.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
An hon. member introduced the discussion, but I thought that he intended to make only a passing reference. I did not anticipate that he would open the subject for general discussion and I allowed his remarks. I must now rule, however, that those remarks were not in order.
. Mr. MARCIL:	Following up the question of advertising, I see you require a statement from the candidate or his agents; but do you require a statement also from any outsider who might pay for subscriptions to newspapers which are sent to a number of voters in a constituency, as was done in 1911 when Le Devoir of Montreal was paid for by hundreds of copies and sent to various parts of the province where it would

be most effective? Will any statemeent he required henceforth in connection with cases of that kind?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: There is nothing in the Act to cover that point, so far as I know.

If some outsider paid for 200 subscriptions, say, to have certain newspapers sent to voters, does the minister not think it wise to require that that man shall make a statement in regard to the matter? It is so much less money that the candidate has to spend.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not think it has been sought to fix such a limitation in any British country. If I wanted to send five hundred copies of the Toronto
10 p.m. Globe for two or three months to certain persons and to pay for those subscriptions myself I would have a perfect right to do so.
Sending them to individual voters?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, and I see no harm in such a thing.
It is part of the campaign.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: It is; and if the -candidate or his agents did it a statement would have to be published.
But if the candidate gets his friend to do it he still violates the law.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Then the candidate
would have to go around the corner pretty well, because he has to give a certificate to show that he does not procure any unauthorized person to do these things.

Subsection (13) provides that personal expenses must he paid by the agent if they amount to more than $500. Would it not be wise to fix a limit of $1,000? There are constituencies where it would be impossible for a candidate to cover the ground if his personal expenses were limited to $500.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I cannot add to the discussion we had the other night, which was lengthy. Up to $500 the candidate may himself pay his personal expenses; over $500 he must pay them through his agent. The reason is an excellent one: it is to prevent candidates going around and paying abnormal fees to various men nominally for services rendered but really to influence their votes. The object of the provision is to take away the personal touch as between the candidate and the voter. I think it is a salutary provision.	.
It would take |500 in railway fares to cover my constituency twice during the campaign-

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Not at the next election.

-and I do not see how you can have an agent look after expenses of that kind. As regards the suggestion with reference to paying exorbitant sums, the candidate will have to swear to a statement showing the amount of his expenses, and that statement will have to show what the various sums were paid for. In large- constituencies where you cannot cover the ground with four or five hundred dollars, I think this will work a hardship on many candidates.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I could suggest a way out of that difficulty. I can understand that a man who is not a member of the House may have a heavy bill for railway fares at the next election. Any man who is a member at the time of the next election will not be bothered in that way, but in a constituency where a candidate must necessarily spend five or six or seven hundred dollars for railway expenses, all he has to do to avoid difficulties is to ask his agent to buy him a four- or five-thousand mile ticket as the case may be. There is no real inconvenience or difficulty. It is only in a few constituencies that such a thing can happen, and the difficulty can be removed if candidates will adopt the plan I have suggested.

Section agreed to.
On section 100-advance polls for railway employees and others;
In view of the fact that this section is of considerable length, I move that we consider it subsection by subsection.

Motion agreed to.
On subsection (1)-advance voting by railway employees, sailors, etc.:

When we were considering
this clause a few days ago I objected to it on the ground that it was class legislation. It is going to give certain people a chance to vote and other people will not be able to vote. I therefore say, Mr. Chairman, that it is class legislation, and in the interest of every voter in Canada the clause should be struck out.

There is one
feature of this subsection to which the attention of the committee should be drawn.
123$
As drafted it Teads: "Every railway employee, sailor, commercial traveller or other person," and so on. Well, "or other person"' includes "any other person." I think the classes who have the advantage of that advance poll ought to be specially named and cited in some way if this clause is to be permitted to stand. As drafted, it is pretty broad, and "any other person" may enjoy the advantage of an advance poll.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Read the words which follow later: "and whose employment and calling is such as to- necessitate from time to time his absence from his ordinary place of residence-
How are you going to define that?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
-and who has reason to believe that, because of necessary absence from such place of residence in the pursuit of his employment or calling:, he will be unable to vote on polling day, may vote in advance of polling day-
I will give my hon. friend a case in illustration : In the fall of the year the people up where I live go out as apple-pickers, and they are away two and three weeks at a time. Or I take the ease of lumbermen; they are away a considerable number of days at a time. There are people who cannot be described as commercial travellers, and who are not railway men, who are not sailors, but their duties do call them away for periods of time and they -have reason to expect they will be away at election time. Surely it is not unreasonable to permit them to make that statement. to the election officer and obtain a certificate to vote at an advance poll. Then, of course, the declaration which is required of them, or the oath they have to take, is a very full one. If you are going to limit this to any particular classes you are going to deprive some people of the privilege accorded to others. That is the only point.
What supervision is there over the (polling at these advance polls?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The same supervision
as at any poll. The manner in which these polls are established is simply this: Several days before the election and at irregular hours-or later than the ordinary polls are held-these polls are kept open. A man who is going to be away-and knows it-on account of his business as a railway man, or a sailor or a commercial traveller can go to the returning officer and get a certificate from him that he is on the list. He takes

that certificate to one of these advance polls, where it is received and marked in the book, and he can vote. His vote is deposited in the ballot box, before a deputyreturning officer and scrutineers, just as is the case of an ordinary poll. Then when he obtains a certificate his name is marked from the list. But I can understand that some hardship might arise even from that, and a committee of rail-way men waited on me a few days ago and said that in the case of railway men sometimes their return was uncertain, and although they had obtained a certificate to enable them to vote at an advance poll they might not be able to vote while the advance poll was open, but might be able to be home on polling day and would find that their names had been marked off the voters' list. They asked as a concession that notwithstanding that, they should still be entitled to vote provided they still retained their certificates; they might still be permitted to go on polling day and present the certificates and vote notwithstanding that their names had been marked off when they applied for these certificates in the first instance. I see nothing unreasonable in that request, and when the time comes I propose to move an amendment to that effect. The whole conduct of the advance poll is precisely the same as that of a general poll except in respect of the length of time it is held open -I think it is for some three days.

Speaking of an
advance poll, has the Minister in mind any set period when that poll should be opened? Should it be opened a week ahead of the regular poll?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: That is provided for in this section.
Do I understand the Minister to say that the ballots- will be placed loosely in the box, and left in the custody of the returning officer until the day of the election, say three or four days after?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Why, yes.

There may be a hundred lose ballots, and they are not placed in an envelope, and the returning officer will have charge of them. Does the Minister mean to say that in the case of a man voting at an advance poll and who marks his ballot and it is put in the box, the ballot will be left there loose in the box, and the returning, officer will have charge of the box until the election day, and that that ballot will be counted with the others?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Why, certainly.
And the ballots will not be sealed up, or any precaution of that kind adopted?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The ballots are to be sealed, certainly, and every scrutineer present can - see the box sealed up. I do not know whether it makes any difference that the ballot is left loose in the box or that it is tied up or covered with something. It certainly will be in the box loose, and the box will be sealed and will not be opened until the regular count is made.
And the returning officer will have charge of the box from the time of the advance poll until the election?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Certainly
. Mr. MACKENZIE KING: The point my hon. -friend has made is not whether the ballot box itself will be sealed but whether the ballot will be placed in an envelope to distinguish it from the others.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The ballot box will be sealed up, and the candidate or his agents may assist in the sealing, and may examine the seals to see that they have not been broken.

If a certain [DOT]class are to have the 6-pecial privilege of putting their ballots in the box three days ahead of the elections what objection is there to having tihe ballots placed in an envelope? It is an extra precaution. Is [DOT]there any objection to it?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Is it for the purpose of identification?
My suggestion is for the purpose of identification, not of the voter but of the number of votes cast.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I do not see how. There is the poll book, there is the whole election machinery, and you would vote just as you would in an ordinary polling booth.
May I explain to my hon. friend that three hundred men may vote at an advance poll-

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
-and there are five hundred votes afterwards in the same box.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: No, no, not in the same box, that box is sealed uip. Every advance polling division has its own box. That box is used only for the purpose of the particular poll and for nothing else.
What is the duration of the voting at an advance poll?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: It is three days in all.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must point out to the committee that the leader of the Opposition submitted a motion which was adopted, that" this clause be considered subsection by subsection. We have not yet adopted subsection one and yet hon members are now considering subsection 15. If my hon. friend wishes to withdraw his motion, well and good. If not, it is my duty as Chairman to require hon. gentlemen to adhere to the subsection under consideration.
If the effect of the motion to consider the clause subsection by subsection will be to restrict discussion I certainly will withdraw it so that the whole section may be reviewed at once.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Is it the pleasure of the committee that the hon. gentleman have leave to withdraw his motion?
Motion (Air. Mackenzie King) withdrawn.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The entire section is now open for discussion.

How many electors
in a given polling subdivision would have to be absent to secure an advance poll, and what steps would they have to take to that end? At my election last fall a number of men who work in the woods were absent, some having left a week before the election, and in that way many of my electors did not have the privilege of voting.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The schedule to this Act sets out where the advance poll shall be. I may say that that schedule has to undergo a good deal of amendment, a great many places having been suggested since the schedule was first compiled, and when we take up this schedule if there are any other places to be included we will certainly add them. There is no limitation as to the number of persons necessary to secure an advance poll at any place, but if the vote falls below a certain number, at the next election there may be no advance poll at that place. Subsection 3 provides that the Chief Electoral Officer shall amend the schedule under the following circumstances:
