(a)	If a total of less than fifty votes is polled a;t the advance polls held within any such place at the election which immediately preceded the amendment, he may strike off the name of that place; or,
(b)	If he is advised and believes that a total of fifty votes will be polled at any place
in case an advance poll is established there, he may add the name of that place.
If my.hon. friend has any point where he would like an advance poll established, we will be glad to give him one if there is good reason for it.

The minister states that
the boxes may be in the hands of the returning officer for two or three days for the purpose of the advance poll. Where will the unused ballots be at that time?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I suppose they will be
in the custody of the returning officer. Subsection 14 provides that:
At the dose of the poll each day, the deputy returning officer and every candidate or agent present who desires so to do shall affix their respective seals to the ballot box in such a manner that the box cannot be opened nor any ballots be deposited therein without breaking such seals.
Will they break the seals next morning?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes. The other ballots that have not been used will, I assume, be in the custody of the deputy returning officer.
Afr. DuTREMBLAY:	Why should not
those votes be counted on the same night as the election?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: They are to be counted on the same night as the election, but they are not to be opened before the election. The idea is to maintain secrecy and to treat the advance poll for all purposes as it it had been a poll established on election day.

We had a similar clause in operation in the last provincial election, and in my riding it worked very satisfactorily and there were no complaints from any one. The railway men found it of great advantage-in fact, I believe that these advance polls were in the Ontario Act confined solely to railway men. The poll was opened a week prior to the election exactly as any other poll, with a deputy returning officer, poll clerks, and candidates' agents in attendance. Any railway men who had reason to believe that they would be away on election day took advantage of these advance polls, and the ballot box was sealed at night, as the hon. minister has pointed out, opened again on the following day, and re-sealed at night, and the votes were counted on the night of the election. Many railway men go out from divisional points and do not return for two or three days. In fact, in my constituency some of the men may not get

back for a week if they are operating on the Canadian Pacific running out of Havelock to Smith's Falls and Toronto, for they may be sent back on the shore line up the Trenton division, and in some cases it may be ten days before they return-to Havelock. I think this is a good clause and should be adopted.

I have not the slightest objection to either railway men or commercial travellers getting this advantage provided they are treated no differently than the other classes of the community. I notice that a sailor will be allowed to vote under this section, but it would be absolutely useless to our deep-sea fishermen, 99 per cent ' of whom leave home at certain seasons and are absent from two to six months; in fact only our sailors on the Great Lakes would be able to take advantage of this provision.
If a sailor was leaving three or four days before an election for a year's trip, this section would give him an opportunity of voting.

It might give that opportunity to six sailors in the whole of the Maritime Provinces. My argument is that we should treat all classes of the community alike, and if we are going to make provision for railway men and commercial travellers, we should also make similar provision for sailors who are away for from two to six months. In my constituency if an election were held next week 4,000 deep-sea fishermen would not have a chance to vote, and I say that my constituents should be treated just the same as our railway men and our commercial travellers. But in view of the difficulties of meeting these cases I think the proper way is not to pass this clause at all, and so treat everybody alike.	,

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
As we have arranged for all the subsections to be considered together, I will now formally make an amendment to meet the objection of the railway men which I have just mentioned to the committee. It will appropriately go in as -an addition to subsection 10 at the foot -of page 74. It reads as follows:
Provided however that if an elector who has obtained a certificate in form TT is unable to vote at an advance poll, he shall nevertheless be entitled to vote on polling day at the polling station at which his name appears upon the list of voters, and at no other polling station. Before so voting such elector shall surrender his certificate in form TT to the deputy returning officer who shall then and there cancel such certificate and the entry concerning the same on the official list of voters, and such
IMr. Sexsmith.]
elector shall then be entitled to vote as if such certificate had never been issued.
This is an amendment prepared to meet the objections of the railway men who waited upon me.

Does he surrender
the certificate?	_

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: In the first instance he gets the certificate. His name is entered upon the list of voters as having the right to vote at an advance poll and when he so votes he must surrender the certificate. If he is not able to get home on time to vote at the advance poll but does get home on election day he may still present himself at his own polling subdivision, surrender his certificate-that heing evidence that he has not voted,-and be entitled to vote.
Gan a railway man vote in any other constituency than his own?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: No, he must vote in his own division.
Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
There will be two consequent amendments. In subsection 10, the following words will be struck out:
The vote of such elector shall thereafter be pollable at an advance poll, and not otherwise.
Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
A further amendment will be necessary on page 76. Paragraph (d) of subsection 16 will have to be struck out. It reads as follows:
After having obtained from a registrar, revising officer or returning officer a certificate in form TT votes or attempts to vote at any other than an advance poll.
This will be struck out because the amendment that I have just made will permit him to vote on election day at other than an advance poll.

There is no provision for the ballots to be deposited in the ballot box, and I do not see any provision for reopening the ballot box after it has been sealed. After the first day the ballot box is sealed; the scrutineers may affix their seals in such a way that no ballots can be deposited in the box. But I do not see any way whereby the unused ballots themselves must be deposited in the box, or the box must be opened in the presence of somebody.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: You could not deposit the unused ballots in the box.

What are you going to
do with them?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Surely the returning
officer has some way of keeping his book of ballot papers. The idea is to keep the ballot box absolutely secret and at night to keep it sealed up. The number of ballots is recorded. The agents know the number that have been used or spoiled. They know that at night and by a simple process of arithmetic they know how many the returning officer should have on the following morning. If they are about their business at all they will know the number that the returning officer should have.
Where is the provision that they have the right to do that?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
What are they there
for?
What authority is there for that?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The general authority
that the agent attending the poll would have, to see there was no crooked work done.

This is a special clause for
carrying on the work at the advance poll.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: There is nothing special about it. The agent has a right to be there.
What right has he to insist on the returning officer counting the ballots?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
If I were there I would
see that it was done.

That is not a fair answer.
Is there any provision in this section that would give the agent that authority? A poll is held from seven to ten o'clock, and they use so many ballots between the opening and closing of the poll. Then, the poll opens again. Has the agent representing the candidate there a right under this section to demand of the returning officer that he permit the counting of ballots after the first night.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
He will have all the
powers of the ordinary scrutineer under this Act.
This section only applies to an advance poll and the general law does not apply.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Before allowing hon.
members to continue a general discussion of the section I must point out that the last amendment made by the Acting Solicitor
General has not been adopted. That is the amendment to strike out paragraph (d) of subsection 16. When that is disposed of this discussion will he perfectly in order.

I am afraid
that the effect of striking out that paragraph will be greater than the minister intends.
I would suggest that instead of striking out the paragraph altogether he leave it as it stands and add the words " except upon the presentation of such certificate on election day as herein provided." The paragraph is to prevent a man who has already voted at an advance poll from voting somewhere else on election day or some other time. Leaving that provision in and adding the words which I have suggested would cover what the minister has in mind.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I will accept that suggestion. I therefore beg to move, instead of striking out subsection (d), to add at the end of it the words " except upon presentation on election day of such certificate as provided by this section."
Amendment agreed to.

This is a special section for holding an advance poll, and the conduct of the business of the poll must be surrounded with the same safeguards and secrecy as surround any other poll held in the regular way on election day. On election morning the deputy returning officer goes into the polling booth, the poll clerk is there, the agents of the respective candidates are there, and it is their duty to count the ballot papers that are in the hands of the returning officer.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Where do they get that right?
My hon. friend said they had the right.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: They get it, just the ordinary agent's right, under clause 52 of this Bill.

I was right before, and my hon. friend said that I was not right, but now he admits I am right in regard to this point-that is, the agent's right to count the ballots is a matter of custom. Let us assume that. The election continues throughout the day; the scrutineers are there to watch the voters as they come in and get their ballot papers from the returning officer, properly initialled by him. Each voter goes into a compartment, marks his ballot, comes out and places the ballot in the ballot box. When the time comes for the closing of the polls the ballots are

counted and put back into the box, the box is sealed in the presence of the scrutineers, and each agent of a candidate has the count as taken at that time. But this advance poll is open from seven to ten o'clock in the evening of three days. My hon. friend says that the ballot box is sealed, but that means simply that a slip of paper is pasted over the slit in the ballot box through which the ballots are inserted. The agent does not know how the vote stands in the ballot box; the returning officer takes the ballot box home with him, and the next night it is opened again and more ballots are put into it. The third night it is opened again and more ballots put into it, and at the close of the poll the third night the ballots are counted. The proper way in which the matter should be handled would be that each night the poll is held, the ballots should be counted and the count taken and preserved by the different candidates at the advance poll. When you have a ballot box, with simply a slip of paper pasted over the slit, left in the hands of the returning officer over night, he could put in or take out twenty-five ballot papers, and in that case, there is no secrecy nor safeguard.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: If my hon. friend thinks it would help, I do not object to putting in a general clause to the effect that the provisions of secions 52 and 54 of this Act ielating to agents at polling stations and their duties and powers shall apply to advance polls.
W7ould that mean the counting of the ballots each night?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Counting the ballots, opening the polls and examining all election documents but I do not think the ballot boxes should be opened and the ballots counted each night.
That is the safeguard.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I shall have to disagree with my hon. friend on that point.

May I suggest this to the minister, merely as a suggestion for his consideration? These advance polls are certainly going to give rise to a good deal of suspicion one way or another, and if it is possible to avoid that it is well to avoid it. Personally, I am in favour of advance polls for certain classes that may be specified. But it might be well that every ballot that goes into the ballot box in an advance poll should be placed in an envelope which should be sealed, and that envelope should bear some designation of [Mr. Copp.l
the returning officer and each of the agents. Let those ballot papers go into the ballot box in that form. Then, only ballots that are in envelopes that have those three signatures could be counted when the count takes place. Otherwise, it is going to be possible to stuff the ballot box.
Why can they not be counted each night?

I am inclined to agree with the general view taken by the leader of the Opposition. (Mr. Mackenzie King) that unless some further safeguard is provided, there will be a suspicion. I am absolutely opposed on principle, to the suggestion that the ballots should be counted each night, because I think the result of the election should be counted as a whole and known as a whole; otherwise the counting of those ballots each night might have on an election an influence which it should not have.
It would have the effect that you would have an honest election and an honest count.

That is another question. We have operated under the law as it stands in Saskatchewan; at our last election we had some twenty-five advance polls in our province, and as far as I have heard, there was never the slightest complaint as to the manner in which those polls were held, and I believe the same thing is true in regard to Ontario, because I have not heard of any complaints there. Nevertheless, those ballot boxes are in the hands of deputy returning officers over nigth for three nights, and a suspicion. is liable to arise as to what might happen to those ballot boxes during that time. If some provision can be made whereby that suspicion may be absolutely removed, that would be in the interest of everybody. The leader of the Opposition has suggested that each ballot be put into a separate envelope and those envelopes identified. I cannot agree with that, because when those envelopes are opened, those marks may be of such a character as to identify the voter, and I think that is objectionable. But I would throw this out as a suggestion, namely, that at the end of the voting on each evening, the ballots should be taken out of the ballot box just as they are, folded, without being openend out, and placed in a fairly large envelope, which will then be properly sealed and put back into the box, and the box sealed. Then on the following day when the box is opened, the only thing

in the box would be one large envelope containing the ballots. The same process would be gone through each evening.

A separate envelope would
be used each evening?
Yes.
That is all right.
That envelope can be properly sealed by the returning officer and all of the agents who are present.

According to this law, a
returning officer will carry in his pocket at night the unused ballots. That is against the present system of election laws in Canada, and it is against the interest of the Canadian people to have unused ballots floating around loose anywhere. Is there any penalty in the event of a returning officer losing those ballots that are in his custody, that are not locked up and for which no person except himself is responsible. I would suggest that instead of putting the ballots, into envelopes, you should have a separate ballot box for each day. You are not going to have so many of these advance polls, and you can very well have a ballot box for each day with a sufficient number of ballot papers in that box for the business of the day. When the ballot box is opened the scrutineers are ' present; and at night when the poll is closed, the unused ballot papers are put back into the box and the box is sealed and put away. The next day the second ballot box, with a sufficient number of ballot papers in it to cover the business of that day, is opened, and at the end of the day the unused ballots are put back into the box and the box sealed and put away like the first. In that way, you are not asking any person to carry around unused ballot papers in his pocket. Such a person might lose one, or two, or five, of those ballots; a sufficient number might be lost at each poll to affect the result. My hon. friend knows what might be done with floating ballots of that kind. I am more concerned with what might be done with floating ballots than I am about stuffing one particular box, because you might not be able to do a great deal of damage with that one box, but you might do a great deal of damage with floating ballots. A separate ballot box each day would overcome the whole difficulty and would safeguard the interest of the electors.

The suggestion by my hon. friend (Mr. Cahill) and also by the Minister of Immigration an Colonization (iMr. Calder) meets what I have in mind by way of greater security as concerns these loose ballots. I really think the suggestion made by my hon. friend (Mr. Cahill) is a little better than the one made by_ my hon. friend the minister (Mr. Calder). The only difference is this; in the one case it takes a few more ballot boxes, and in the other a few more envelopes.

If the other suggestion is carried out, then in the evening at the close of the poll the ballot boxes are opened and the ballots are put in an envelope. There is no reason why the remaining blanks should not be put in another envelope and put in that box, which rwould be closed and sealed for the night. The following days, open up the box and take out the blank ballots. If you are going to open that box at night after the poll is closed, you can put your blank ballots in that box. I cannot see any necessity for having three boxes.
I cannot see any necessity for opening a ballot box after it has been closed.
What harm is there?
Why is it closed at all? Why do we seal the box except to protect the franchise of the people from corrupt politicians? There is every reason for it.

What we are attempting to do is to provide for secrecy; that is what we are aiming at. Now the suggestion is that the ballot box at the close of the poll should be opened in the presence of the deputy returning officer and the officers on both sides. They will be there, and the ballots before they are unfolded and examined should simply be put in an envelope which should be sealed by all parties. You are not violating any secrecy in that. You are attempting to make an arrangement so as to secure us .secrecy. There is no harm in opening the ballot box for that purpose. After sealing that envelope, put it back in the box and seal the box, and then on the following day when the deputy returning officer and the agents are there,' again open the box and get out these blank envelopes.

That suggestion involves the handling of the ballots two or three times. The suggestion of my hon. friend (Mr. Cahill) would mean that the ballots would not be handled at all. The box would be sealed. It vrould mean two

or three boxes, but it would give an additional sense of security to have the box sealed until all the ballots were about to be counted.

Personally the objection I have to that feature is this: We all know how ballot boxes are sealed. Many of them are sealed in a very flimsy way, and the seals may possibly Joe removed without suspicion. You have a tin box that is very difficult to seal, but we have had a provision in the law that boxes should be sealed ever since we have had an election law. I have seen hundreds of ballot boxes turned in with practically no seals .at all. I say that, in order to remove suspicion, it is far better to have that sealing done on an envelope than to attempt to seal the box itself.

May I suggest that both plans be adopted that the ballots be put in an envelope and sealed, and the ballot box itself be sealed. That would be a double precaution. At the end of the day have all the ballots put in an envelope, and the envelope and the ballot box sealed. Then remove that ballot box, and the next day do the same thing with another box. It would involve having two or three boxes, but it would be a double precaution and give a greater sense of security.
What would be the object of having three boxes?

Just to double the precautions. My hon. friend has said that his experience with ballot boxes goes to show that the seals can be broken very easily. If both these methods were adopted, any one wishing to tamper with the ballots would have to break open the seal on the ballot box and the seal on the envelope containing the ballots, and they might hesitate to go to that extent.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: This is more in line with the suggestion of my hon. friend (Mr. Cahill). Suppose at the end of the first day's polling a box is sealed land the scrutineers exercise the privilege given them of putting their own seals on it. The unused ballots are placed in an ev-velope which is sealed by the two scrutineers. Then in the morning examine your seals on the box and on the envelope and start out for the second day's work, and so on at the end of the second day and the third day. Seal the ballots in a special envelope, and let the scrutineers put their signatures on the seals on the envelope.
That is a good suggestion.
And mark on the envelopes the number of ballots enclosed.

Those suggestions are very good, but I would bring before the committee the suggestion of hawing a particular method of sealing the box and the envelope. There are methods by wbcih the envelope [DOT] and ballot box could be sealed so that the seal could not be broken without detection. The minister (Mr. Guthrie) has just said that the seals on the boxes are easily broken, and that is true. It does not mean much simply to say that the officials must seal the box or the envelope, because we know how it is done. The deputy returning officer simply closes or seals the box as he may see fit. If he does not know how to seal it, it will not be sealed, or the sealing will be done in such a way as to be useless. I would suggest that a particular method of sealing be adopted, and that a system for doing so1 be provided in the law. My suggestion is that each 'box and each envelope should be sealed by using a sheet of paper upon which the deputy returning officer, his clerk, and the agents of the candidates will jput their signature, and that the sealing be done in such a way as to leave the signatures exposed. 'Suppose II want to seal this -book. If 'I seal it with an ordinary sheet of paper, the seal might be broken and a new seal substituted and you would not. be able to detect the difference, but if I take a blank piece of paper on which I write my signature, which cannot be imitated without exposing oneself to a charge of perjury, and then the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Immigration also put their signatures on, and we use this sheet of paper to close this book, bind it and seal it, it is absolutely impossible to break the seal without its being known. I am not the inventor of this method. It is already in use now for loose-leaf ledgers. You close your ledger with a key, but the key locks with a little piece of paper on which you put your name, and no one can open the ledger except by breaking the little piece of paper. If this method is not adopted,
I would suggest that some other be adopted which would give good results. This strikes me as a good means of avoiding fraud, and I submit it to the consideration of the committee. If we adopt a safe method of sealing either the envelope or the ballot box there will be no trouble.

If the minister is still prepared to receive suggestions I have one

to offer. I agree with the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) that it is a bad practice to handle ballots at any time previous to the final counting of them. I would suggest that the boxes for the advance polls be constructed with three compartments, each having its own separate opening, and each opening being sealed. On the first day number one would be opened and at the close of the day, after the ballots had been put in, it would be sealed; and the same procedure would be carried out on the second and third day. In this way you would avoid interfering with the ballots until the box was opened on the closing of the poll on the final day.

I do not see any objection to the suggestion made by the Minister of Immigration (Mr. Calder) of putting the ballots into envelopes and marking them. Nothing has been said to show that there is any danger in putting the ballots at night into an envelope in the presence of all parties, and certainly there is no other way by which you can so well identify them the next morning. The suggestion of the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. Denis) might be all right with experts at that sort of work, but it might lead to blunders, and I do not think it is a wise one. Any man can easily put his name on an envelope, and if the ballots are put into an envelope at night I fail to see what harm can be done. I think the unused ballots might also be counted and put into envelopes.
That is a good suggestion.

I have never seen a ballot box sealed in such a way that it could not be broken and sealed up the same way. The suggestion of the Minister of Immigration is worthy of consideration. I was not in Saskatchewan during the provincial election of 1912 but I heard no complaints in regard to the operation of the law there. Every one was satisfied with that particular part of the Act and the way in which it had worked out. No fault was found, and it seems to me that the suggestion of the minister, who has more experience in regard to this matter than any one else in this House, should be well considerd. The simple and effective way is to seal and initial the envelopes at night, and all unused ballots could be cleaned up and put into an envelope and sealed.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Let us thoroughly understand the wish of the committee in this
matter. We may agree on this to-night, and to-morrow when other hon. gentlemen are in the House we may find ourselves disagreing on the question. If I
11 p.m. understand' the suggestion it is this: We should make a provision that at the end of each day the box shall be opened and the ballots, without being unfolded, shall be placed in an envelope and sealed, and that the returning officer and agents shall, if they so desire, seal the envelope with their own seals and signatures. That envelope shall be placed in the ballot box. The unused ballots shall be placed in another envelope and sealed in a similar way, being also placed in the ballot box. The ballot box then shall be locked and sealed. On the following morning the ballot box shall be unlocked and unsealed, and the envelope' containing the unused ballots taken out, the other envelope, containing the used ballots, not to be opened until the close of the poll. The same procedure is to be followed each day until the final counting of the votes. If that is right, I shall have an amendment drawn to cover the suggestion and shall submit it to the House when the Bill comes up again. If, on the other hand, I have not expressed the wish of the committee I shall be glad to know just what is desired.

There is just one additional feature to the suggestion that has been made, and that is that the envelopes should bear on the cover the number of ballots enclosed. I would ask the minister also whether it would not be well, instead of opening the unused ballots, to begin with a fresh book,of ballots and alloiw the two envelopes to remain sealed. I think it might be well to start the next day with a fresh book.

I think that if you go to all this trouble you will destroy the effect of the advance poll. Suppose you have an advance poll where there may not be more than fifty votes during two or three days. A dozen or two dozen voters may come in during the first day and at night you take the trouble of putting those bollots into an envelope and marking the number and putting the envelope into the box.
What objection could there be, before the ballots were finally counted ibn the third day, to opening the three envelopes and mixing the ballots together?

It does seem to me that we have not very much confidence in humanity. You have a returning officer, a re-

sponsible deputy returning officer, a sworn poll clerk and the sworn agents of each of the different candidates. You have, say, twenty ballots marked on the first day of the advance poll, and they are put into a box and sealed at night. I cannot see any sense in trying to put these in an envelope and marking them so that when the envelope is opened you may know how these men may have voted, but I do see some sense in taking care of unused ballots. There are not two or three hundred ballots issued to these branch polls. There are a small number of ballots and only a certain number of men vote the first day, and the scrutineers, the agents and the poll clerk, together with the deputy returning officer, I believe, would do their duty. They would be there in the morning, at the hour when the poll is open, to count over the unused ballots they may have. If there were eight or ten-or even fifty for that matter-of unused ballots, those unused ballots pould be put in an envelope and the envelope sealed by the agent and by the returning officer, and that would be sufficient, without sealing the other ballots that had already been placed in the box.

I have not had the
opportunity of making a very close study of the provisions for these advance polls, nor have I got into my head a true conception of the machinery which is to be provided for them. I simply want to put myself on record as being absolutely and entirely opposed to the whole business.
Hear, hear.

I think it is an invasion upon the old, well-established, and well-understood principle of holding the elections and having everybody vote on the same day, and the feeling of security and satisfaction that that gives to the whole community is a greater consideration to the Canadian public than the convenience of the few who might vote at these advance polls. I simply speak for myself and say that I am absolutely and entirely opposed to it as an expedient that should not be practised in this country. Everybody should vote on election day; and there are. very few people indeed-if they choose to put themselves to a little inconvenience, and if they are anxious to exercise the franchise-but can be present and poll their votes on the day. The polls are now open in most towns at six o'clock in the morning; and in the case of anybody who is going away, if the train were delayed half an hour in the morning in order to give them

an opportunity to poll their votes before they leave the station from which they are to depart that would be all right. I repeat that I wish to put myself on record as being opposed to creating difficult machinery such as is provided for here, and which is bound to result in no end of dissatisfaction.

I think that when this clause was under consideration some days ago I was the first to express' my opposition to advance polls, as I thought the public at large thought more of the secrecy and sanctity of the ballot than of the granting of such a special privilege as this to a few people. I believe that having the polling take place on the one day has been adopted by democratic nations in order to insure secrecy in elections, and at the same time to prevent the exercise of certain influences which might be brought into play if the polling was extended over a number of days. I am very pleased now to see that I am supported in my opposition by my hon. friend from Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie), and my hon. friend from Lunenburg (Mr. Duff).'Apparently the chief object of the proposed innovation is to give commercial travellers the privilege of voting without great inconvenience. But we know' that there are certain periods when commercial travellers are at home, more particularly iSunday. Iif the polling were to take place on Monday every class of the community that are not usually at home would have the opportunity of knowdng four or five weeks in advance that the elections would take place on Monday, would make their arrangements accordingly and W'ouid vote on that particular day before starting out on their business. Fishermen in the Maritime Provinces would prefer Monday as the day on which polling should take place in preference to any other day in the week because they leave home early on Monday and do not return until the following Saturday. Possibly some people may not be able to he home on that day, but that would occur no matter what day was chosen. For the convenience of railway men living in the cities or suburban districts I previously suggested that they should be allowed to vote early in the morning and late at night. That is the best suggestion I can make to the committee in order that we may adhere to the present system and thus preserve the secrecy and honesty of the ballot. You may adopt whatever safeguards you like but nevertheless these advance polls will result in many acts of corruption in certain parts of the country.	_

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Do I understand that the statement I made as to the proposed amendment, added to by the suggestion of my hon. friend (Mr. Mackenzie King) is in line with what the committee thinks proper to adopt? If so, when the committee next meets I will have such an amendment prepared and laid before it.

With the- understanding
that the boxes are to be opened in the presence of the returning officer and the agent.?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I am giving the agents at the advance polls all the power they have at any other poll, but I do not quite agree that the envelopes containing unused ballots should not be re-opened for use on the following day.
I will withdraw that suggestion if the minister says that the unused ballots will be sealed as well as the others.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Then I move that clause 100 stand.
And the agents will be there to put their seal or signature on the envelopes?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada

Yes, if they-want to.

speechtext: Section 101 was carried, but I find that the Under Secretary of State, who has the administration of the Canada Temperance Act, thinks that that section will have to be further amended, and that probably some amendments will also have to be made to the Canada Temperance Act. I have not got these amendments yet, and would therefore move that we reopen section 101 for further consideration and then allow it to stand. Motion agreed to.
On section 2-Interpretation:

The form of
this section, I think, will depend a good deal upon what we decide with regard to other sections.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I do not think the
form taken by other clauses can affect the interpretation clause. I have gone over it very carefully and have some suggestions to make. It is difficult to keep track of them all. That is the reason why I wished to get back to this section.
I know that one or two members on this side of the House have something to say about the necessity of more specifically defining the rural polling division.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: When we get down to that paragraph, I want to have it fully discussed. It is for the purpose of reaching it that I want to proceed.
I was going to suggest that" a schedule containing the names of the cities and towns-

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I am prepared to discuss that when we get to the paragraph, but it is at the very end of the section, and we may not reach it for several days.
Is not the minister proposing to take up that section now?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, but I desire to move that the section be considered paragraph by paragraph.

Alotion agreed to.
On paragraph (a)-"advance poll."
Is it the intention that any paragraph must stand as carried?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It is not possible for the committee to definitely adopt a subclause or a paragraph. When one paragraph has been fully discussed and adopted we pass on to the next, discuss and adopt that. Before the entire section is finally adopted the question is always put: Shall the clause carry? Then any paragraph may be again referred to and discussed.
On paragraph (b)-"candidate":

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: That is practically the same as the former law.

This seems to me to be rather a peculiar provision. I do not remember having seen it in the old law, but even if it were there I do not think it is a reasonable provision. "A candidate is a person who is declared by himself or by others to be a candidate." That would include anybody whom, for instance, the newspapers might mention as a candidate. It very often happens prior to an election that the newspapers get busy with the names of men, prominent or otherwise, in the locality and say that Air. So-and-So is to be a candidate. Mr. So-and-So might be very seriously inconvenienced by such a clause as this.
What is the object of the words "or by others"?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: This is to prevent a man giving private information to some of his friends and saying to them: "Go on with the work of the election; I will not be bound by any corrupt act you may do." Or a man may be in Great Britain, and his friends may go ahead and canvass on is behalf. But that man has not announced himself as a candidate, and in that way he might corrupt the whole riding. It is an old law in this country and I have never heard it questioned. I think it is a very wise provision. In the case of a newspaper simply announcing a man as a candidate, I do not think a judge would hold him to be a candidate in such an isolated case. But anything like an organized effort on the part of one's friends to carry on election work, even although the candidate had withheld his positive assent to their action, is wrong. If a man wishes he can very soon stop such work. This clause is intended to prevent a man using his friends to do what the law will not allow him to do personally.

But in a large number of cases a man is not going to take the trouble to deny a report. In our province previous to an election we invariably have a large number of candidates announced, and if any corrupt practice occurred apparently those men would be held responsible.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Does my hon. friend know of any wrong or injury done to any man since this law has been in force?

No, because I am under the impression that most of our population never knew such a law was in force. Otherwise, I am sure that in a number of cases they might have been able to use it to the detriment of prominent respectable citizens. As things are now a prominent citizen will have to communicate with all the newspapers and go around to all the political heelers and tale-bearers to stop them calling him a candidate and so save himself from being held responsible for something they may do without his authority.
I think that part of the clause should be stricken out.

I quite agree with the hon. member. I can conceive of a case where people for their own benefit would set up the name of a man as a candidate who never had any intention of running. Surely it could not be said that that man is nominated as a candidate. In fact, I have heard it repeatedly said during elections that Mr. So-and-So was running, this report being

circulated simply for the purpose of influencing votes. If a man whose name is put forward as a candidate without his authority is going to be held responsible, I think that the words "with his consent" should be inserted after the words "by others."

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Of course, if he does not eventually become a candidate that report does not make any difference one way or the other; it is only when he does become a candidate that the section has any operation at all. I have no objection to the words going in.

I would direct the attention of the minister to the fact that this section will apparently lead to considerable controversy. I think he was in the House this afternoon when the Acting Prime Minister (Sir George Foster) told us that the Government would be inclined to be reasonable with the committee in the matter of late sittings. It is now half-past eleven, and as we have done a very good day's work, I think the minister might very well agree to left the committee rise and report progress. I am sure I can promise that he will make just as much progress as if he continues the sitting.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: We might just as well make it bold and plain. This promise is made, as was the promise on Thursday night, meaning: If you don't adjourn now, why we will see that you don't pass any more of this Bill. My hon. friend speaking in the House to-day said that the minister used the threat that the committee would sit until two o'clock in the morning. I made a suggestion and not a threat. I would suggest, not by way of threat, but merely by way of getting on with this Bill, that we sit until two o'clock this morning. However, let it be distinctly understood that while we on this side are -anxious to go on, the disposition on the other side is not to go on. It is now less than half-past eleven. It is my view that we should pass the uncontested sections to-night, and another hour would probably enable us to do so. There are seven or eight sections before us that will, of course, have to be threshed out. However, in the face of what my hon. friend intimates in effect, if we have to do it we will do it. I take it that no further progress will be made to-night, and we may as well adjourn.

I would like
the minister to appreciate our position on this side of the House. After the adjourn-

ment comes we are informed what the business is to be to-morrow. We have no opportunity to consider those measures until to-morrow morning, and that means devote ing to-morrow morning to work of the afternoon. It is all right for the minister himself, for he is here as an individual, but if he. looks at the seats about him he will find that for the most part the House is empty. A few of us who are endeavouring to follow legislation carefully are obliged to remain here till on in the morning each day. We are beginning another week and if the minister proposes to keep this committee in session every night until after midnight, let him say so. If he wishes to be reasonable he will consent to allow the committee to rise now.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think that half past eleven is unreasonable, but after the way the matter has been put before the committee I suppose there is nothing for me to do but to move that the committee rise and report progress.

I think the
minister might have done that without having to be asked.
Motion agreed to; progress reported.

subtopic: THE REPORTED MERGER DISCUSSED ON MOTION BY MR. RICHARDSON TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the right hon. the leader of the Government (Sir George Foster) and hon. members for giving me this opportunity to proceed. Were it not that I expect to have to leave Ottawa to-night I would have been very glad to postpone until to-morrow my remarks on this question.
My attention was directed to this matter in various ways, but I was especially struck with a letter which I received from a very prominent capitalist residing in Toronto, in which he says:
The job is being put up, I believe, by London and New York financial manipulators, the latter group being closely connected with the United States Steel Corporation, with which this " British Empire " (they are hell on loyalty these cosmopolitan grafters) affair is to " compete." It is, of course, another gigantic stock-watering enterprise, and it would be very interesting to know before any Canadian charter or franchise is granted whether the Government has detailed knowledge of the actual money to be invested, of the "securities" to be issued, of the valuations to be placed on the existing property, and securities which are to be included in the merger, and of the names of the persons actually interested, who are the real projectors, and who are really putting up or finding the money. It would also be highly interesting to know whether the Government, in view of the country's past experience with the actual meaning and cost to the public of " vested rights," is taking such measures as shall ensure that nothing shall be conceded to this enterprise which will warrant its projectors or manipulators or those to whom they may dispose of their franchises in demanding at any time in the future that the people of Canada shall pay such prices for metal products and water transport as shall enable them to pay fat dividends on a hundred millions or so of wind and water as was done in the case of the United States Steel merger to the ' 
extent of nearly seven hundred millions. This is obviously an attempt to duplicate that swindle. It is these flaunting, posing ballyhoos like Morden, and still more the men at the back, who make the bullets and aim the guns, who are the real Bolsheviks, and whose goings-on afford a sort of excuse for the other kind.

speechtext:
I do not think it makes any difference what the name is; this House has only to deal with the matter dealt with in the communication.
In addition to what I have read, I noticed in one of the Toronto joapers recently the following statement:
The biggest industrial company in the British Empire is being organized in Canada by Colonel Grant Morden, M.P. for Chiswick, in the British House of Commons. He is identified with big interests in England, and has come to Canada to effect a merger that will include the great steel and iron companies of Nova Scotia, the Canada Steamships Company and other concerns.
The new company will be known as the Bri-ish Empire Steel Corporation It will have a capitalization of two hundred and fifty million dollars, and will be able to compete with the United States Steel Corporation, which has been dumping its products into the British Empire market.
" I cannot give you the details of the new company for the present," said Colonel Morden,
" but it will compare in size with the Canadian Pacific railway and will be the biggest industrial concern in the British Empire."
I also observed that iColonel Morden addressed the Toronto Board of Trade yesterday, and I clipped from a Toronto paper a summary of his speech on that occasion. If the House will permit me, I would like to read a few figures in order that hon. gentlemen may be fully seized of the situation:
Col. W. Grant Morden, promoter of the big merger known as the British Empire Steel Corporation, member of the British Parliament for Brantford and Chiswick, England, and a former Toronto boy, gave an address to the Toronto

Board of Trade to-day. Col. Morden said: " Proper combination to-day in trade is essential, just the same as in all united efforts. There has been no consolidation of industries, to my knowledge, that has ever taken place which has worked out so scientifically, so fairly, and on so conservative lines as the consolidation to be known in future as the British Empire Steel Corporation."
Col. Morden compared its position with that of the United States Steel Corporation, which had started without a dollar of assets behind its common stock. The British Empire Steel starts out by simply assuming a nominal funded debt of $43,000,000.
" We assume and put against the outstanding preference shares of the constituent companies an equivalent amount of preference shares, namely, 37,000,000 dollars," Col. Morden said. x " We issue 25,000,000 dollars of Oight per cent preferential participating shares as against an equivalent amount of cash, and we pay for the combined properties sixty-eight million dollars in seven per cent non-cumulative preference shares, and seventy-seven million dollars of common stock. That makes a total of 250 million dollars." '
"What do we pay for it?" the colonel asked. " We have an appraised value that has been substantiated by the greatest experts obtainable on the North American continent and in England, of four hundred and three million dollars of assets plus a surplus of some forty-two million dollars of quick assets over current liabilities. In other words, we have a net asset value there of four hundred and fifty million odd dollars."
I went over to the office of the Under-Secretary of State this morning and I was there allowed to inspect the fyle in connection with this merger. I find that these people applied for incorporation under the Joint Stock Companies Act of a company capitalized at $200,000. Notice, however, was given in the correspondence that the capitalization would be increased to $500,000,000 and intimation was also given-that the company might be capitalized at a billion dollars Now, the point I want to make is that ii they secure all these assets for something around $40,000,000 and if they are allowed to capitalize at $500,000,000, dividends will be paid on the $500,000,000 and not upon the actual amount of value involved in the properties acquired.
The great curse of high finance in this country, Mr. Speaker, has been over-capitalization, combinations of people buying up corporations and vastly increasing the capitalization, putting millions, tens of millions, sometimes hundreds of millions of wind and water into the enterprises, and the public have usually been obliged to pay dividends on these vast amounts. In a matter of this immense importance to the country I think it highly necessary that the attention of the Government should be directed to the situation. It is probable that the members of the Government are 124
thoroughly seized of the gravity of the situation; and that they thoroughly understand the desirability of guarding the public interests in a matter of this kind.
It is true that this company is being incorporated under the Joint Stock Companies Act of the Dominion. I learned by looking over the correspondence that the fee for incorporation of a company capitalized at $500,000,000 is $100,000. The lawyers for the corporation notified the Under-Secretary of State that they could obtain from Parliament an Act authorizing that capitalization at a cost not exceeding. $50,000, and they thought that a portion of the fee should be remitted. However, that request was refused.
It must be perfectly clear to hon. gentlemen that the Government have a special duty in this regard. The Canadian people have been exploited to such an amazing extent that were there no great papular ignorance throughout the oountry, I believe we would have had an outbreak time and time again. But the time is coming when an absolute limit should be placed on capitalization.
It may be that the Board of Commerce, which was appointed a year ago, could exercise control in a question of this kind. In fact, a reading of the Act constituting this board will make it clear to hon. gentlemen that the board have a right to take cognizance oif the actual value, not of the capital stock authorized upon which dividends are paid. But the (Board of Commerce, as everybody knows, is at present an impotent body. Its jurisdiction has been challenged and is now being considered by the Supreme Court, and so far as the exercising of its functions are concerned practically nothing is being done.
Although I fancy it is not desirable that I should tell what I have heard about the Board of Commerce and many of the things which have led almost to its destruction, the facts will, I hope, come out a little later on when this House and the country will see how the Board of. Commerce has, as I believe, been betrayed, and the dangerous position in which the people of this country stand because of the private onslaught against that board in an effort to destroy it. Unless the board is made a virile one and given full power to cany out the mission for which it was created, I do not think we need look for any protection in that quarter. It is the duty of the Government, therefore, very carefully to look into this merger and to see that the public interest is fully and absolutely safeguarded.

Parliament is
not all-powerful. It cannot override laws that are higher than those it makea- it cannot override the laws of nature. The effort to adopt daylight saving was extremely foolish because the attempt on the part of a human being to interefere with the sun, to interfere with regulations that have come from a scientific study of astronomy-that by way of illustration-is a thing that Parliament cannot do. Parliament is not all-powerful it is only all-powerful in its sphere of operation.
Now there are certain laws, just as irrevocable as the laws of astronomy, that regulate the formation of a merger, and those are the laws of economics; and I want to tell the House and the country that the creation of a merger like this is only possible in normal times because of a protective tariff, and I am going to prove it from the mouths of those who make it. How does the tariff act, Mr. Speaker? It acts by raising the price of the article carrying the tariff. If I wanted to reinforce my opinion upon that subject I would do so by quoting one to whom I venture to think every one in this House would be inclined to pay attention. My right hon. friend who leads the Government at the moment, once said in this House-he has never given us any Teason to believe that he has changed his opinion, and I call the attention of my right hon. friend and of the House to the 4*cidity and the emphasis of the language-that the effect of a tariff is to raise the price of the article carrying the tariff by about the amount of the duty. He went on to say if it did not do that what would be the use of it. Well, that is a question he might put to the protected

speechtext:
I do not know how far I should be in order in extending my observations on this question, but if I have the permission of the Chair and of the House I would answer my hon. friend in this way:	wages have to be looked at not *
only in the light of the actual money value of the wage, but in relation also to the rent of houses, to the price of what the wages buy, to the hours of work, and to the conditions of the labour. Now I am going to answer my hon. friend in this way:
Every labour member of Parliament in the old country has studied these labour conditions all his life, and his opinion clearly is-because they are all free traders- that protection has done nothing for the wage earners of the United States or they would not want the same benefits as the Briton enjoys. Let me come closer to the question. The cotton operatives of Lancashire, through their trade union, some years ago sent a delegation to the United States to examine into conditions in connection with the cotton industry in that country. They made an examination along all these lines,-the actual money wage of labour, the actual value of the money wage-which is a very different thing, because the value of the money wage is estimated by what it will purchase-the conditions of labour, and the hours worked; and that delegation went back and reported to their union in Lancashire and said: "For goodness' sake, say nothing about the aristocratic labour of the United States." Now, that is the fact, and that is my answer by way of comparison with the conditions in the United States.

speechtext:
My hon. friend must really take my word for the fact as far as my memory carries me. I could not give the date. How could I when I did not know that the question under discussion would come up? I have been studying these
things for a long time, however, and if my hon. friend, while he was overseas as a warrior, had been disposed to take some little time from the castigation of the Germans to go to Lancashire he would have derived sufficient information to assure him of the truth of what I have said. It is an old trick to call upon a man on the spur of the moment to give dates: "Have you the date, can you say when so-and-so occurred?" What does the date matter? It is the fact that matters, Sir.
One -word more, Mr. Speaker. I apologise for having spoken at greater length than I had intended, but I think it is highly essential that we should understand what we are doing. What are we doing? We are increasing the price of steel and iron products to the consumers of the Dominion for the benefit of British financiers. We are increasing the price of transportation by making it more difficult to build railroads; because no one will try to pass off the suggestion upon this intelligent assembly that you can make it easier to build railroads by making steel dearer. I think it is an absurd proposition. If you make steel dearer you increase the difficulty of building railways, you increase the difficulty of making agricultural machinery, and preventing production in that way, you increase the difficulty of making everything into which iron and steel enter as products; you increase the difficulty of developing your country, and you restrict its population, its wealth and its prosperity. I say population because people will come more readily to a country where the conditions of life are good than where they are made bad at least by increasing the price of the commodities they require. Now, Mr. Speaker, I apologise again for having occupied so long a time, but I thought it was only right that my hon. friend's deficiency in the statement as to what the Government should do to prevent the formation of mergers should be supplemented by this economic presentation of the case. There is only one way to deal with the matter, and that is to get rid of a protective tariff.

speechtext:
Before the hon, member proceeds I must direct the attention of the House to the rule, which is very rigid in its application, that debate on a motion of this kind should be confined strictly to the specific subject under discussion. It would be unfortunate if we should have a Budget debate on this motion.

Mr. NEiSBITT: I assure you, Mr. Speaker, I shall confine myself to the question before the House. I am glad that my hon. friend from Springfield (Mr. Richardson) brought this matter before the House, because if the situation is as serious as he depicts it, there may be room for apprehension. I am one of those persons who are not afraid of big business or big corporations. I think that big corporations, as any one who has had any experience with large business concerns will agree, are capable of turning out goods cheaper in proportion than small corporation's, and therefore I have nothing to say against them. I am opposed to over-capitalization. I think there should be value behind all incorporations; that is to say, there should not be a dollar of stock issued behind which there is not full value. I believe that there is a certain amount of value in goodwill, and this depends on hoiw well the business has been established. It is apparent, I think, that goodwill is sometimes as valuable an asset as anything else, and I am not particularly opposed to the practice of issuing a certain amount of stock as against goodwill. In regard to this particular quev.ion before us, I think it would be wise for the Government to investigate the matter now that it has been brought up, and if it is in their power they should prevent the- issue of what is known as "promotion stock." A great many of these concerns are incorporated and sometimes a large .1 >ck of promotion stock is given to some individua1 or individuals for the purpose of organizing the corporation, and fortunes have been made through this sort of stock. Personally I am strongly opposed to that p notice, but if this corporation has value behind it we should not be afraid of two hundred oi two hundred and seven millions of dollars, or whatever may be the amount wh;ch it is proposed to issue, or even five hundred million dollars. I do not see that there is any reason for anxiety if there is good solid value behind the stock and if these people can show an honest intention to operate on sound business principles. The United States (Steel Corporation has been mentioned. Undoubtedly, when that enterprise was organized a lot of promotion stock was issued, but I will say this for the United States Steel Corporation-for I have dealt *with them for a number of years-that in my opinion there is not an organization in the world that uses its customers more fairly. This corporation is highly honourable in all its dealings and sells goods cheaper than almost any of its opponents. In other words, the United States Steel lHr. Speaker.]
Corporation's goods constitute the standard of the market. Others follow where this corporation leads, and no other Corporation can raise the price of goods hi the United States unless the United States Steel Corporation is willing that this should be done; and my experience has convinced me that these people have no desire to raise prices so long as the cost of production does not warrant any increase. With regard to the remarks of my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) touching the tariff, let me say that neither the United States Steel Corporation nor any of the other steel corporations in that country require any protective tariff. As a matter of fact, they have invaded England for the last five years and have sold their goods right undeT the Englishman's nose in competition with goods -produced in England as well as goods produced in Germany previous to the war.

I know that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Nesbitt) has one of the fairest minds of any member of this House and that he does not want to incorrectly state my position. He says that he does not know where I got my information. I got my information from a copy of the British Weekly about six weeks ago. I have the sheet cut out and I will produce it, chapter and verse, before the session closes. The article is written by Sir Ernest Hodder Williams, who has been making

periodic visits to the United States to gather information in reference to this question and who gives his United States authority for everything that took place, and everything that is quoted in the article.
Mr. NtESBITT: What I said was that I did not know where my hon. friend's informant got his information in the United States. That is what I said and I will say that it must have been in some secluded spot in the United States where they did not know what was going on in other parts of the United States where they were working their men twelve hours a day. Some of these men might work twelve hours a day but they get additional pay for every hour < they work over eight hours in all large industries in the United States and in all large industries connected with steel in this country.
I have nothing further to say except that I think it is well that this question has arisen and that the Government should investigate very carefully to ascertain whether there is anything in the nature of watered or promotion stock in this enterprise. If they have not good, solid value behind it, and if there is any way to stop it, I would not like it-to go on. There has been too much of this sort of thing in the past. The public have these great corporations thrown before their eyes, they are quoted other corporations that have paid large dividends and by that means they are induced to buy the stock. I do not believe in paternal government in any shape, manner or form but there is a limit to everything and we have a right in certain instances to interfere to see that the great public are not imposed upon. 'I hope, if the Government have the power and there is anything wrong with this corporation, that they will interfere. At the same time we have to bear in mind that this proposition, as planned and written up, has great opportunities for the future. There is no possible doubt what my hon. friend from Toronto (Mir. Bristol) stated, that we have the basic, raw product in Nova Scotia and Newfoundland very close together and that this corporation with the lowest possible carrying charges and the best possible organization can reduce the cost of steel to a very great extent in this country and can also assist the Mother Country in producing steel as it should be produced. We know 4 p.m. that the Mother Country has been in difficulty in competing with the United States in the last few years in the steel industry. But there is no use
in complaining about that. Those of us who have followed the steel business of the world in the last few years know that there has been great difficulty in England in competing with the United States.

speechtext:
I am quite ready to abide by your ruling, Mr. Speaker; but I was drawn into that discussion by the interrogations put by my hon. friend. If he questions the exactness of my statement as to the fixing of a minimum price for wheat, I am compelled to state that to the best of my recollection the Government last year, if not 
this year, fixed a minimum price, which was removed when the current market price rose above that minimum. But I never heard that the grain growlers asked the Government to fix a maximum price beyond which their wheat could not be sold.
I was illustrating the fact, Mr. Speaker, that big combinations are necessary for the western grain growers, as big combinations are necessary to defend our economic "place under the sun." My hon. friend from Red Deer mentioned a minute ago that such a combination as the British Empire Steel Corporation would enhance the price of steel to the consumer. I think my hon. friend is wrong in that respect. Does he imagine that if we had no steel industry in this country steel would sell at a lower price? I submit, Sir, as a result of the better organization of our steel interests, such a competition will be created in this country that the price of steel will be reduced. I quite appreciate that if this new combination were asking the Government for an increase in the tariff to protect their industry the price of the commodity would be enhanced to that extent. But that is not the question. I do not believe that in connection with this merger it has ever been mentioned that those connected with it would ask for higher protection.

maintopic: STEEL AND SHIPPING INDUSTRIES OF CANADA.
subtopic: THE REPORTED MERGER DISCUSSED ON MOTION BY MR. RICHARDSON TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE.
speechtext: They have got it now.

maintopic: STEEL AND SHIPPING INDUSTRIES OF CANADA.
subtopic: THE REPORTED MERGER DISCUSSED ON MOTION BY MR. RICHARDSON TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE.
speechtext:
On the contrary, Sir, I think that the only way of putting steel on the Canadian market at a lower price to the consumer is to insure the life of our steel industry, ahd to do that there must be combination. We have the example of the United States Steel Corporation,-and* some hon. members have cited that corporation to show how stocks are watered in the United States. But, Sir, if our Canadian industries do not combine they will not be able to defend even their home market. On account of the huge profits made during the war by the United States Steel Corporation their capital investment is practically written off; that is to say, they are so strong financially that they can reduce their fixed and overhead charges to a minimum. Therefore unless our steel interests combine with other steel interests in the British Empire to defend their commodity on the home market and to take their place in the markets of the world in competition with the United States Steel Corporation, our steel industry cannot live. We have coal, we have iron ore, we have rolling

mills-we have everything necessary, to build up a big steel industry that will be able tc hold Its own in the markets of the world; and unless we apply all our efforts to developing that industry, adopting the methods that have proved successful in other countries, it is absolutely doomed.
As a result of this combination I think the Brit'sh Empire Steel Corporation will be in a position financially and economically to compete in the world's markets with the United States Steel Corporation. And it is important that our exports should be greatly increased, otherwise we will never be able to pay off the huge debt that this country has incurred in bringing the war to a victorious conclusion. But how are we to develop our exports if whenever a corporation is organized on a big scale somebody jumps up and says: "Here is a corporation which is going to exploit the poor [DOT]consumer again." The hon, gentleman who preceded me was absolutely right when he said that we should see to it that no watered stock is allowed. But according to the laws of this country no watered stock can be issued.

maintopic: STEEL AND SHIPPING INDUSTRIES OF CANADA.
subtopic: THE REPORTED MERGER DISCUSSED ON MOTION BY MR. RICHARDSON TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE.
speechtext: What about the paper companies; is there no watered stock there?

maintopic: STEEL AND SHIPPING INDUSTRIES OF CANADA.
subtopic: THE REPORTED MERGER DISCUSSED ON MOTION BY MR. RICHARDSON TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE.
speechtext: If my hon. friend thinks there is watered stock in the capitalization of our paper companies, he can set the law in motion against them. But this has nothing to do with the question before the House. I am simply trying to convey to hon. members the idea that we should not cast a slur on any corporation that is organized just because its capitalization runs into the millions. I do not believe that hon. members who have advocated an investigation of the organization under discussion have shown to this House any irregularity in connection therewith. It should not. be blocked or criticized simply because it has a capitalization of $500,000,000. If we want to oppose such an organization we should be able to prove that there is something fundamentally wrong in its formation, but we have heard nothing that would warrant an investigation of this British Empire Steel Corporation. I think that we should give to the men who have initiated such a huge undertaking due credit for their courage and for the spirit of enterprise which they have manifested in furthering a project which iwill surely he greatly beneficial to this country.

maintopic: STEEL AND SHIPPING INDUSTRIES OF CANADA.
subtopic: THE REPORTED MERGER DISCUSSED ON MOTION BY MR. RICHARDSON TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE.
speechtext: Is my hon. friend ware that this merger will acquire practically all the coal deposits in Nova Scotia, amounting to over ten billion tons?

speechtext: This merger will not control the coal deposits of Nova Scotia to any greater degree than they are controlled by the coal companies which manage them at the present time.
