speechtext:
Does my hon.
friend believe that the bringing about of this merger will reduce the price of coal in this country?	'

maintopic: STEEL AND SHIPPING INDUSTRIES OF CANADA.
subtopic: THE REPORTED MERGER DISCUSSED ON MOTION BY MR. RICHARDSON TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE.
speechtext: I think so.

maintopic: STEEL AND SHIPPING INDUSTRIES OF CANADA.
subtopic: THE REPORTED MERGER DISCUSSED ON MOTION BY MR. RICHARDSON TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE.
speechtext: How?

maintopic: STEEL AND SHIPPING INDUSTRIES OF CANADA.
subtopic: THE REPORTED MERGER DISCUSSED ON MOTION BY MR. RICHARDSON TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE.
speechtext:
My hon. friend laughs. I
think I can prove to him, however, that this merger will reduce the price not only of coal, but also of steel. It will reduce the price of coal by wiping out large overhead expenses and fixed charges. The combination will co-ordinate the management of these various companies and wipe out many expenses which are necessary when different companies are separately managed. I think, Sir, that the combine which is now proposed will have the effect of reducing to the consumer the prices of the commodities which will be produced by it. We should not cast any imputation upon any big business which is organized in this country. W e should give credit to business men who put their money into such an enterprise and who invite foreign capital to come to Canada to be used in the promotion of our industries and in the development of our natural resources. We have had coal and steel in our land for hundreds of years; the trouble has been that our coal and steel industries have not been developed to a sufficient degree. The organization now proposed will, I think, meet this requirement of our Canadian industries and will have the effect of offering to the consumer at a cheaper price the commodities of which we stand in need.

maintopic: STEEL AND SHIPPING INDUSTRIES OF CANADA.
subtopic: THE REPORTED MERGER DISCUSSED ON MOTION BY MR. RICHARDSON TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

speakeroldname: Rt. Hon. Sir GEORGE FOSTER (Acting Prime Minister):
maintopic: STEEL AND SHIPPING INDUSTRIES OF CANADA.
subtopic: THE REPORTED MERGER DISCUSSED ON MOTION BY MR. RICHARDSON TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Perhaps hon. members
will permit me to intervene for a moment, at this stage in the interests of economy of time if for nothing else.
The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark) harked back to the old, familiar fighting ground of the national policy and free trade and all the subjects connected therewith. I do not propose to go in that direction at this particular time, though as an old warrior myself in these fields the reminiscences which he evoked raised a bit ot

the warlike spirit in me. But I shall restrain myself until another occasion, and if I restrain myself may I ask the House to restrain itself as well, because just as sure as fate, all these arguments will be brought up again next week when we are upon the Budget,-there now, I have really said something, haven't I?-and they will lose much of their freshness at that time from having been aired in the House on this occasion. So in the interests of all of us I would counsel the House to reserve the particularly argumentative points connected with free trade and with national policy and with tariff rates until we are in the proper field for that work. That, I think, would help us to economize our time and to get through with our business.
My hon. friend from Springfield (Mr. Richardson) was perfectly within his right in directing the attention of the Government and of the House to what seemed to him a danger threatening in the capitalization of a company about which the papers were talking and with reference to which speeches were being made in the country. That company is not yet incorporated. It has applied for incorporation. It can only get incorporation through coming to Parliament for an Act or through the facilities afforded by the Companies Act. Its application is before the Government. The Government are looking very carefully into the grounds upon which the application is made. Before my hon. friend from Springfield brought it to their attention- we thank him just the same for bringing it to our attention-the Government had been looking into the matter and will make a very thorough inquiry into it preceding the granting of the papers for which the company are applying.
I have only one more word to say, and that is this: Whatever may be the extent of our natural resources, we also need capital in this country for their development, and we musit -be reasonable in trying to join the two together as far as we possibly can. Before we raise a cry against the corning of capital into this country we must be pretty sure that we are on reasonably good grounds as to the basis upon which that capital proposes to come in. Now, that will be all threshed out in the application for the papers and in the action of the Government upon the applications which have been made. I do not want to shut off any member from the expression of his opinion, *but I would just place before them the question whether, this m-uch having been said, we may not better reserve the rest 
of our fire until the Budget has been brought down and we get on the old, familiar and much-loved fighting ground.

maintopic: STEEL AND SHIPPING INDUSTRIES OF CANADA.

speechtext: If it is the opinion of the Government that it would be not in the public interest to grafat this charter, have they any means now of preventing the Secretary of State from granting it?

speechtext: If it is found in the course of the investigation that the granting of this application will be prejudicial to the interests of the country, the Government either has means of its own or, relying upon the good sense of this House, it can get power from the House to see that the public interests are thoroughly protected.

maintopic: STEEL AND SHIPPING INDUSTRIES OF CANADA.
subtopic: THE REPORTED MERGER DISCUSSED ON MOTION BY MR. RICHARDSON TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while I appreciate what the Acting Prime Minister (Sir George Foster) has said, I feel that the thanks of this House are due to the hon. member for Springfield for bringing this matter before the House, and that I should at least say a few words on this occasion.
I am confident that the Government should make a thorough investigation of this whole merger. I feel also that this merger should have been compelled to come before Parliament' for a charter instead of going to the Secretary of State and saying: Well, we would rather pay you $100,000 and get the charter from you than go before the House and get it for only $50,000. Then, there is another matter which is worthy of consideration.

maintopic: STEEL AND SHIPPING INDUSTRIES OF CANADA.
subtopic: THE REPORTED MERGER DISCUSSED ON MOTION BY MR. RICHARDSON TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE.
speechtext: Will my hon. friend permit me a question? Why make an exception to the rule so far as this company is concerned?

maintopic: STEEL AND SHIPPING INDUSTRIES OF CANADA.
subtopic: THE REPORTED MERGER DISCUSSED ON MOTION BY MR. RICHARDSON TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE.
speechtext:
This project
is undertaken to bring together several of the large combinations of capital in this country and to make pf them the second largest merger in the Empire.

maintopic: STEEL AND SHIPPING INDUSTRIES OF CANADA.
subtopic: THE REPORTED MERGER DISCUSSED ON MOTION BY MR. RICHARDSON TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE.
speechtext: In the world.

maintopic: STEEL AND SHIPPING INDUSTRIES OF CANADA.
subtopic: THE REPORTED MERGER DISCUSSED ON MOTION BY MR. RICHARDSON TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE.
speechtext:
In the world, that is right. My hon. friend (Mr. Vien) says that they are perfectly justified in undertaking the work. He believes in mergers, in big combinations. He says we shall get cheaper steel products and cheaper rates. Let me call attention of the hon. gentleman to the fact that the very gentleman who is at the head of this merger, Colonel Morden, is the man who organized the Canada Steamship lines into the com-

bination in which they are to-day. What is the Tesult of his merger? It is that rates on our inland waters and our ocean-going vessels have doubled and trebled and quadrupled.
Let us look at these things in a practical, commonsense way. How did they come to make this tremendous capital that they now have and to be able to pay the interest on the money? They claim to-day in their annual statement that they have a capital investment of $44,500,000 and they have a surplus of $6,700,000, and the money to pay our dividends on this has been taken out of the people in the way of excessive freight rates. The hon. member for Toronto Centre (Mr. Bristol) said the other night that a few years years ago the capital investment amounted to $16,000,000. I am not going to argue that point with him today, although I am prepared to say that the bulk of that was water. But the position is that a capital of $16,000,000 of a few years ago has increased until it is now $44,500,000 with a surplus of $6,700,000. What is this same company being put into this merger at? The other day this same watered stock was being sold for about eighty cents because of the profits this company was able to make on account of excessive freight rates, and they place this same stock into this merger at $1; with 45 cents of common stock thrown in, all this being added to the value of what was already watered stock. I do not dare to refer to a previous debate, but it is a matter that is worthy of the attention of this Government.
The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. M. Clark) speaks about the tariff, saying that the tariff has had everything to do with this matter. If he will look into the excessive freight rates that are being charged on the water-borne traffic of this country, both coming and going to our shores, he will find a much more vital question to deal with than even the tariff question in connection with the benefits that should accrue to the people of this country. I might also call his attention to the fact that in free trade England he will find accounts of large mergers that have been lately con-sumated in that country.
I rose particularly to call the attention of the Government to the fact that the time has come when we should investigate these mergers instead of permitting them to say that they have a capital of $207,000,000, and that they are going to put in enough watered stock or common stock to make up $500,000,000. The other $200,000,000 is
nothing but water, and they will compel the people of Canada to pay increased water rates and increased freight rates on steel and nails and everything else that goes into this combination, and they will see, no doubt, that the interest is paid on this watered stock as well as on the other.
It is not my intention to take up any more of the time of the House, but I hope the [DOT] Government will thoroughly investigate this question.

maintopic: STEEL AND SHIPPING INDUSTRIES OF CANADA.
subtopic: THE REPORTED MERGER DISCUSSED ON MOTION BY MR. RICHARDSON TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to have asked the hon. member for Toronto Centre (Mr. Bristol) if, when he was quoting the assets of these various companies, he had gone back for two or three years and taken the assets at that date. He .stated that the assets amounted to over $400,000,000. If the Government would take the combined assets of these companies, say two or three years ago, I think they would find that they have an excellent opportunity of getting .some revenue for the treasury of this country. If the assets have increased as much as they apparently have, the Government have not been getting a sufficient amount of the increased earnings from those companies, and before the leader oi the Government grants this charter, it would be well fox him to find out what the real assets of these companies were a few years ago, because it iis well known to all promoters that you can value, say the coal in a mine at anywhere from ten cents to a dollar a ton; that you can value vacant land or timber limits or any of the assets of this combination at any amount you wish. If their valuation three years ago was $400,000,000 and they are going to put their stocks into the merger at that amount,
I do not know that'I would have any great objection to the combination if it is going to be able to produce something to better advantage than it is being produced now. There is no more reason to my mind why a company should not have a capital of $500,000,000, if that capital is neocessary to do the business than why a company should not have a capital of a million dollars if that amount of capital is necessary. But I do not like this promotion business, and the Government should be very careful about granting a charter to any combination of promoters whereby they may be able to increase the cost of living to the people of this country and keep down the wages, because, after all, when the combination is formed of all the steel magnates of the country, competition for labour is practically gone and the workers will not

be able to change from one position to another if the first position does not suit them. When these people get this combination for the production of steel, they will be in a position to dictate prices, just as the United States Steel Corporation did until prices became so high that other companies were able to produce steel and steel products in competition iwith them. Those companies did that while they were small, and when they got larger, they also formed combinations just as the Bethlehem Steel Company did. This merger is not for the benefit of the people; it is for the benefit of the persons who organize it and put theii money into it, and these persons are organizing it solely for their selfish benefit. That is only human nature after all, but it is the business of this Parliament and this Government to see that these mergers are not oppressive on the people. If the Government find that they have $400,000,000 worth of assets, as I very much doubt-I do not care who the appraiser is-and it they find that the assets have been written *up, say $200,000,000 in the last three years, it would be the business of the Government to see that they get a good fair share of the excess profits that they should have had instead of allowing them to issue watered stock. If the Government find that the assets are absolutely worth the money; that the companies have paid their fair share of taxation during the last few years and that this combination of shipping, coal and iron industries is not going to be a -hardship on the people, then the merger might be all right; but certainly it is the business of the Government to see that, if at all possible, no more watered stock is issued in this country, because twe have had far too much of it already. We are dipping into the treasury to-day to pay interest on w'atered stock, to pay deficits of companies on account of watered stock. While we may not find this company coming to Parliament for assistance, the money nfust be paid by the Canadian people just the same, and it does not matter whether this combination takes the money out of the [DOT]treasury or in some other way. It is the interest of the Government to protect the interest of the common people of this country, and the interest of the common people is not being safeguarded by this merger.	,	*.

maintopic: STEEL AND SHIPPING INDUSTRIES OF CANADA.
subtopic: THE REPORTED MERGER DISCUSSED ON MOTION BY MR. RICHARDSON TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct the attention of the leader of the Government (Sir Robert Borden) and the leader of the House (Sir George Foster) to the point raised by the IMr. Cahill.I
hon. member for Lambton East (Mr. J. E. Armstrong), which point I will present in a somewhat different way. I am a believer in public ownership and public control of the transportation facilities of this country, and that applies to railways as well as to steamship lines. This Government, as a Government, has em-barked-with its credit, with its legislation, and with its assistance-upon the creation of a great oceanic marine. We are putting hundreds of millions into that, and we are intending to put more. We are creating in this country to-day what has been described as the greatest merger we ever had in Canada. I am not raising the question now, in regard to this merger, as to its application to the production of steel. I believe in the production of steel. I believe Canada ought to be one of the greatest steel and iron producing countries in the world; but merged with this proposition to-day is a marine company that we know something of and which has been discussed in this House before.

maintopic: STEEL AND SHIPPING INDUSTRIES OF CANADA.
subtopic: THE REPORTED MERGER DISCUSSED ON MOTION BY MR. RICHARDSON TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE.
speechtext: Would my hon. friend permit me? Did he say he would be in favour of public ownership of water transportation?

maintopic: STEEL AND SHIPPING INDUSTRIES OF CANADA.
subtopic: THE REPORTED MERGER DISCUSSED ON MOTION BY MR. RICHARDSON TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE.
speechtext: Certainly, and we have it now. I hope my hon. friend will not be offended with the information that the Government of Canada is to-day embarking upon the creation of a great oceanic marine, to be allied and associated with the railway transportation of this country and the National railway.

maintopic: STEEL AND SHIPPING INDUSTRIES OF CANADA.
subtopic: THE REPORTED MERGER DISCUSSED ON MOTION BY MR. RICHARDSON TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Yes, but we are not
nationalizing private companies.

maintopic: STEEL AND SHIPPING INDUSTRIES OF CANADA.
subtopic: THE REPORTED MERGER DISCUSSED ON MOTION BY MR. RICHARDSON TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Yes, we are.
We are creating to-day a great oceanic marine which is largely the property of Canada. We have subsidized it, we have put our money into it, we have provided steel plates for it, we have encouraged the production of steel ships in this country. Now I want to warn the Government-and I want to direct the attention of the right hon. gentleman who leads the House to the matter, after what he said to-day-I want to warn the Government to exercise the greatest possible care in connection with this matter. Why should transportation-oiie of the fundamental interests of this country-be mixed up with the production of steel ? Why not limit this merger to the coal and iron resources of Canada? I say there is a menace in this merger in the association of transportation with steel and iron. I only

wish the Minister of Marine was in the Chamber at the moment. I gathered from his manner at an earlier stage of the proceedings that he looked favourably on this idea of a merger iir connection with iron and coal. That may be right, but I enter my protest-as one who has taken some interest in the transportation problem in this country, and I think I speak for some of the Canadian people-against the transportation facilities of this country being associated with the great steel and coal merger. And especially I want to make this prophecy at the present time: One of the menaces of transportation in this country, and one of the great menaces of the big oceanic marine which we are now creating, will come from this steel merger. They will not stop, after their success in connection with merging the inland marine of Canada, until they get control of the national marine that we are now creating; and I want to advise the Government that when they are investigating this thing fully-and they propose to investigate it fully-that they inquire whether it is necessary to menace .the ocean marine that we are now establishing with the opposition of a greater merger that primarily has for its object the production of iron and steel. Of course it will be said "So much the better for the country. I we get a great merger that will undertake to make iron and steel plentiful in' this country and if they choose to go into the building of ships, all well'and good." But I do not like that idea. I do not want to see a company created under the Companies Act of this country to compete with the greatest interest that we have in Canada to-day, that of transportation, without getting that authorization from Parliament when the whole question could be opened up and discussed in this House.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: STEEL AND SHIPPING INDUSTRIES OF CANADA.
subtopic: THE REPORTED MERGER DISCUSSED ON MOTION BY MR. RICHARDSON TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I should like to join with other members in expressing appreciation to the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson) for bringing to the attention of Parliament, and particularly to the attention of the Government, the significance of this vast industrial enterprise which is now being promoted, and which has a possible far-reaching bearing upon the well-being of different classes in this country. If it has served no other purpose than to bring forth from the Acting Prime Minister the assurance that the Government, at the present time, is carefully looking into this proposed merger, and if I gathered aright the words of my right hon. friend (Sir George Foster) that no charter will be granted unless the
Government is fully satisfied that public interests are going to be adequately protected -I think the purpose the hon. gentleman had in view will have been well met. It is to be remembered we are living in an age of industrial competition. It is no longer a matter of competition between one industry and another industry, between one country and another country; industrial competition has now got to a stage where there is 'competition, one might almost say, as between continent and continent throughout the world. The fact that these very large developments are part of the inevitable trend of economic development in our day makes it absolutely imperative that there should be the fullest publicity possible as to the significance and the possible bearings of such vast combinations when proposed in this country. I feel that it is well, inasmuch as this proposal is to the fore at the present time, that gentlemen who are connected therewith, as well as the country itself, should be apprised more fully, than I believe is the case, of a statute respecting combines and mergers which is a part of the law of Canada at the present .time, but which has not yet received the attention throughout the country that I think it should have received. The Act was drafted largely in view of the possibility of these vast commercial and industrial organizations being created in accordance with the trend of the times, and was passed by this Parliament in 1910. It is known as an Act to provide for the investigation of combines, monopolies, trusts and mergers, or by its short title, as the Combines Investigation Act. My purpose in bringing this Act to the attention of Parliament at the moment is that the people of Canada may know it is open to any six individuals who are in a position to make out a prima facie case before any judge of a high court in Canada to the effect that a merger exists which is about to enhance prices or restrain trade, or operate otherwise to the disadvantage of the public-to compel a full investigation into all the circumstances of the merger-into its possible baneful influences

and that the law provides where consequences of the kind are shown, means .whereby the Government itself, of its own motion, may take the necessary steps to protect the public interests.

maintopic: STEEL AND SHIPPING INDUSTRIES OF CANADA.
subtopic: THE REPORTED MERGER DISCUSSED ON MOTION BY MR. RICHARDSON TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE.
speechtext:
Do I understand the leader of the Opposition to say that it is better to deal with the evil after it has happened than to try and provide a cure for it-to prevent the occurrence before it

really happens? Because that is the question at issue to-day, and my hon. friend is not dealing with it.

maintopic: STEEL AND SHIPPING INDUSTRIES OF CANADA.
subtopic: THE REPORTED MERGER DISCUSSED ON MOTION BY MR. RICHARDSON TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE.
speechtext: My position at the moment is the very one that I think my hon. friend has in mind, that namely of trying to prevent evils from arising. I think when the provisions of this statute are fully known they will constitute one of the best guarantees it is possible for the country to have against the possible inimical effects of large combinations. There are evils which publicity will cure much more effectively than .penalty, and the evils arising from industrial combinations are, I believe, of that nature. Now my purpose in making the few remarks I am at the moment is that I would like the gentlemen connected with this proposed industrial organization to understand that it is not only open to the Government of Canada to investigate the affairs of this merger, but that it is open to any six individuals in this country to place upon a board .of investigation some one nominated by themselves who will hold a position akin to that of a judge of a high court and have power to compel the production of documents, summon witnesses, take evidence under oath, and prepare a report upon the bearings of the combination in its social, industrial, financial and other aspects. I believe it is helping to prevent possible evil arising out of large combinations to have the existence of such a law fully known, and it is opportune in order that, on the one hand, gentlemen connected with a large business enterprise of this kind may know what to expect if they exceed what is right and proper in industrial relations, and on the other hand, that some feeling of security and safety may be afforded the public at a moment when any large business development of this kind is proposed. The statute to which I refer is 9-10 Edward VII, Chapter Nine. It was passed by this Parliament in May, 1910. It is known as the Combines Investigations Act, and it Telates particularly to any business in the nature of a trust, monopoly or a merger. I shall not take up the time of the House by reading any of the provisions of the Act. I simply wish to place myself on record as one who feels very strongly that wherever there is any increase in the size of a business organization there should go with -it an increase of opportunity for the fullest publicity on the part of the community and of all individuals who may be directly or indirectly concerned.

maintopic: STEEL AND SHIPPING INDUSTRIES OF CANADA.
subtopic: THE REPORTED MERGER DISCUSSED ON MOTION BY MR. RICHARDSON TO ADJOURN THE HOUSE.
speechtext:
I
have no desire to protract the debate, as the time is approaching when we shall have an opportunity of discussing, in the consideration of the Budget, a great many of the questions that have arisen this afternoon. The matter that has been brought to the attention of the House by the hon. member for Springfield is one which, to my mind, should be given ample attention. It strikes me that the Government are virtually out of court so far as they may attempt to deal with this matter. The company is applying for a charter under the Dominion Companies Act and this country will be benefited to the tune of $100,000 on account of that charter. It is quite true that the company could get a private Bill through the House for possibly less money, but the company and its promoters are not confined to the Dominion Government in their application for charter. They can go to my one of the provinces of Canada, which all have Companies Acts almost identical with the Dominion Act, and this company could get more favourable terms for its charter from any one of the provinces than from the Dominion. So that So far as that is concerned, I do not think that this Government would be justified in refusing to grant the charter, nor should they compel the company to do anything which they should not necessarily have to do. But not only has the company the option of applying to any of the provinces for a charter; it, can go to Great Britain and obtain its chapter under the Companies Act Imperial, which is identical with our Act. And there is no reason that I can see why the company could not go there. The Dominion Government will therefore have only restricted ground for the exercise of their prerogative in dealing with this matter, and the only question which they have to decide is whether op not it is in the public interest that the charter should be granted.
Having paid some attention to the capitalization of these companies-I am not personally interested in this matter-I feel that this corporation is acting very modestly. A great deal has been said this afternoon in regard to the question of values. Now, values are of two kinds, so far as 3/ company of this kind is concerned. There is a value which might mean the original investment, and there is also a value which is placed upon an asset as an earning proposition. The assets that are to be brought into this company are all splendid earners and in nearly every case the stock is paying good dividends. There appears to be good value in the assets, and there does not

seem to be a tremendous amount of watei in their capitalization. But in the capitalization of many companies, the so-called "water" sometimes proves to be very strong. Let us take some Canadian companies. Take the case of the Canadian Pacific railway, for instance. Every dollar of its common stock was watered when it was issued, but those who were interested in the enterprise were confident that they could make that company earn dividends for the common stock, and having stuck to it they have been richly rewarded. The same is true in regard to a number of other companies. I might mention the steamboat merger olf a few years ago. A number of farmers invested their savings in a small steamship which earned 3 per cent per annum, and from that undertaking they were able to purchase a larger steamer, and the year before they entered the steamboat merger the earnings which those people were rceiving amounted to 80 per cent. Those earnings represented not exactly the amount of fixed capital first invested, but the amount which the assets had been able to earn. As regards those steamships, the fact that they have merged has had nothing to do with the excessive freight rates. My hon. friend from Lambton (Mr. Armstrong) if he knows anything in connection with shipping, must be perfectly aware that the war has destroyed a great many ships, and that the freight rates of ships that operated throughout the war, even if the ships made large earnings, were entirely at the mercy of the Government. The earnings of the steamship lines on the Great Lakes were under the control of the Government, as the Acting Prime Minister (Sir George Foster) who was then in charge of the Department might tell the House. And while they have made large earnings, they have increased the assets from time 'to time. I can remember when I first came into this House In 1908, and even as far back as 1900, that the number of iron ships owned by Canada could be counted on the fingers of one hand, but men had faith in the shipping industry and Canadians invested their money until to-day they have a magnificent fleet. The original investment in this steamship company amounted to something like $100,000, and operations were begun with two or three wooden ships. The enterprise has grown with time, and now we see a great fleet. I think that most of the men connected with that fleet are still with this company, and I believe that the interests of the public will be well preserved in every dollar that is put into the new corporation.
With reference to the suggestion that the new proposition is in the nature of a monopoly, contrary to the expressed views of the House it may surprise a good many hon. members to know that the United States Steel Corporation for years have been selling steel at least from 15 to 20 per cent below all their rivals in the United States.
*I hold in my hand a copy of the Iron Age of last week, and I shall quote one paragraph for the information of the House. It deals with a line of business in which I am interested, and I believe that hon. members will be interested in the facts which I shall cite. The paragraph in question appears at page 1262 of this publication and is dated Pittsburgh, April 29:
We quote wire nails at $3.25 base, this being the price of the American Steel and Wire Co., and $4 base on the new card recently issued by four or five of the independent mills. We quote bright basic wire at $3, this being the price of the American Steel and Wire Co., and $3.50, this being the price of most of the independent mills.
This absolutely upsets all the preconceived notions of hon. members who have dealt with this question without any knowledge of the subject. This is only one line of business, and in regard to other lines, such as plates, sheets, etc., that are produced by the United States Steel Corporation, the same proportion obtains. Hon. members may ask, why do not the independents quote the same price as the United States Steel Corporation? The United States Steel Corporation can only fill a tonnage of about fifty per cent of the total market, and the result is that those who are not fortunate enough to get on the books of the United States Steel Corporation for the products at these low prices have to pay the independents a higher price. A few days ago I had the pleasure of going through a number of plants in the United States that are interested in the manufacture of steel. I have also gone through the plants interested in this merger, and I thoroughly understand their situation and know what the possibilities are.
Of all the corporations in the world there is no other steel corporation that would have any greater assets in the matter of' raw material, coal and iron than this will. The United States Steel Corporation have great assets but they pale into insignificance when compared with the assets of this company. What is the trouble with our steel corporations in Nova Scotia at the present time: It is lack of capital to increase their producing capacity. 1 was in a large mill in Youngstown, Ohio, a few days ago where

they produce sheets for the manufacture of automobile bodies. The plant was fully a quarter of a mile long, with mill after mill, ranged like desks with a man working in front of each, and the mill manager told me that they made enough profit for the corporation that owned it to pay for the mill once a month. We have not $5,000,000 or $10,000,000 in this country to put into these corporations. If somebody proposes to put that amount of money into a corporation here a question will be raised in this House or some place else. This corporation will have hundreds of millions of capital to put into plants of this kind to produce sheets. They are producing plates now but they had to get the assistance of the Government to help them before they could do it. The so-called steel cor-5 p.m. porations in Canada may have been wisely managed but they have been up against great difficulties and the greatest of these has been the lack ot capital.
The only question that may arise under the statute which has been referred to by my hon. friend the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) is the question ol restraint of trade. There is no restraint oi trade in so far as the steel corporation ot the United States is concerned. For the last six or seven years the United States 'Steel Corporation has been threatening to build a plant in Canada that would put the Canadian plants out of business. They have projected a plant at Windsor where they propose to expend $50,000,000 or $60,000,000, where they are going to duplicate all our fabricating plants, and the result will be that all our Canadian plants wil be put out of business. In the interest of self protection these industries in the east must of necessity come together and form themselves into one large corporation.
There are other large steel corporations in Canada. The Steel Company of Canada is not in this corporation so far and it is a large producer. The Algoma Steel Company is not of this corporation; so that there are several independents outside of this corporation altogether.
What is this corporation going to do: Great Britain is running short of iron ore and it can almost see the end of its coal measures. Of necessity that country, which is producing finished material in the way of steel, has been purchasing its iron ore, some of it from one of these companies in Newfoundland and some from iSpain, Norway and other countries. But these other countries are adopting the policy of- com-
[Mr Mackenzie King;.]
pelling the British companies to manufacture the steel where they get the ore just the same as the state of Minnesota has taken the United States Steel Corporation by the throat and said: "You cannot take ore out of the state of Minnesota unless you build a plant and manufacture steel here." The result is that the United States Steel Corporation has had to spend hundreds of millions of dollars in establishing a steel plant at Duluth. Foreign countries are threatening to compel Great Britain to manufacture in these countries.
The other great source of iron and steel is India and one of the corporations that it is proposed to bring into this merger is a corporation in India where they manufacture pig-iron cheaper than they can do it in any other place in the world. Mr. Farrell, President of the Steel Corporation, was examined by a committee of Congress in Washington and he was asked various questions with reference to the manufacture of iron and steel. He was asked if the United States Steel Corporation could not manufacture iron and steel in competition with and cheaper than, any other country in the world and he turned and pointed out to them that there were two companies in India who -were large iron and steel producers and that they could produce pig-iron at less than $7 per ton whereas the steel * corporation could not produce it-this was some years ago-at less than $15 or $16.
Bear in mind that at the present time steel is selling for much higher prices than it has been for many years the reason being the scarcity of that commodity. For four years the greatest nations in the world were destroying all the steel they possibly could get hold of and not one pound of that steel comes back to the furnaces. They were blowing steel into the air by the thousands of tons daily and none of it will ever come back. Ordinarily a large percentage of steel used in commerce returns again in the form of scrap but a large proportion of the steel used in shells during the war was destroyed, it was blown into the air, it is now buried underneath the ground and it cannot be recovered. It is therefore not difficult to understand why the prices of steel should be high.
Objection has been taken to the fact that this corporation is going into transportation.
It is well known that the ore deposits are in Newfoundland and Belle Isle and that the coal and furnaces are in Nova Scotia. We are bringing this raw material from Newfoundland to Nova Scotia, we are converting it into iron steel by Canadian workmen

and Canadian capital and we are going to produce the iron and steel of the world. If these furnaces and these plants at Sydney, Nova Scotia, were properly provided with all the wealth of the United States Steel Corporation you would very soon see that their output would be quadrupled-yes, increased by 500 per cent. That is what we expect is going to happen now. It will benefit this country in the matter of exchange. With regard to transportation, if they had to bring the ore from Newfoundland to Nova Scotia, necessarily, they must have ships. Then, they expect to distribute their products to the four corners of the globe, because Canada can compete with other countries in steel products. This corporation will be badly handicapped unless it controls its own transportation. I noticed by the Iron Age that there is a shortage of 150,000 tons of iron and steel in the United States caused by iack of transportation. The Steel Corporation of the United States is dependent on transportation by rail for its ore and coal and these small, petty strikes that are occurring in the railway world are tying up its furnaces. The result is that there is a shortage. This emphasizes the importance of this company being provided with its own ships to handle its ore and finished products so as to place itself beyond the danger of having its operations tied up through lack of transportation.
I think it will be a sufficient answer to the question that is raised with regard to prices to point out that the policy of corporations such as the United States Steel Corporation has always been to undersell its rivals and that it has done so by some 15 or 20 per cent. That is a well known principle to everybody who is in the steel business. The hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Cockshutt) knows that is true. This illustrates the fact that the public derives some benefit from corporations of this kind.
I am satisfied that unless a merger of this kind is consummated now, and all these Canadian companies pass into the hands of a large Canadian corporation, such as is proposed, it is only a matter of five or ten years until the United States Steel Corporation will own every one of them. Just picture to yourself that great corporation with its enormous capital establishing a large plant at Windsor, Ontario. It has its own sources of ore, its own coal and coke, it can produce and manufacture cheaper and with its enormous capital it can control the price and force the Canadian companies out of the market. It is neither in their interests nor in the 125
interests of this country that this should occur. As long as the company looks after the investment of the Canadian people in these mines and furnaces I think we should be satisfied. If this company were buying up these plants in order to close them down or move them to some foreign country, we might very well object, but evidently the intention is to increase the output of these plants, I think we would be acting against the best interests of this country were we to refuse the charter, because I believe in the end the earnings of this corporation will be made in Canada. Supose this corporation earns big dividends on its capital, the production of which those dividends are earned will go into the markets of the world, and every dollar will help to reduce our enormous debt due to the war. And unless we make up our minds to put more money into our factories and increase our output generally-and our manufactured products represent one-half of our exports'-there is no help for us in the future.
I am sorry that my hon. friend from Red Deer is not in his place. He cries .aloud that the rich are getting richer and the poor poorer. Where did we hear that sound before? We have heard this socialistic talk from Fournier and Karl Marx down to Lenine and Trotsky. It is the same cry against capitalism. I hate to think that my hon. friend belongs to the Reds, and I hope we will not hear any more of that bunkum talk in this House, nor any more of that cheap form of political economy with which he endeavours to enlighten us from time to time. If I were going to discuss the question of wages in Great Britain as compared with those in Pittsburg, I could find dozens of books in the library with parallel columns of figures. Here is the Speaker's Handbook for 1919-

Mr. Speaker, I am not
going to make my Budget speech, so do not be alarmed. But in a moment I could quote parallel columns of wages paid in the United States as compared with wages paid in Canada. However, if the hon. member for Red Deer were making a funeral oration he would always end it by a diatribe against the tariff.
I think I have met the objections with reference to the question now before the House. The tariff does not enter into this question, because the corporation will expect to do the largest amount of its business in foreign countries. And the only



way that I can see of putting the products of our great iron and steel resources on the foreign market is by increasing the capital in our steel companies and building more mills so that we can employ more men and produce more materials. As far as the granting of the. oharter is concerned, I am sure that the gentlemen connected with this company cannot but merit the approval of the (House. I understand that Mr. Beardmore, the well-known steel magnate, is one of the directors, and associated with him are Mr. Boy Wolvin-one of our brightest young men-Mr. Elkins-a member of this House-and Sir Trevor Dawson, of the firm of Vickers, Limited. I understand that five of the greatest steel corporations in the world outside of the United States will be associated in this merger. Therefore if we have the principal part of their production in Canada it will all be for the good of the country, and I do not think we can make the slightest objection to the granting of this charter.
With reference to other corporations that have come here seeking charters, one of the greatest in the world to-day is the Imperial Oil Company, which is virtually the Standard Oil Company. It is a Canadian corporation and has expended hundreds of thousands of dollars in" Canadian plants, and has been in every way friendly to this country. Therefore I do not like the attitude of some hon. members who are constantly complaining against capitalists. It does seem to me as if at the present moment there w.as a crusade against our manufacturers. What will this country do, what will our men who have returned from the war do, what will those who cannot work on the farms do if we are going to close all our mills and factories and deny any rights to our people to put more capital into Canadian companies so that they may enlarge their operations and increase production? I cannot see what is to be gained by pursing such a course. I think this corporation in asking the Dominion for a oharter has made a concession, because it could very well have got a charter from Nova Scotia, Quebec, Ontaria, or from any of the other provinces. I used to be in favour of granting charters for the building of railways-not so much for the building of those railways that we have had to carry-and in the old days there was always a sheaf of independent railway companies making application every day for twenty or .thirty charters, and the Government took the money and granted the charters, .the Minister of
	t
Railways usually saying: The Government wants the money and we will take it and grant the charters. Those were the days of free trade in charters. But we did not lose anything by that: I do not think more than 10 miles of independent railroad were built during those days, but the country benefited largely by the fees. And in this case the country will also benefit by the fees. But the men associated with this corporation are, to my mind, men who can virtually guarantee the success of the undertaking, for every one of them is a specialist in his own line of business. For instance, there is to-day no greater transportation authority so far as steamships are concerned on the North American continent than Mr. Wolvin; Sir Trevor Dawson is a man of great scientific attainments and is at the head of the well known firm of Vickers in the Old Country; Mr. Beard-more's name is a household word so far as the iron and steel industry is concerned. In fact, so far as I can see, nothing but good can come from this so-called merger.
The only thing that the Government will have to keep an eye on is to see that as much of this product as possible shall be manufactured in 'Canada rather than that the ore and coal be sent abroad. We should fabricate as much of the steel as possible in this country. The one great province that will need this steel for fabrication is Ontario. .-We have no steel industry there native to the province, but we have vast resources of iron ore which some day will be developed, and we will have a real industry using our own raw materials. The extension of the Hydro-Electric enterprise has made it possible for us to fabricate iron and steel more cheaply than any other place in the world, and naturally we would look with a jealous eye at any attempt to take our raw materials out of the country and give us nothing in return. We suffered for a long time in respect to our timber resources, all our timber being taken over to the United States in log form, and the only beneficiaries by the transfer were the black bass that swam under the logs! Finally that great free trader, Sir George Boss, said the province would not allow any more of our timber to go over to the United States in log form, and that one act conferred millions of dollars on the people of Ontario; in fact, it was the most effective stroke of policy in favour of protection that we have ever had. The same thing is happening with our pulp timber, and if we allowed our friends to the south of us they would take all that timber over to

their own country instead of manufacturing it into pulp on this side of the line. I hope the minister will get a pledge from the British Empire Steel 'Corporation that they will not beggar our manufacturers by taking all our raw material away.
I am very thankful to the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson) for bringing this matter before the House, as I am sure we all are, because this discussion is not lost on the country.

Mr. Speaker, practically the whole of this enterprise being in the county of Cape Breton, which I represent in part, I feel that I should say a word on the subject before the discussion closes.
I do not think that there is such a strong feeling abroad in this country against capital as my hon. friend (Mr. Currie) seems to believe. At all events, that is not the feeling in the part of the country from which I come. We are very well disposed toward capital, but we want to have capital well harnessed so that it shall be a servant rather than a master. I am sure that the very excellent legislature of Nova Scotia will see to it that this vast addition to capital now contemplated will also' be the servant of the people and will serve the same good purpose that investments of this character have served in the past.
It has been said that the capitalization [DOT]of this concern is going to be very large. I do not know whether the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Richardson) knows the county of Cape Breton or knows the immense deposits of coal that are involved in [DOT]this merger. If he did, perhaps he would hesitate before complaining about the capitalization. We have in the island of Cape Breton the greatest virgin deposit of coal, [DOT]perhaps, to be found in the world, and certain features connected with these coal [DOT]deposits aTe certainly absent anywhere else in the world, except possibly in England. We have a deep navigable waterway following these coal seams around the shores of the province, and one can imagine the possibility of practically [DOT]switching the coal into the ships as it comes out of the mine. Across the gulf in Newfoundland there are inexhaustible quantities of iron ore, and, these two elements of commercial advancement being so dlose together, all that is really necessary is the capital to bring about the required developments. No one who has money to invest in this enterprise need be afraid that the natural resources are not there. All that is necessary is proper and careful management to make of 125i
these industries a greater success in the future than they have been in the past.
In the county of 'Cape Breton and the province of Nova Scotia we are not afraid of mergers. There sits in this House to-day the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) who for fourteen years or more fwas premier |of Nova 'Scotia^ Iff 1893 he remembers well that the first real mergeT of these great properties took place in the county of Cape Breton. Through his hands passed a charter which made possible the amalgamation of nine or ten separate coal mines then existing in the island of Cape Breton. These nine or ten small mines were unable to compete in the world, unable to hold their own against big corporations. They came together in the Dominion Coal Company, and out of the Dominion Coal Company grew the Dominion Iron and Steel Company. Mr. Whitney, a distinguished American and enterprising capitalist, was really the man who promoted the merger of the coal mines in the island of Cape Breton. He realized that he must create a market for his own coal, In creating that market he established steel works at Sydney, and the coal which he produced from his coal mines was used in the production of steel. In 1893, 750,000 tons of coal were produced out of the mines; that was the highest notch that we ever reached under the national policy, which, of course was supposed to be the great protector and preserver of the coal industry [DOT]in that 'country. To-day, under that merger, we produce something like 6,000,000 tons of coal a year, and a large quantity of that coal is being used in the production of steel. Recently a plate mill has been built at Sydney in connection with steel production, and now we are getting this large amount of money into this undertaking, which, of course, will produce larger and larger quantities.

There are on the stocks in the city of Halifax four magnificent ships which are to be clad with these steel plates, manufactured out of our own steel, by our own enterprise, and by our own workmen. I am sure that the hon. member will be delighted to know that we have in Canada the raw material and the capital behind it and that those magnificent greyhounds of the sea that are being

built to-day 'in Halifax are entirely Canadian and are being produced by what, we might call a merger of money and influence in the little province of Nova Scotia. These are the results of the eo-operation of brains and capital in. our province.
I fully concur in the point raised by the hon. member for Springfield that we should Keep a tight rein on every corporation in this country and see to it that no fictitious values are held up to the people and that when stock is issued it actually represents something. While agreeing with that idea I submit that at the same time we must give some scope for the imagination of such men as Colonel Morden, who is at the head of this enterprise. Let me say as a matter of history that in the very early days of coal development in the island of Cape Breton the father of the present Parliamentary Counsel, Mr. Gisborne, was one of the pioneers in that work. Then, we had the further development of Mr. Whitney, and now a Canadian who seems to be capable of giving further impetus to this development, Colonel Morden, is taking the matter up. I am sure, Sir, having regard to the magnificent resources at the disposal of this company, the brains that are behind it, and the various elements which are entering into the combine-all necessary to the success of the enterprise-that with proper *management the enterprise will attain that success which it merits, deserves and commands.

speechtext:
If you had let me alone, Mr. Speaker, I would have been through with it by this time. I just want to say, in reply to a remark made by the hon.

member for Toronto Centre (Mr. Bristol), that, speaking of the values of the assets these companies have, he refers, of course, to the potential values. I suppose he takes the quantity of coal, iron ore and so on in these deposits and makes an estimate that they are worth four or five hundred million dollars. But the whole point is-what are these promoters acquiring these assets for?
I think if the amount is placed at thirty or forty million dollars, it will be placed at a very' large sum. Therefore, why should they be allowed to capitalize for $500,000,000, because if they do capitalize for $500,000,000 and distribute stock for that amount, those who buy that stock will expect dividends on that capitalization, and a sufficient amount will be charged upon the output of those industries to provide for the payment of dividends on this vast overcapitalization? It seems to me that such a capitalization as is spoken of is unpardonable. If the capitalization is limited to the amount that is being paid for these companies or a reasonable amount beyond that, no complaint might be made; but the Government ought, if possible, take steps to see that the amount of capitalization is limited.
For instance, this merger is acquiring the Nova Scotia Steel Company by paying 90 per cent in preferred stock and 40 per cent in common stock. As a matter of fact, I learn, by looking up records, that when this Nova Scotia Steel Company was first formed, much of the stock was given away and anybody could buy it at from seven to eight cents a share. A little later on every holder of one share got three shares, and now it is proposed to give 90 per cent in preferred stock and 40 per cent in common stock. Therefore, hon. gentlemen will see just how a transaction of this kind is manipulated against the interest of the people.
I am gratified that this discussion has taken place, and I am much pleased with the tone of most of the speeches that have been made. I believe that, as a result, the people may expect that their interest will be ultimately protected.

On motion of Hon. C. C. Ballantyne (Minister of Marine and Fisheries), Bill No. 94, to amend the Canada Shipping Act (Pilotage), was read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 1-section 434 with respect to the mode of altering pilot rates for and below Quebec repealed as from 12th June, 1914.

I understand the system of pilotage or the laws dealing with pilotage in Halifax and Sydney have been changed. Is there any change in method, or is there any proposed change in method of operating those pilotage systems or combinations in other parts of the country, or.,are they to go on as before?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The hon. member
will no doubt recall that, at the session of Parliament a year ago, I introduced in the House a Bill that was passed giving the Governor General in Council authority to make the Minister of Marine the pilotage authority and to take over such districts as Sydney, St. John, Vancouver and Victoria. The pilotage districts of Montreal and Quebec have been under the Minister of Marine for quite a number of years, and the pilotage authority at Halifax was placed under the same minister under the War Measures Act in 1918. The Bill that I introduced a year ago vested the pilotage districts that I have mentioned in the Governor in Council and the Minister of Marine. I shall be very glad to give further details when the pilotage items in the Marine Estimates are reached, which may possibly be to-night. The object of the present Bill is merely to make a change in the shipping law so that it will be possible for the Quebec pilots to get an increase in tariff if that is found necessary. If we do not make the change that the Bill calls for there can be no increase in the pilot's tariff until the minimum salary of the Quebec pilots for three consecutive years falls below $600 a year. I am sure hon. members will agree that $600 per year as a remuneration for pilots may have been all right a great many years ago, but is altogether too low at

the present time. While the subject is not up at the present time, I am having this change made in the Act so that if it was thought fit in the future to make any change in the tariff with respect to the Quebec pilots I might be free to do so.
What was the average amount received by the Quebec pilots last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The average earnings of the sixty-one pilots in the Quebec district last year amounted to $2,452.30.

Then this Bill relates not to the salaries of the pilots but to the Tates to be charged by the pilots on shipping coming up the St. Lawrence. Am I not correct in that? There is a restriction in the law at present against increasing the rates to be charged ships iby the pilots until the salaries of the pilots shall be less than $600. That is not likely to take place because the pilots are getting about four times as much at the present time, but this legislation, as I understand it, opens the way to an increase in the pilotage rates.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The hon. member is quite correct, but even if it were mutually agreed between the Quebec pilots, the Department of Marine and the Shipping interests that the present tariff of the pilots should be increased-which would mean that their earning power would be greater than the average I have given-I would be quite unable to make the increase because of the existence of the old statute referred to which provides that no change can be made in the pilotage tariff unless the annual income of the pilots is less than $600 per year for three consecutive years. No such restriction as this exists in the case of any other pilotage system, and I desire to have it eliminated1 so that if the time should ever come when it was deemed fair and right to increase the tariff we may be able to do so.
Then it is not intended at the present time to make any increase in the rates?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
No.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

On the motion of Hon. Mr. Toimie (Minister of Agriculture, Bill No. 103, to amend the Oleomargarine Act, 1919, was read a 
second time and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in. the Chair.
On Section Three^The Governor in Council to make regulations.
What regulations are proposed to be made by the Governor in Council?

We have a large number of regulations at present in force governing the manufacture of oleomargarine that were published in the Canada Gazette of February 10, 1920. It is proposed to add to that list certain other regulations, one of which will make it compulsory to have the word "oleo" on each package of material that is turned out-that is printed into the material itself. We hope that doing that will help to keep down the selling of oleomargarine as 'butter as much as possible. In addition, we hope to increase our police work in regard to the enforcement of the provisions of this Bill, and with the additional fine, which has 'been materially increased, to stop the fradulent sale of oleomargarine to a very great extent.
Has the minister considered the advisability of regulating the size of the package containing oleomargarine? ,
The matter is under consideration at the present time. We are looking for a little more information along these lines, and if, after due consideration, it is deemed advisable we may adopt the idea.

It seems to me that the committee is entitled to have all the regulations which have been passed on this subject brought down before it passes this Bill. The measure confers a blanket power on the Governor in Council to make regulations, hut we do not know what those regulations are. This question is a very serious one, not only from the point of view of the dairy farmer, but also from the viewpoint of the whole country. I do not altogether agree with the remarks upon this subject which were made the other day by my hon. friend from Dufferin (Mr. Best), but there is no question that if the dairy industry is injured the whole country will be hurt to an even greater extent. I do not oppose the importation into and manufacture of oleomargarine in Canada, providing the commodity is not sold as butter, but up to now there have been no regulations in force which would prevent that substitution. I do not think that the dairymen of the country have any objection to anybody eating oleomargarine if they wish to do so.

What they do object to-and certainly what the people of the country have a right to object to-is that the public should be given oleomargarine when they want butter.
I have another suggestion to make which may sound rather radical but which I think will meet with the approval of the minister. If he adopted it his troubles would be over and every opportunity of the public being imposed upon would be removed. I would suggest that oleomargarine be coloured by some vegetable substance which is not yellow and which would instantly identify the article. If the minister went into a hotel and was served with oleomargarine which was pink, or let us say green, he would be at once assured that something spurious was not being foisted upon him under the guise of good butter. In all seriousness, however, I offer this suggestion to the minister as one that should be carefully considered. Some people of course might have some qualms about spreading any green substance on their bread, but if the minister encountered any great objection to that colour then he could make it pink. I am putting this forward in all seriousness. People eat pink ice cream and ice cream of other artistic colours, and I see_ no reason why oleomargarine should not be given a specific colour that would distinguish it from butter and would always infallibly reveal its identity. The great importance is that the public shall not be imposed upon, and the minister will be well advised to adopt a suggestion such as that which I now make that would absolutely and for all time remove the possibility of deception in the sale of this article. If you colour oleomargarine in the way I have suggested, that is all the protection which I conceive the dairymen would require or could reasonably ask for, and it is all the protection the public would need, for they would always have the assurance that when they bought butter they were not receiving an inferior foodstuff.

There are some twenty-four regulations covering the sale of oleomargarine, and the hon. member can find them in the Canada Gazette of Tuesday February 10. The proposal to colour oleomargarine has received a good deal of attention, but as the natural fats of the animal are yellow or light yellow, it would hardly be fair to compel those who sell these fats in the form of oleomargarine to colour them pink or blue or anything else while the dairyman was allowed to sell his butter under its natural colour. Even the
dairyman at certain seasons of the year uses colouring to bring his butter up to the natural colour in June when the grass is rich and the butter is of the highest natural colour. As regards the suggestion that oleomargarine is injurious to the dairy business, I do not think that we have seen very much evidence to support such a supposition up to the present time. Some of the greatest competitors of Canada in the British market are those countries, such as Denmark and the United States, where oleomargarine has been manufactured and consumed for years without any serious injury to the dairy business. Our own experience in Canada shows that since the manufacture of oleomargarine has been permitted the prices of cows and butter have gone up higher than ever, and there is a big demand for our butter overseas. Our butter prices in Canada will not be controlled by the manufacture of oleomargarine bu.t, in my opinion at any rate, rather by the prices prevailing in the export market of Great Britain. I propose during the coming year to study the whole situation very carefully. Naturally, I am a dairyman, being at present a breeder of pure-bred dairy cattle, and up to a few months ago I was president of one of the largest dairy associations in Canada. I am therefore heartily in sympathy with the dairy business, but there is a demand for this material by poor people who cannot afford to buy first class butter, and I think that they should be allowed to use it. I shall do my very best, and I can assure hon. gentlemen that the officials in the Department of Agriculture will also exert their best efforts, to enforce the regulations to the limit in order to prevent the fraudulent sale of oleomargarine as butter.
Does the minister consider that the regulations which he intends to bring down will prevent the selling of oleomargarine as butter?

It will to a great extent. In all restaurants where oleomargarine is sold it is necessary that there shall be hung up a placard stating the fact that oleomargarine is served there; and I may inform the hon. gentleman that only this morning one person was fined $50 for an attempt to sell oleomargarine for butter.
Has the minister ever himself seen such a placard displayed in a restaurant?

Yes, on several occasions; and sometimes, I may add, I have been

served with an article that tasted like oleomargarine although there was in the restaurant no placard such as I have described.

If the minister is not disposed to accept the suggestion offered by my hon. friend (Mr. Kay) to colour oleomargarine so as to prevent any possibility of its being sold as butter, perhaps he will accept another suggestion, namely, to prevent the manufacturers of oleomargarine from putting any colouring into that article. As a matter of fact, the grocers who sell oleomargarine also sell a powder for colouring it, so that oleomargarine can come to the table ^ coloured as butter. Perhaps as an additional safeguard to the dairy industry the minister might prevent the -sale of any colouring matter or the putting of colouring matter into oleomargarine.

Under the law now no artificial colouring can be used in the manufacture of oleomargarine. I assure the hon. member that any regulations that are suggested by our experience during the coming year and which we may consider useful in preventing fraud will be enforced.

Would the minister 'consider the merit of a regulation making it an offence to colour oleomargarine after it has been purchased from the retailer? It may be true that the manufacturer cannot legally colour oleomargarine, but in the United States a grocer may sell a pound of oleomargarine together with a package of powder and the purchaser can colour the oleomargarine after obtaining it from the retailer. There is no doubt that oleomargarine is coloured to imitate butter, and in view of that fact I think it is due to the public to provide protection in some way that would prevent the sale of oleomargarine as butter. The man who goes into the restaurant should have some assurance that he will not be given this inferior article for butter. I would suggest that the use of butter should be prohibited in the making of oleomargarine.

I said that the clause in the regulations dealing with the question of colour says that:
No substance intended for the colouring of oleomargarine shall be imported into Canada in packages containing oleomargarine, and no manufacturer, wholesaler or retailer dealing in oleomargarine shall deal in, sell or give away any substance intended for colouring oleomargarine.
[Mr. Tolmie.l

Nevertheless oleomargarine
is sold -and given out to the public in restaurants as fully coloured as butter.
iMr. TOLMIE:	I suggested that I proposed to meet that situation by much closer policing and a closer application of the law as contained in the regulations during the coming year.
Mr. SEX8MITH: Do hotels and restaurants that use margarine have to notify the public to that effect?

They have to hang up a
sign in a conspicuous place stating that "oleomargarine is served here."
Mr. MoGIBiBON (Muskoka): What steps does the minister intend to take to protect the buyer?
It is intended to print immediately in the package of oleomargarine the iwords "oleo."
I do not want to obstruct this Bill but 'I would like the minister to say definitely what objection there is to having oleomargarine distinctively coloured.

I stated a few minutes
ago that the natural colour of oleomargarine, or the fats from which oleomargarine is made, is a light yellow just the same as the winter production of butter, but the butter maker adds yellow colouring to his butter to give it a June appearance and I do not see why the manufacturer of oleo should not have the same right to increase the density of the material he is turning out.
The manufacturer of oleomargarine colours his oleomargarine in order to imitate butter. That is the very thing that the public and the dairymen should be protected against.

He is not permitted to
use colouring substances to colour his oleomargarine but he mixes June butter with it.

Is it -the intention to
still allow him to mix butter with it.

There is nothing in these regulations yet to prevent him mixing butter in the manufacture of oleo for the reason that butter is a higher priced product and certainly a better product and must improve the product of the oleomargarine manufacturer. It would be quite a different situation if the butter -manufacturer were allowed to mix a cheaper quality of oleo in making butter.

On section 5-penalty:

What is the penalty under
the present Act?

Not less than $10 and in this we are making it not less than $50.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

House again in committee on Bill No. 57 (from the Senate) to amend the Industrial Disputes Investigation Act, 1907-'the Minister of the Interior. Mr. Boivin in the Chair.

I understood
that we were going on with the Franchise Act this evening.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I saw the order of proceedings in the hands of the Acting Prime Minister (Sir George Foster), and this Bill came after the Oleomargarine resolution; it was also mentioned in the House last night.

I am perfectly agreeable to go on, but I might mention that the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Angus McDonald) is expecting to leave the city to-night and has asked that this measure might stand over.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He is here.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When this Bill was
last in committee all the clauses had been read and discussed, but clauses 1, 2 and 3 were allowed to stand over for further consideration. The question is now on clause 1:

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Clause 1 was allowed to stand in order that consideration might be given to a suggestion of the leader of the Opposition that the definition of "employees" should be made wide enough to bring within the scope of the Act municipal and provincial employees. Upon reviewing the matter I find that Hon. Senator Robertson, the Minister of Labour, is in agreement with the leader of the Opposition as to the wisdom of including municipal and, indeed, for that matter, provincial employees, provided there is no constitutional objection to so doing. But I am informed that in the past the Department of Labour has, at the
request of municipal employees, appointed boards of conciliation, but its jurisdiction to do so was questioned, and the opinion of the Department of Justice leaned to the support of the position taken by the municipal authorities. Consequently the Minister of Labour does not think it would be wise to seek to invade that realm, because such action would certainly be resisted by the municipalities.

Might I draw ' my hon. friend's attention to the fact that within the last week a conference composed of the representatives of the provinces and of the Dominion, has been sitting in the Department of Labour for the purpose of considering the unification of labour laws, and, as I understand it, that conference has unanimously recommended this very feature namely, that the employees of municipalities and of Provincial Governments should be brought within the scope of this Act. I do not know whether the Department of Justice gave its ruling because the Act was not sufficiently comprehensive to include these different classes; but it seems to me that if both federal and provincial authorities called together for the purpose of considering this matter favour such a course, the Act should be so extended in its application as to include these classes; and if the constitutionality of the amendment is called in question it can be threshed out in the courts. I would be sorry to see this opportunity go by without an amendment of this kind being adopted, because I think it will be a matter of only another year before we will be asked to amend the Act in this particular.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The Department of Justice could not have proceeded upon the principle the hon. member has in mind. The Department of Labour has regarded the Act as being wide enough to include municipal employees, and has proceeded on that assumption. The memorandum placed in my hands states:
The department has in many instances established boards upon the application of municipal employees, such as policemen, firemen, etc. Instances have arisen, however, where municipalities have questioned the jurisdiction of the department to establish a board without the consent of the municipality, which contention the Department of Justice was inclined to uphold.
That is to say, there must be consent by the municipality before such jurisdiction can be exercised. That opinion clearly proceeds upon the assumption that the Act is wide enough in its original form, because undoubtedly the employees of municipali-

ties would be employed in a public capacity by a public body. That would lead to the opinion that it would be wise for us to leave the Act as it stands, in which case the department will doubtless proceed as it has done before-will appoint a board in all cases where applied for, provided the municipality does not take exception.

It would seem to be in the public interest that it should not be possible Jor a municipality to' take exception. Take the case of the strike of employees in the (waterworks department of the city of Montreal during last winter. Had the Act's provisions been applied the strike would never have taken place. The Act is framed with a view to protecting the public quite as much as the parties to a dispute. If we are passing an Act which applies to the Dominion generally, which is for the peace, order and good government of Canada, certainly it should be made to include such a provision. It would be a pity, simply on account of a ruling of the Department of Justice, to forego that extension of the legislation, especially as many requests for it have been made by employees and on behalf of the public.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Well, I will try to put the matter from the legal standpoint as clearly as I can. The Act reads now that "employer" shall extend to and include "public service utility." Now, a man employed in a municipality may be employed in a public service utility; consequently if the Department of Justice is wrong the Act is wide enough as it is; there is no need to amend it. But the question arises, is the Act, even in its present form, not wider than we can enforce?
