The opinion of the Justice Department seems to Ibe that when dispute arises between a municipality and its employees, the Parliament of Canada is powerless to say to the (municipality on the one hand and to the employees on the other; there must ibe no lockout on the one hand or strike on the other until the board that we provide for in this Act has been appointed and has done its work. The municipality .says: We are not created by you; we are not subject to your jurisdiction in this regard; we are created by the province; jurisdiction over us rests in the provincial parliament and that alone. That may foe right or it may be wrong, but it is not a question of the wording of the Act; it is a question of the interpretation of the British North America Act. The Minister of Labour regrets that that is the state of

the distribution of the constitutional authority, because he is of the same opinion in ipoint of policy as the leader of the Opposition; he believes that it would be very much in the public interest if municipalities and their employees could be brought within the scope of the Act.
I rather think that the opinion of the Justice Department goes further than the minister says-

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Possibly so.

-or has a deeper meaning. For instance, policemen in this city are servants of the city, are appointed and paid by the city, but from the constitutional standpoint and .from the standpoint of the protection of the public they are the servants of the Crown. The moment that we .concede that they are servants of the Crown we cannot interfere with them by any statute unless the Crown is specially mentioned therein. If the town treasurer, the municipal clerk, and all such officers are in theory officers of the Crown, that is the reason why the Department of Justice says we cannot interfere with them. Take the simple question df taxes. Taxes due to a municipality are, in theory, taxes due to the Crown and for that reason the Statute of Limitations does not apply. Summonses that issue under this Act for the calling of witnesses issue in the name of the King; the board is appointed in the name of The King. If, then, in theory you are creating a court to which The King is a party, you act contrary to the principle that no person can foe a judge in his own case. 1 believe that the Department of Justice is reasoning on the basis that you cannot make a court which is binding upon The King or (The King's officers or The King's exchequer unless The King is mentioned in the Act.
Do I understand from the minister that the provincial Governments might authorize the bringing of municipalities under this Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No; whatever the distribution of constitutional power is as between the provinces and the Dominion, it cannot be altered at the will of either or both; it can only be altered by amendment of the British North America Act. That is to say, if the authority is now reposed in the provinces, they are powerless to divest themselves of it and to transfer it to us; that would have to foe donp- by constitutional amendment. Of course, all the municipalities 'could agree to waive it and

to submit to the jurisdiction. A great many of them do, and wherever they do we exercise jurisdiction.

It seems to me that this leaves the whole question of employees of municipalities somewhat in the position of Mahomet's coffin, suspended between Heaven and earth. There ought to be some way of providing that this clas3 of employees shall get the benefit of this . legislation and also that the public shall get the protection which this legislation is intended to give in the case of strikes of employees of municipalities. The form in which the minister is leaving the matter is very unsatisfactory. I shall not press my view any further, but I certainly think that some method should be devised of bringing this class of employees- under the provisions of this Act.

Some years ago, when Mr. Graham was Minister of Railways, he appointed a board to deal with employees of the Government railways. This question was up then and it was conceded by everybody that it was simply by consent of the Crown that the matter could be dealt with at all, regard being had to the principle that we cannot sue The King in his own court.

Is it not the case that within the last few weeks a deputation of working men from the city of Montreal waited upon the Government and asked that the Act be so extended as to bring municipal employees within its scope?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not know of that personally, but I think, if they came, they would be in entire agreement with the opinion of the minister which he expressed in this way to me:
While we would be glad to regard the municipal employees, such as firemen, policemen, waterworks men, as coming within the scope of this Act, yet it does not appear possible to so regard them.

Section agreed to.
On section 2-signatures requisite for applications to refer disputes to boards and for statutory declarations accompanying them:
Mr. MEIGlHEN:	This clause was also
reserved, considerable discussion having arisen as to whether or not the unit of employees, a majority of whom had to requisition for a board, was too large. When the subject was under discussion, I expressed the view that, inasmuch as it required only
a majority of the union, and as "union" was defined so as to include a local union, then only a majority of the local union was required. I have, however, (taken the matter up with the Minister of Labour who naturally is more familiar with the Bill than I am, and he has called my attention to the definition of the word "employee" .as appearing in paragraph (d), as follows:
" Employee " means any person employed by an employer to do any skilled or unskilled manual or clerical work for hire or reward in any industry to which this Act applies.
The definition of "dispute" follows:
" Dispute " means any dispute or difference between an employer and one or more of his employees as to matters or things affecting or relating to work done or to be done by him or them.
And so forth. Clause 16 as amended by this Bill will read:
The application and the declaration accompanying it shall he signed, if made-
(d) by employees who are members of a trade union.
If you take the definition of "employee" as found in paragraph (d) of section 2 of the old Act, paragraph (d) of the clause 2 of the present Bill would read:
By any persons employed by an employer to do any skilled or unskilled manual or clerical work for hire or reward in any industry to which this Act applies, who are members of a trade union, by two of its officers duly authorized by a majority of the members of the union.
The intention of the Minister of Labour was, and his contention is, that that means a majority of all the men employed by that employer who are members of the union. That is to say, the unit is the men employed by that employer. If there is any doubt as to that being the effect-and it would not appear to me that there was- it is (the intention of the Minister of Labour that that shall be the effect. All that he insisted upon is, in every case, a majority of those affected; he does not want it possible for a mere minority that may get together at some meeting to be able to do this. But he is quite prepared that the ambit of those affected shall be those in a single industry under the single employer where the grievance occurs. That is to say, his intention is that the unit shall be just as described by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Angus McDonald).

I assume that what my hon. friend says is correct as to the intention of the Minister of Labour, and possibly what he has in view in regard

to his intention thus expressed, is correct. But let me draw the attention of the minister to this, that the change that has been made in the legislation is of an entirely different nature. Since last night I have taken the trouble to look up what was more or less considered when this section was drafted, and I will bring the point to the minister's attention, when, I think, he will see in a moment that the essential feature in this section has been, either intentionally or unintentionally, overlooked in the amendment suggested. Paragraph (d) reads:
By employees who are members of a trade union, by two of the officers duly authorized by a majority, of the members of the union.
The original section is the same as that with the addition of the word " vote." It reads:
Duly authorized by a majority vote of the members of the union.
In deciding upon an application for a Board of Arbitration, a group of men together in a meeting may make an appeal, and if the meeting decides that a majority have asked for a board, the hoard shall be granted. When this law was drafted, it was thought advisable, inasmuch as the constituting of a board was a serious matter, that precautions of a reasonable sort should be thrown around it, and it was thought reasonable that the employees, before asking for a board, should vote on the subject. There could be no dispute, when a vote was taken, whether the majority desired the board or not. By eliminating the word" vote," that feature is done away with and the clause as it reads makes it possible for any two members to go throughout a camp and to request different men one by one to ask for a board and they can get a board if they have a majority of the men without having a meeting called for the purpose of discussing the matter or any vote taken. Unless the minister intends to do away with that precaution which, it was thought at the time of the drafting of the Act, was in the interest of the parties in whose behalf the Act was drafted, he should have made that clear. My hon. friend has said nothing to us about any thought in the mind of the Minister of Labour to do away with that feature-of requiring a vote to be taken. Unless that is his intention, it would be a mistake to amend the law in the way suggested.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I agree fully with t! e leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie

King) as to the meaning of the old law in this regard and as to the meaning of the present amendment. Under the old law, a vote was essential, but it required to be only a majority vote of those who took the pains to attend a meeting called for the purpose. Under the present law it is not the meeting but the majority that is essential; but the majority may be secured if they can secure it, without a meeting at all. Any two officers may get the authorization that they require by merely taking round a peti- < tion, so long as it is signed by a majority of the employees affected. The Minister of Labour is of opinion that they ought to have that privilege. A meeting is not essential at all, the essential thing is that a majority of the men affected shall express a desire that a board be granted; and the Minister of Labour does not seem to fear that any danger or any abuse can creep in providing that a majority is required. He does think it should be put out of the power of any minority to precipitate the proceedings, but so long as the majority of the men want it they ought to be allowed to express their desire in any way they like, and that is evidence that those two men have authority to ask for it. Thereupon the board must be granted.

If that is the intention of the Minister of Labour I think my hon. friend should have so represented it to the House and saved a great deal of discussion. That is an entirely different thing from the reason alleged by the minister (Mr. Meighen) yesterday, and alleged earlier this evening. The essential change being made 'now, as I see it, is doing away with the precaution of a vote being taken and recorded before an application is made.
If the minister wishes to have the law changed in that form I have nothing further to say about it; but that is not the position of the amendment as set out by my hon. friend until this moment.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not think I have changed my expression-I know I have not changed my opinion-as to the meaning of the amendment in the slightest degree, and that being so I could not have changed its substance in the way I put it. It is true that under the new law the majority is always essential. There are two ways under the proposed new law by which that majority of the men effected may express its will. They may authorize, by requisition in any form they desire, the two officers to ask for a board, or they may give

authority by a vote by ballot at a meeting called at three days' notice. The object is not to- do away with the meeting, but to give the two methods to the men, while insisting on the majority. That is not only consistent with what I expressed to-day and yesterday but it is the same thing. 'I emphasized, of course, yesterday, the one feature: I emphasize the other to-day because it happens to be up for discussion.

All these large bodies of men are organized under a local statute in our part of the country. They have their own by-laws and their own regulations as to meetings, and I venture to think that nothing is done affecting the body of workmen belonging to any of these associations except at a meeting where those who choose to attend will have a voice. Nothing at all is done by private canvassing and by somebody going around with a book in his hand to the different members and asking them to consent to a resolution which he has written in his book giving him some authority. I venture to think there is no such resolution in the case of any large body of workingmen, and that if this new method is taken the workingmen, at all events in the part of the country I belong to, will rebel against it and say, "You are passing a law by which you are taking out of our hands a rule which we have always exercised and for which we have organized." They have organized for the purpose of having the united opinion of labour men at a meeting, and assembled, if you please, after they have had notice of what the purpose of the meeting was. I think you will find that these men will not for a moment tolerate the hole-and-corner methods of somebody going around and getting the consent of per-sgns to do things which have not been considered by a deliberative body. I know there is not very much difference between this Bill and the old Act, but personally I complain of the old Act too. I say that the matter should be left open and free for the men to get together and decide for themselves what their position shall be.
Now the minister has given ps his definition of what constitutes the scope of a union. If that is applied to the people in the service of the Dominion Coal Company, for instance, it means something that has never been carried out in practice in that part of the country.- The Dominion Coal Company have a large number of men at Springhill and in Cape Breton and in Newfoundland as well, Now if -the men at the mines at New Waterford say there is some
difficulty which they want to put before a board, it has never been the practice that the employees in Newfoundland or at Springhill should be consulted. The men -at New Waterford got together according to their rules, and passed a resolution as to whether or not they would apply for a board, and that was the end of it. Leaving the Dominion Coal Company out of the question and taking the Nova Scotia Steel Company, it will be found that there are something like a couple of thousand men at New Glasgow in the county of Pictou and five or six thousand men at Sydney Mines. If the people at New Glasgow had any trouble they never used to bother the people at Sydney Mines; they passed their own resolutions and settled their own difficulty. The same thing was done in the case of the employees at Sydney Mines. I can only say to the minister, it would be well worth while to ascertain what has been done in practice without adhering strictly to the legal interpretation of this law. Surely the officers in the Labour Department know how these things used to be brought about. I can say to the minister, I think with certainty, that the view now expressed has never been acted upon in our part of the country when an application of this kind was made.

I do not wish to cast any reflections on the minister or to be understood -as doubting his word in regard to this amendment. I am quite willing to accept his explanation as to what he intends by the amendment; but his explanation of what he intends and the way the amendment is worded are, in my estimation, two entirely different things. The present Minister of Labour may not be holding that position four years hence and the man who will succeed him may place an entirely different interpretation on this, -and he will have the amendment to go by. Now I wish to give a concrete illustration of what I am trying to point out. For instance, the carpenters to-day employed on this very building, we will say, feel that they ha/ve a grievance against the contractor. They desire to geit redress, to have their grievances adjusted by honourable methods, by constitutional means. They apply for a board without going to the -trouble of getting the approval of every member of the union working on the other buildings in Ottawa. But under the amendment there has got to be a majority of that union in favour of making the demand for the board before they are able to obtain it. I cannot for the life of me see how you can place any inter-

pretation on that amendment other than the one I have stated, and that is what I object to. If trouble is threatened among the men on any given property, I contend, it should be the prerogative of the employee's at work on that property to obtain a majority vote of the men employed right there, and if the majority decide to apply for a board the board should be granted. That, I believe, means what it says, but when it comes to a matter of law and the legal profession begin to interpret it, I believe that they will be able to drive a carriage and pair through it. I contend that we should make these things so plain that the ordinary workingman can Teadily understand them. If we do we shall be able in time to avoid some of the disputes that are occurring from time to time in connection with various industries in the country. I am sorry that I shall not be able to remain for any considerable length of time to-night, and I desire to offer an amendment. I move-that the words "of the union" be struck out of line 24 and the word "affected" be substituted theTefor.

I am sorry that .the hon. member who has just submitted his amendment will be forced to leave the House so early, because I think that if he analysed the matter a little more closely he would realize that the amendment to the Act as drafted meets the situation which he put before the House so clearly. The amendment reads: "By employees who are members of a trade union," etc. If there should arise any trouble between any group of employees and their employer it is obvious that the designation here given "employees" would embrace the men who were working for that particular employer if it took in all the members of that particular union. If any members of that union were not working for the - employer concerned they (would not be "employees" in the sense of having a grievance in that particular case. The use of the term "employees" in this connection immediately makes it clear, in my judgment, that the men referred to are those who have the grievance with the specific employer. They are not members of a union in general; they are not employees at large, but employees of the man with whom they have the difficulty. There is very much more involved in this question than perhaps appears on the surface, and very much more than has so far been brought out, and the elimination of the amendment as drafted would strike at the very Toot of what the mem-

bers of organized labour have regarded as the basis of collective bargaining. If collective bargaining is going to be of advantage to either employer or employees it must necessarily rest on the inviolability of contracts made. If collective bargaining is to be of any service to the employees, it will be because they are in a position to feel that the employer will carry out the contract he makes with them. Similarly, if the principle is going to serve the employer or society as a whole, the employer and society must be assured that the employees will fulfil their contract. What would be involved in -the elimination of this amendment and the continuance of the law as it stands to-day P It would simply bring about a condition like this. We will take the carpenters' union, for example, which has been referred to by my hon. friend (Mr. McDonald. That union, let us say, makes a contract as representing all the employees in that particular business working for a particular employer. But after the contract is made a dissatisfied minority amongst these men make another demand, and in violation of their contract, and in apite of the efforts that have been made by the organization itself, they decide that unless they get something further they will strike. What is immediately involved? It follows that if the contract is to be of use the whole union must be bound, both the union in that particular business and the men employed by the particular employer. We have a striking evidence of this in the recent railway strike in the United States, and the same thing is occurring from one end of this country to the other. The efforts of what are termed the "pirate" labour organizations are all directed towards one end, and that is to break down the contracts that are made by recognized bodies of organized labour in order to get an excuse for undermining organized labour as we have had it and as we have understood it in this country; and to attain this end any number of men, without regard to any contract that has been made by their organization, come along and demand from the employer something that is not in harmony with what their own organization thinks they should get, and if they do not get it they declare a strike, such as that which was declared in connection with the railways in the United States, but which fortunately is gradually subsiding. Efforts have been made in this direction in this country, and they will continue to be made; and the amendment introduced by the Min-

ister of Labour-I am speaking merely on the strength of a perusal of the Bill and without having consulted the minister in any way-seems to me to afford a provision that protects not only the legitimate 'body of organized labour, that class of men who want to play fair and who are anxious to protect the workingmen and at the same time to see that contracts are honoured, but also honest employers and the public generally. Unless something like this is aimed at, organized labour will have the very foundation on which it rests out from under its feet. I would urge the House strongly to ponder well before making any change whatever in the provisions of the Bill as introduced by the minister.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for East Algoma (Mr. Nicholson) has given considerable attention, in his remarks, to my proposed amendment to the amendment. 1 wish the hon. member for Algoma, and not only the hon. member for Algoma but other hon. members of this House, to understand that I belong to what the Government of this country, and what the hon. the Minister of Labour choose and desire to call the bona fide labour movement on this continent and that I do not belong to what the press and certain politicians have held up to the four winds of Heaven in the last three or four months as the Bed or Socialist party. I belong to an international movement of the bona fide trade unions of this country. When the hon. member for East Algoma says that we are asking for something that will give to a small, disgruntled minority a leverage over the saner elements in the labour field he is certainly going very far afield. We do not ask you to change one word of this excepting those words which will place control in the hands of a majority of manufacturers, and which will take the matter in dispute beyond the boundaries of the locality, where the organization my hon. friend may be making reference to exists, to soime other part of the country entirely. We are not asking for anything but that the law shall be stated in plain English, that it shall be freed from ambiguity, so that every man who comes in contact with it may understand it without the necessity of going into the courts to get an interpretation, which interpretation may be injurious to his welfare.

If the minister is determined to press this change I shall certainly support the amendment moved
by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. McDonald), because I think it is in the right direction and the minister's is entirely in the wrong one.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: il have moved no amendment.

The minister is amending the Disputes Act. This law has stood for thirteen years, and until the minister came forward with his amendment I never heard of the slightest exception being taken to the clause providing that parties grieved were to have the right to apply for a board and prescribing the manner in which they were to make application. The only reason the minister has given us why he has suggested a change is that the Minister of Labour wishes to make it perfectly sure that the minority shall not have the right to have a grievance investigated and to make it more difficult for boards of investigation to be granted. That is entirely wrong. The whole purpose of the Act is to avoid the grievance of a minority growing into the grievance of the majority and finally into the grievance of the whole community. I am perfectly sure that by the amendment that he is introducing the minister is making the situation unnecessarily difficult and obscure. The Act is perfectly plain, and it is understood by the workingmen and employers of this country. I noticed that the minister in referring to the 9 p.m. amendment last week said it was perfectly acceptable to the employers. Why the Minister of Labour is so particular about it being acceptable to the employers and should make no particular reference to it having special application to the employees, I am unable to understand. It would have been much better to have brought in an amendment which was acceptable to the employees in a situation of this kind rather than one which was specially acceptable to the employers. I would suggest to the minister (Mr. Meighen) that he allow the original Act to remain as it is and not attempt to introduce an amendment which, according to the explanation which he gives to the House, will make it necessary in order to ascertain what is meant by the word "employee," to look up another section and see what is meant by "employer." This is making confusion worse confounded, and in these industrial disputes there is enough difficulty without adding to it difficulty in the interpretation of the Act. I am strongly in favour of keeping the original Act on

the statute books, but if the minister persists in the change I shall support the amendment of the hon. member for Timis-kaming because it is in harmony with the spirit which it was intended should pervade the Act.

I am sorry if anything I said gave the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. McDonald) the thought that I was referring to any particular organization to which he belongs. Such a thought was not in my mind, I was merely referring to the whole principle underlying the relationship that necessarily must exist between employer and employee, if the employee class are going to be represented by bodies of organized labour. I was only referring to the fact that to make contracts between employers and' employees that are worth the paper they are written on we must have some responsible body to whom we can look to carry out the contract that is entered into. The hon. the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), referring to this amendment, speaks of the obscurity that is written into it by the use of the term "employee." I must confess to some little surprise that an hon. gentleman who was for a number of years Minister of Labour should profess any doubt as to what is meant by the term "employee" or by the term "employee" as we find it in this Act. When we refer to employees who have a grievance, we refer, I submit, not in legal terms but in the terms of ordinary common sense, to those who are employed by a particular employer. They are not employees at large. The simple fact that they are members of an organization, numbers of whom may be employed in one particular part of the country and others in some other part of the country, does not make the situation in the least bit different. The organization to which the hon. member for Timiskaming belongs has members, I am perfectly certain, all through the United States. No one would suggest that because these terms "employee" and "members aggrieved" happen to be written into this Act they refer to men who are employed in Colorado, Nevada, or any other section where members associated with my hon. friend may happen to be working. They refer specifically to members aggrieved and members of the union. I take it, as a member of a body of organized labour, that legitimate organizations, such as the one to which my hon. friend belongs, Will not gainsay the fact that labour does look to organized labour to protect its interests [Mr Mackenzie King.]
and that it does not recognise a contract that is not made by a recognized labour organization. I repeat,, the moment you write anything into the law of this country by which you recognize the right of a minority, whether they belong to some outlaw organization-as they are sometimes termed-or not, you undermine the very ground upon which collective bargaining must rest and it is going to be no advantage to the employees whatever. In the interest of organized labour I urge the minister not to make any change in the amendment of the law he has introduced into this House, because just as sure as he does just so sure will a condition develop such as we have evidence of in the United States at the present time when organized labour is going to fall to the ground like a house of cards. That is why I am urging the minister to pass this amendment.

I would ask the hon. member (Mr. Nicholson) if he sees any objection to the law as it stands without the amendment. What is the need for the amendment? I have not heard a single reason urged other than the one put forward a moment ago, namely, that it was to make more difficult an application for a board than it has been in the past.
I never heard the complaint that employees have been taking undue advantage of this Act, and I do not think the present Minister of Labour would say that any such unfair advantage has been taken. I cannot see that the amendment is in the slightest degree necessary, on the contrary I think it will provoke all kinds of difficulties in the future administration of the Act.

If my hon. friend (Mr. Mackenzie King) has not heard of efforts to take advantage of the Act he has not been keeping in close touch with the labour movement on this continent; and if he has not heard of cases of outlaw organizations attempting to break down organized labour by encouraging violation of their contracts, he is out of harmony with what is taking place in the industrial world on this continent. Such attempts were made in Chicago last month, and efforts of a similar character were made in this country last year, and will be made again.
I have not had the privilege of discussing this amendment with the hon. Minister of Labour, hut I think I know his mind sufficiently well to feel assured that he has drafted it with a view of protecting not only our workingmen and their employers, but also society as a whole, and to see m

it that wnen a contract is entered into between an employer and his employees, the labour 'body making that contract shall be of sufficient stability to insure the contract being lived up to until it is amended in the way that is always provided for in contracts of this kind.

I happen to be an employer of labour and have had occasion to make agreements with labour unions; consequently I can appreciate the position taken toy the hon. member for Timis-kaming as well as by the hon. leader of the Opposition; tout I do not think there is anything to be concerned about in the change proposed. Take the typographical union, for instance: It makes agreements with all the union offices in a city. Difficulties may arise in one office; the employees of that particular office go to the union and present their case, and under this proposed law, if their case is good enough, they can ask for the appointment of a board to deal with their complaints, without affecting the men employed in the other union offices. That is my interpretation of this particular provision. But this cannot toe done without the support first of all of a majority of the members of that particular union. Now, if in any one office difficulty arises, and the men go to their union with their case, the union surely will ask for a board if the case has any merit at all. I am also familiar with the coal mining industry in Alberta. In the Lethbridge field the workers in each mine are organized as a union, but in the Taber field there is one union to cover the whole district. If there is trouble in any one mine, the miners present their case to their union, and I think I am safe in saying that under the Act local differences have been dealt with by boards of conciliation without the other mines being affected. I do not see why there should be any trouble about this proposal, for it certainly seems 'to me that if the employees in one particular concern go to their union with a really good case they may rest assured that their union wiill support them and ask for a board to deal with their complaint.

When my hon. friend from Lethbridge (Mr. Buchanan) refers to the mining industry he is nearer to the Act than when he refers to the typographical union, because this law does not apply to the latter except by the mutual consent of the parties involved. The Act relates to industries in the nature of public 126
utilities, and I think that the greater part of this discussion has arisen from a lack of appreciation of the purport of the Act and what it is that this particular section refers to. The Act is for the purpose of securing investigation of grievances where a body of men believe they have a grievance that requires^ investigation. The Act as it stands provides that any group of men who feel they have a grievance may call a public meeting which any one interested may attend, and if it is a union matter that is under consideration it is open to all the members to be present and to participate in the proceedings. If the majority at that meeting say there shall be no application for a board, there can be no board granted under the Act as it is at present. So, to speak of any effort to defeat the wishes of a union is altogether beside the mark. All the members of a union have to do if they do not not want a board of conciliation is to attend the meeting, three days' notice of which is required to be given under the Act, and to vote against the application. All the Minister of Labour has to do when the application comes in is to ascertain:	How
many were at the meeting-how many votes were passed-was there a majority of votes in favour of the application? What could be fairer than that? But the minister proposes to cancel that provision and to take away from a group of men the right they have to take proceedings I have outlined. In its stead he proposed to substitute a clause under which two officers are allowed to get sufficient names to a list which they pass around without the necessity of any meeting whatever, and in that way apply for a board. That is a move entirely in the wrong direction. That is not the way to heal industrial unrest; it is more likely to add to unrest.
When a board has been appointed what are its powers? Those of investigation. There is nothing obligatory in the findings of such a board. All the board can do is to make known the facts relating to the case it investigates. What has any legitimate union to fear by having the facts clearly demonstrated in relation to any matter affecting the men belonging to its organization? The very purpose of the Act is to let in the light, and no body of men are likely to ask for an investigation to expose their own weakness, or to expose some difference with another group of their fellow-men that will not stand the light of day. For the life of me I cannot see why the ministry in the interests of labour and



the interests of the public-and it is vital to the public that no dispute shall develop into a strike or lockout-I say I cannot understand why the ministry should try and shut the door upon publicity of that kind. Assuredly when you take away from men the right to ventilate their grievances, they will naturally suspect that justice is being denied them and that their interests are being jeopardized.
Supposing a group of men in a coal mine, or on a railway system, or connected with any other public utility, want to have a grievance investigated; the company may be interested in not having an investigation, even although a large body of men ask for a board, and it may contend that the law requires that the application shall be made by a majority of the members of the union. But these men have not a majority of the union behind them, at least, it cannot be proved that they have. Then, it will be contended, they have no right to secure a board of conciliation.
The minister referred this evening to the Department of Labour wishing to have the employees of municipalities brought within the Act, and said that cannot be done because the Department of Justice has given a ruling that this law does not apply to such employees; whereas it was drafted with that as one of the purposes in view. *Now he is proposing to add a provision which will make possible further objections of the kind. There has been no difficulty under the Act up to the present time, and it has been in force for thirteen years. The minister is trying to drive through a piece of legislation against the advice of those who have given careful study to this question. Nothing has been put before the committee to justify the adoption of the proposed amendment at this time. This Act is a bit of legislation that the Dominion has reason to be proud of and around which we should wish to establish every safeguard. .Believing that, I for one do not want to see the workingmen lose their confidence in this Act because of the involved nature of the provisions which form part of it.
If the leader of the Opposition knew a little more about the practical side of the operations of organized labour and perhaps a little less about the theoretical side, he would take a different view.

Oh, oh.
'Some hon. MEMBERS:	Order.

Ask the member for Timiskaming.
[Mr Mackenzie King:.]

I have said
nothing that I am called upon to take back. I say that if the leader of the Opposition knew more about the practical working of bodies of organized labour, and less, perhaps, about the theory, he would take a different view. Bodies of organized labour do not work just in the way that my hon. friend has stated. They have a very clear and definite line of action in dealing with matters of this kind they never have any difficulty in showing to employers or to the ^Government or to the public whether a majority of their members are behind any particular position which they take. The Act provides for what must be done by every regularly constituted body of organized labour in this country before they can reach the point where they ask for a board of conciliation. Every man who is or has been associated with organized labour knows perfectly well what a board of conciliation means. It is not a board of arbitration; it is simply a board of conciliation; "a board created for the purpose of finding out what is in the minds of employees on the one hand and employers on the other; to show up to the public, if you will, who is right and who is wrong, and then to let public opinion be the final arbiter. Take the case of locomotive engineers on any of our railways. Does my hon. friend think that upon two or three or four days' notice any one of these bodies may call a meeting and ask for a board of conciliation to inquire into any specific grievance, and that that is going to be the end of it? Not at all; they have a constitutional course to follow, and they have not completed that constitutional course until they have taken steps to do just what this Act provides, that is, get the opinion of the majority of their members. All that is aimed at in the amendment introduced by the Minister of Labour is simply this: to provide that after a recognized body of organized labour representing employees have entered into a contract with an employer, that contract will stand until the majority of the members employed by that particular employer determine that it should be changed. If the contention of my hon. friend is correct, what follows? A small group, four or five if you will, of these men located at any one point may ask to have the contract abridged or changed, and if their desire is not acceded to they may go to the Department of Labour and ask for a board of conciliation. They get the board of conciliation, and the employer says: I am not going to meet this board; I have a contract with the majority of my employees and I am going to stand by that

contract. Then the employer is held up to the odium of the people from one end of this country to the other; is looked upon as a man who does not want to meet his employees on a fair basis. I am confident that the Minister of Labour knew what he was doing when he drafted that clause. If it means anything, it is designed to protect organized labour; to make the contract that organized labour enters into of some use, of some service, not only to one employer or employee, but to the public in the way of protecting them against illegal strikes. Its purpose is to provide that when a minority in any group of employees make up their mind that they are not going to stand by a contract made with an employer the public will know that they are out of harmony with the organization which made the contract in the first place.

Was this proposed
change in the law asked for by any labour organizations? I have not heard of any labour union or other large body of organized labour that has asked for it. My hon. friend (Mr. G. B. Nicholson) seems to be strongly in favour of it. So far as I know, when a contract is made by a trade union with employers it usually stands. Of course, employers, if they are strong enough and if economic conditions change very largely, will not respect the contract any more than anybody else; that has often been the experience in the past. You may say that the same things happens so far as trade unions are concerned. It may be, but numerically the position of the employer is quite different from the position of the trade unions. During the last two or three years contracts between large associations of employers and small associations of employees have been broken, by direct or by indirect means, when conditions generally have changed. I do not see how the amendment is going to improve that situation; it may simply make things more difficult for the workingmen. My hon. friend seems to lay great stress on the assumption that the effect of the amendment may be at a certain moment to break up a trade union movement. He says there is a certain way to go about it; that the trade unions have to meet before they can take a vote. Well, the constitutions of these organizations set forth the manner in which they are supposed to take a vote. No trade union to-day will take a vote on a matter of such importance as a strike without first having notifications sent to all members. In fact, the principle of the amendment is already recognized among most of the trade unions. Further, a secret 126i	,
ballot is taken, and then if the majority are in favour of doing so, they will ask for a board. If this law were to apply to municipal employees, for instance, the case would be different. But the trade unions have been well taken care of so far as these boards are concerned. We do not want to make it difficult for them to obtain these boards. If we want to safeguard the interests of the trades and labour movement we want to throw just as much light on their operations as we can.
They have nothing to hide. A trade' union that has anything to hide should dissolve right away. While I admit that the present law may not have always given entire satisfaction, at the same time it has not, so far as I know, prevented in any case the granting of a board provided that the matter came under the rules and regulations of the board. Let us have as much light as we can, because under this change in the law a small group would be prevented from asking for a board, and there are ways by which the matter can be worked out in the trade union itself, ways which may be dangerous, in preventing the asking for a board. If you leave the law as it stands, the matter is wide open; the labour men of this country understand the Act well, because they have used it for many years, and the employers also understand it. Have any trade unions aAed the Government to make this change? If they have not done so, this request must have come from the other side, and if so, I am very doubtful whether the change will be in the interest of trade unions.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have not addressed the committee, since the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. McDonald) moved his amendment. In the interval we have had some addresses from the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) and another now from the hon. member for St., Denis (Mr. Verville). I can follow very ' clearly the desire and also the reasoning of the hon. member for Timiskaming; but for the life of me I am not able to follow either the reasoning or the desire of the leader of the Opposition, nor the purpose of the hon. member for St. Denis unless his purpose is to follow, as closely as he can understand it, the course outlined and pointed out by his leader.
That is a very fair remark for the minister to make.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Very fair, I am quite certain it is. I could only learn from the hon. member that he desired to be on the

same ground as t'he leader of the Opposition, and his leader's ground being somewhat confused, I am sorry to say his was confusing to me as well. I will point out what I mean. The Act as it has stood all these years, has been in this form, that in the case of employees, members of a trade union, desiring a board, they, might secure that board by getting a majority vote at a meeting called, as the Act provides on three days' notice and specifying the purpose. The Act as it will read if this amendment passes, will call for a majority in every case, though that majority may not express itself at a meeting; it may express itself by petition or otherwise, authorizing two of its officers to demand a board. Under the old law a meeting was necessary; a majority of the meeting was necessary; but a majority of the members, whether of the employees, or of the union, was not necessary at all. Under the new Bill, a majority of the members of the union will be necessary. The hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. McDonald) moves in amendment to the new Bill that "a majority of the members affected" shall be the words employed instead of ''a majority of the members of the union." As I tried to make clear at the opening of the discussion this evening, the Minister of Labour has taken the view-and I think he is right-that all along, under the old Act and now under this Bill, the effect is just the same, because under the definition of the word "employee," the word "employees" must mean the employees of an employer, and consequently a majority of those employees is sufficient. That has been the practice under the Act; I havff not heard the minister say that it was the practice previously to his coming into office, but I believe that to be the case, and certainly that is the present practice of the Department of Labour. If we take that view, the amendment moved by the hon. member for Timiskaming is only another way of expressing the effect which the Minister of Labour intends by this amendment. If the provision as I introduce it does not mean what the hon. member for Timiskaming wants it to mean; if it calls for a majority of the whole union, however wide, and not a majority of the members of the union, employees of the employer where the grievance is, then the old Act did not mean that either, for the very same words are used. The old Act reads:
A majority vote of the members of the union.
So the old Act must have meant that it must be a majority vote of all the members
[Mr. Meighen.j
of the union altogether. Under the old Act all may not go to the meeting, but all had a right to go, and indeed that is what the leader of the Opposition argues. Therefore, members of the union employed in industries that were not affected at all and that had no grievance, could go to the meeting and outvote members of the union who had a grievance, being employed in the particular industry where the grievance arose. Therefore, if there is need for a Change in the provision which I have introduced, there was the same need as regards the Act when it was passed into law in 1907. Consequently I am a little confused when I am urged on the one hand to leave the law as it is and by the very same hon. gentleman to accept the amendment moved by the hon. member for Timiskaming, because if I leave the law as it is, there is just the same need of the amendment of the hon. member for Timiskaming as there is if I bring in this amendment to-night. That is why my confusion exists.
. Mr. MACKENZIE KING: You are changing it.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I am changing it in another regard, so as to require in every case a majority of the employees, members of the union, in the industry affected. The Minister of Labour says: Leave the words as they are; then a majority of those employed by a single employer may demand a board and get it. That is what the hon. member for Timiskaming wants to make more clear. That being the case, there is no reason for refusing the amendment of the hon. member for Timiskaming.
Mr. VKRV1LLE: I am not refusing it.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I know that, but what confuses me was an urging on the one hand to leave the law as it is and an urging by the same hon. member to accept the amendment of the hon. member for Timiskaming. The two things are utterly inconsistent,- and I do not think I was unfair in saying that I was confused by any one taking that position.	.
Before I refer to another phase of the discussion, let me re-emphasize what I tried to make clear a minute ago. I know this is a question of interpretation and questions of interpretation are always more or less difficult to expound. Under the new Bill, members of the union must always have a majority to demand a board. Under the old Act, they did not need to have a majority; all that they required was a majority vote at a meeting, and that might be only one-fifth

of the employees, members of the union, concerned. That is the essential difference. There is no difference in any other regard than that under the new Bill it will not be necessary to express in the notice calling the meeting, the purpose of the meeting. The minister does not think that is necessary, because when you demand a majority, he is not particular how the meeting is called; as long as he is sure that a majority of the men affected wants a hoard, then he is ready to grant a board, no matter how the majority expresses its desires. The leader of the Opposition says:	There
is no need for this amendment at all; the law as it stood was fine. My hon. friend regards the old Act as an Ark of the Covenant. I can understand that one has some particular regard for a piece of work of his own creation. But the difficulty is this:	In the Grand Trunk
Railway Company to-day, for example, there are four different organizations demanding to he known as "the union," and demanding jurisdiction in this regard. While that exists the necessity for a majority is only too apparent. The minister does not care which it is so long as he knows that he has a majority of the men affected asking for that hoard. But the one disputes the right of the other; the other disputes the right of the one, and there it stands. Not only does the Minister of Labour want that situation cleared up, but organized labour wants it cleared up. I was sorry to hear the intimation from the hon. member for St. Denis (Mr. Verville)-particularly because I know he has confidence in the present Minister of Labour, just in the relation in which he expresses suspicion tonight-I was sorry to hear the intimation that this was something demanded by employers and not wanted by employees at all. Now the Minister of Labour informs me, on the other hand, that this very amendment has been approved by the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada who have recognized the difficulty under which he labours-has been approved by them through their executive-and that is the approval which comes to this House. Now that surely should convince the hon. member at least that there is some need for the amendment, and should convince him still more emphatically that it is not designed to assist employers-it is only designed to make the Act more workable and to remove the difficulty that now is pressing for amendment. To show that there is no objection to the amendment moved by the hon. member for Timiskaming, I would
suggest that the approval be by a majority of union members, and having it read:
by a majority of the union members affected.
It was just to make clear that this covers the case of union members. I do not know that it is essential but I think it would be clearer that way, and that is the opinion of the Minister of Labour. It does not change, in our opinion, the effect of the Act as it reads, but it will at all events make clear to him and certainly makes very clear to everyone the purpose of that section -perhaps clearer than it is. Consequently there is no objection to the amendment. But let me add again, if it is necessary to make the language in the Bill clear it was just as necessary to make clear the language of the old Act as it existed, because the words in the present Bill, even if they are obscure, were the same words as were used in the old Act.

May I ask the minister whether, in the event of the majority of the members of a local organization voting that a board be named they will have the privilege of selecting imembers from another organization-for instance a district organization or a national organization- to represent them?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not so understand the Act, if I apprehend the question rightly. Any two officers of the union may be authorized by the members of the union affected, but not two officers of any union.
What I mean is this: Supposing the majority of the members of ' a local organization select two officers of the district organization or a national organization to represent them.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.

Could they do it
under this?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I would say so, if they are members of the same union. Do you mean that the two officers could ask for a board, or the appointment of an officer on the board?

The local union may be asking for a board and they may ask, for instance, that the members of another organization-that is to say members of the district or national organization-represent them instead of the two officers who may be members of the local organization that are selected.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
This clause has nothing to say at all as to who shall act on the

board. That is governed by other clauses of the Act that are not at all affected by this Bill.
Before the clause carries may I ask the minister, who is to decide the question as to whether or not there has been a majority as required by the Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That will be decided just as previously. Previously the minister would be compelled to decide whether or not a majority had voted at the meeting. Now the minister will have to decide whether or not there is a majority either at the meeting or expressed in any other way.

I would point out to my hon. friend that the Act as originally drafted took care of that by providing that when a vote was taken on the question of an application to the board a record should be kept of it. Thus there was something on record for the minister to refer to. That provision has been struck out of the present Bill, and I think it is going to lead to a lot of confusion.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is no call for a record.

The minister said he could not understand how one could support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Timiskaming, and at the same time see any difference between this Bill and the old Act. Let me read the section in the old Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I did not say that. I said I could not understand the argument that the old Act was all right and also the argument from the same person that the amendment of the hon. member for Timiskaming was necessary under this Bill.

The present Bill is departing from the feature in the old Act which gave, upon a majority vote, the right to have a board. Let me read the provision to which I refer:
-if made by employees some or all of whom are not members of a trade union, shall be signed by two of their number, duly authorized by a majority vote taken by ballot of the employees present at a meeting called on not less than three days' notice for the purpose of discussing the question.
Let any group of men who are affected by a dispute call for a meeting and the majority of those affected are entitled to a board by voting at that meeting. That is the principle which ought to be maintained,

and that is the principle which my hon friend from Timiskaming has asked to have recognized by proposing the amendment which he suggested to-night.

Amendment agreed to.
Mr. MACKENZIE. KING: Is the minister aware that the clause as introduced leaves out a very important amendment which was made-to this part of the Act in 1910 at the request of the railway employees of this country? It looks to me as though in the drafting of this particular measure the original Act has been before the minister but not the amendment of 1910. I would ask the minister if his attention has been drawn to the following clause, which is in the Act as it now stands and which was inserted as an amendment in 1910:
-or, where a dispute directly affects employees in more than one province and such employees are members of a trade union having a general committee authorized to carry on negotiations in disputes between employers and employees and so recognized by the employer, a statutory declaration by the chairman or president and by the secretary of such committeeand so forth. I may say that that amendment to the Act was introduced at the time I was Minister of Labour at the request of the railway employees. The employees of the Grand Trunk and the employees of the Canadian Pacific railway requested that amendment should be inserted, and the matter was taken up with the officers of the railway companies. They were wholly agreeable that in the case of the railway organizations it would be quite sufficient to apply for a board, to have the officers of the organization make the application and not necessitate a ballot of the members of the railway brotherhoods in order to get a board. That is a most important amendment, and I think is one that is valued by the railway employees. Unless the minister is prepared to throw it out altogether I think it ought to remain as part of the Act. Nothing has been said by the minister presenting the amendment with reference to leaving out this rather important feature.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. member is right in the assumption that my attention had not been called to that amendment of 1910. I have just received an intimation that the amendment added in 1910 is not affected at all by the amendment now proposed. It does not appear clear to me that such is the case. I would suggest that the section stand; I should like to look into the point raised.
Section stands.

On section 3-clerical correction consequent on amendment of section 16:

This simply
corrects some errors in the previous legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Not errors, just corrections necessitated by the passing of clauses 1 and 2.

Well, the copy of the Bill I have bears the following marginal note:
Clerical correction consequent on amendment of section 16.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, but not any correction of errors in the legislation.
Section agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I move that the committee rise, report progress and beg leave to sit again. .
Motion agreed to, and progress reported.

The House resumed from May 3rd consideration in committee of Bill No. 12 (Hon. Mr. Guthrie) respecting the election of members of the House of Commons and the electoral franchise.-Mr. Boivin in the Chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
When progress was
reported upon this Bill on Monday evening, all of the clauses and schedules had been read and considered. Clauses 2, 19, 28, 29, 30, 32, 33, 37, 44, 63, 76, 100 and 101; the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) to clause 28; the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Turgeon) to clause 37; the amendment proposed by the hon. the Acting Solicitor General (Mr. Guthrie) to clause 44; and several forms of schedules to the Bill, had been allowed to stand for further consideration. The other clauses and forms had been adopted. Clauses 19 and 76 which provide for the expenditure of money by the Government await the approval of the House of the required resolution. Clause 2 is being considered paragraph by paragraph. We have reached paragraph (b).	Shall this paragraph
carry?

There is in paragraph (b)
a bad inversion which I think makes the sense obscure and ambiguous. The paragraph as it is woTded reads:
" Candidate " or " candidate at an election ' includes any person elected to serve in the House of Commons of Canada at an election.
I move to strike out the words " at an election" in the eighth line of paragraph (b) and put them in the seventh line after the word " elected " so that the paragraph may read:
" Candidate " or " candidate at an election " includes any person elected at an election to serve in the House of Commons of Canada.
This would make the sense very much clearer in my opinion.
'Mr. GUTHRIE:	I do not think it improves it at all. The paragraph is just as clear now as it would be if the words were transposed as suggested.
Why are the words " at an election" necessary at all?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: They have been considered necessary for a great many years. We have not changed the language of the old clause.

Are not these words
redundant?
Mr. DuTREMBLAY: I think it is important to retain these words. Sometimes a man is chosen as a candidate a long while before an election, and yet, under the law, he might not be a candidate at the time of the election. A man is considered a candidate only from the moment the writs are out.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
That has no reference
to the object of the words. For the purposes of the controverted Elections Act, a man who has been elected is still properly described as a " candidate;" and for the purposes of this Act, so far as improper or illegal conduct at an election is concerned, he is still to be regarded as a " candidate." The fact that he has been elected does not relieve him of the obligations that are binding on candidates.
Amendment negatived; paragraph agreed to.
On paragraph (d)-"during an election" -"at an election "-" throughout an election."

I move that the following words be struck out:
__or the occurrence of a vacancy in consequence
of which a writ for an election is eventually issued.
We have two classes of elections, general elections and by-elections. Paragraph (d) provides that "during an election" or " at an election " or " throughout an election" shall include the period after the

issue of the writ or after the dissolution of Parliament. The period of a general election begins after the dissolution of Parliament and that of the by-election after the issue of the writ. If a seat becomes vacant to-day the election can be held inside of six months, and whatever may be the length of time before the election is brought on will be deemed, according to this clause, to be the period " during an election," "at an election," and " throughout an election." I think that the period between the occurrence of the vacancy and the time when the elected candidate is returned as elected should be given a reasonable limit.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
These clauses have been prepared by very expert draftsmen and unless there is some good reason for a change I do not see any object dn changing them. My hon. friend thinks that six months is too long a period for a man to be a candidate. From the time the seat becomes vacant until an election must be held, by reason of an Act passed by this House, six months is the longest period that can intervene. In my judgment it is a very salutary provision. If a seat does become vacant we generally hear certain announcements that this man or that man is going to be a candidate. Very often before a vacancy has occurred candidates have been practically, although not formally, nominated. The clause is inserted to prevent corrupt or illegal practices during or after the election and the question is; when is a man supposed to. be a candidate? or: when does the period at or during an election commence and when does it end?
I think it is a very reasonable definition, and unless there is very good reason I would not like to change it. My hon. friend simply proposes that we shall strike out three lines of the section. 10 p.m. That is not very much of a reason in my judgment and I do not think he gave any 'reason to the committee.
The only reason is that according to this section an election is liable to last for six months and over.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: It might last for more than that when there 'is a general election after a dissolution.
It would be an abuse of power to have a general election last for six months.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Not at all. If the House should dissolve to-day and an election were 
held in the fall, it would not be an abuse of power.

The Acting Solicitor General claims that because this Act has been drafted by competent men we should adduce very good reasons for wishing to change it and that we are practically guilty of an offence if we do not agree to it. If I understand my hon. friend (Mr. Denis) his point is this: A vacancy occurs and suppose that a man has been chosen dn a county to run in the interest of one party. He becomes a candidate. For six months he can be spied upon and watched, to see what he is doing, whilst the other man may be nominated only on the eve of the election. His nomination as a candidate would not have any retroactive effect, and he could not be charged with having done anything that might be improper. In that way the candidate who had been in the field six months would be at a disadvantage. The early nomination would put him at a disadvantage over the other fellow who was nominated later.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is the early bird that gets caught.

He would not get the worm this time; it would work against him. Of course we are not supposed to commit any of these illegal acts, but if men are to be charged with things of this kind they should be put upon an equal footing and the time should be restricted to the period dating from the issue of the writs.
In what respect does the proposed section differ from the present Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think there was a definition in the former Act. The courts in Ontario have decided that so long as a man announces himself a candidate, the question of time is of no consequence.
The question has been up more or less frequently in litigation, and that is what caused me to make the inquiry.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
In our courts it has been held repeatedly that there is no limitation of time. Our (responsible officials suggest this change as a limitation which would be reasonable. When a vacancy does occur the public is aware that there is going to be an election-there is bound to be one within six months-and if people announce themselves as candidates they should be held responsible for the conduct

of the election. There is no disadvantage as between the two candidates. One may get the nomination on nomination day.
On moral grounds, no, but on practical grounds, yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: He may have no thought of running till nomination day. The other man may have been six months in the field. We assume that every man is conducting a proper and regular election. What disadvantage can it be to a man who happens to be in the field for six months.
Six months is a long time to remain in purgatory.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I have been longer than that.
Amendment (Mr. Denis) negatived, and paragraph agreed to.
On paragraph (e)-election officer:

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I move that, after the words "Chief Electoral Officer" at the end of line 25, the words "Assistant Chief Electoral Officer" be added.
Amendment agreed to.
Does this paragraph include the officials who would have charge of the advance polls?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, it includes every official who is required to take the oath. The election officer is included in this section, those who attend the advance polls and all who are under oath.

In view of the explanation given by the hon; gentleman and of the language in the last line of this subsection, may I inquire if there are any other officials provided for in this Act who will not be sworn to the faithful performance of their duty?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: No, I think they are all included in this. Every officer, as far as I am aware, has to be sworn.
Is it the intention of the minister that no officers but those mentioned in subsection (e) are to be sworn?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: No, I did not say that. I said that every officer who is sworn is mentioned.
Why not make it "having any duty to perform?"

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: There might be a constable called in to quell a riot and I do not suppose he is sworn. There is a special provision for such.

I move that paragraph (e) be amended by adding after the words "poll clerk" in the twenty-seventh line the words "registrar, revising officer"-those being the two officials left out, probably owing to this section having been taken from the old law which did not contemplate these new officials. I understand that the registrar and the revising officer are on the same footing as the election clerk, deputy returning officer and poll clerk, and, if so, they should be included in the section.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think there is any necessity to include them. The revising officer, if a judge, is not sworn (because he has taken his oath of office as a judge. The registrar and any one else who has to do with enumeration or revision have to be sworn.
The revising officer must be sworn.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, and the oaths are provided in every case, as are also the penalties.

"Returning officer" is
mentioned in clause (e).

Since the minister has just mentioned that the registrar has to be sworn, surely his name should appear in the nomenclature of officers. If there is any objection to including the revising officer let us leave him out, but surely the registrar should be included as he is in the same category as the deputy returning officer, the poll clerk, and so on.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I suppose the constables and scrutineers should appear too, but the clause is general enough to include them all.
Then, if general, every one of these names should be struck out.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
That might be a good
suggestion.
There is no use naming half of these officials and leaving out the other half of the officials whom we know to be controlled by this clause.
Is there any objection to "registrar" being inserted?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I do not want to change the clause. It has been very carefully drawn.

It may have been very carefully drawn, but that is no reason why this amendment should not be accepted.

The returning officer is among those who must be sworn, and certain penalties are provided in relation to misconduct by him and the other officials enumerated. But the registrar is more exposed to temptation to evade the law than any of these other officials, by reason of his office. 'Supposing any penalty is provided for in case of misconduct, and we want to proceed against a registrar, we would probably be met by the argument: This is a penal section and it must be interpreted very strictly; therefore who are the election officers who iare subject-to this penalty? But when we come to enumerate them we find the registrar is left out. I think the contention of my hon. friend from Joliette (Mr. Denis) is well founded, and that the word "registrar" ought to be included, because the registrar is an official who can use his position to party advantage at an election.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Will it shorten the discussion if we include it?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Then we will include it.
Good.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I move that after the
word "returning officer" in the twenty-sixth line we insert the word "registrar."
Amendment (Mr. Guthrie) agreed to and paragraph (e) as amended agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
We have used the term "election papers" in several later clauses of the Bill. I move therefore that a paragraph be added, which I suppose for the present we may term (e-1), as follows:
" Election papers " mean all ballot papers, including those unused, poll books, lists of voters, and other statements used at a polling station, and all other documents sent by any returning officer to the Chief Electoral Officer in compliance with this Act or any instructions issued by the said Chief Electoral Officer.

What does the word "statements" mean?
Mr. GUTHRIE.: A certain statement has to be issued at the end of the poll showing the number of votes cast, for whom, and the number of unused ballots. One of these statements must be returned to the Chief Electoral Officer. These statements would also be called for in the case of controverted election proceedings. Instead of enumerating all these papers in each section we have framed this interpretation clause.
Should not the definition cover instructions issued by the Assistant Electoral Officer?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: That could only happen through the illness of the Chief Electoral Officer, and in that event his assistant would issue instructions as Chief Electoral Officer.
Not as assistant?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: He becomes the Acting Chief Electoral Officer. I have no objection to the additions. I therefore move that the words "or his assistant" 'be added to the proposed paragraph (e-1) after "Chief Electoral Officer."

Amendment agreed to, and paragraph (e-1) as amended agreed to.
On paragraph (g)-"elector":

Could not the words
"whether his name is or is not on any list of voters" be struck out?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
No; "voter" in this Act is a man who votes or whose name is on the voters' list. "Elector" in this Act is a man whose name is not on the list but whose name is entitled to go on the list.
