Paragraph (g) agreed to.
On paragraph (i)-"form":

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I move that we add here as a new paragraph the following words, in order to define the word "hours":
" Hours of the day " when mentioned in this Act shall be calculated upon standard time.

What does "standard time" mean?
Mr.'GUTHRIE: Standard time is defined in our statutes, I understand, as calculated from Greenwich.
There are different kinds of standard time-Eastern standard time, Atlantic standard time, Central, Western and Pacific.
Has the minister the definition of "standard time" at hand?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
No, but our standard time, as I understand it, is twenty minutes after solar time, and solar time in this country is computed so many hours-five hours and something-after Greenwich time. Whether you are in the East, the Centre or the West, standard time is fixed. There are a number of judicial decisions on the question. I know that the Ontario

statute fixes it definitely, and I think it is fixed also by Dominion statute.

I think that this paragraph ought to be further considered, because standard time in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick is one hour earlier than standard time in Quebec and Ontario; it is different in different parts of the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Well, they would all come within my definition. We know what standard time in Ontario is; they know what it is in Manitoba; they know what it is in every province of Canada. The simple term "standard time" is a well known and accepted term.
In a province of large area, the adoption of "standard time," as defined by the minister, might result in the time being different in different portions of that province.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: A very slight difference.

But a very slight difference may be material in this case. Possibly each province has defined what shall be standard time within that province. In that case it would be well to say:	"standard
time as defined by the provincial legislature." But to adopt the term "standard time" alone may give rise to confusion and difficulty.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Well, I do not want any difficulty or doubt to exist on the subject; we will let that definition stand.
Proposed paragraph stands.
On paragraph (Ik)-"list of voters":

If there is any possibility of the provincial lists being adopted, it would be necessary to refer to them as "provincial lists". If this paragraph stands as it is and the lists in Nova Scotia are accepted, they will not have been prepared "as required by this Act." Of course, we are still hopeful that, at all events so far as Nova Scotia is concerned, the electoral lists will be the provincial lists.
Vain hope.

My hon. friend seems to know all that is coming and going; he says it is a vain hope. But we still cling to the hope, vain though it may be; and we shall die with our faces to the foe and fighting desperately.

If this paragraph is to stand, I have nothing further to say. If it is to be adhered to now, may I suggest
that it end with the words "as required by this Act"? Whatever is required by the Act will then be covered by this definition.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Well, there are several places in the Act where the provincial lists are referred to. In clause 32 they are referred to several times; they are made the basis of our voters' lists where those lists are not more . than a year old. I cannot see any objection to having some definition of them in the interpretation clause.

It might be well to let this stand until the "list" clauses are considered. If this were the only clause left,
I would not object, but there aTe several others, and if there is to be further discussion on the "list" clauses, it is only reasonable that this should stand until that discussion takes place.
Paragraph (k) stands.
On paragraph (1)-member:

What is the difference between a "member of the House of Commons of Canada" and a "person elected to serve in the House of Commons of Canada?" The only difference that I can see is the fact that a member of the House of Commons is sworn before he can take his seat. Paragraph (b) defines a candidate as "any person elected to serve in the House of Commons of Canada at an, election." It is difficult to have a man elected to serve as a member of the House of Commons of Canada otherwise than at an election, whether it be by acclamation or at a contested election.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
There may be a great
distinction. A person elected to serve may never sit; he may get into the election courts and find that he was not legally elected although returned by the returning officer. A member of the House of Commons .means a man who has been actually introduced and who has taken his seat.

Do I understand from
that, that a man who has been elected and declared elected and whose election is not protested, is considered to be a "candidate" until after he is sworn?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: A man, for the purpose of those Acts, continues to be a "candidate" notwithstanding the fact that he has been elected, and as such is still liable for anything he may have done during the campaign.

A man cannot be tried
at election trials for acts he has done after

he has been declared elected by the returning officer, and I claim he ceases to be a candidate the moment he has been declared to have been elected by the returning officer. A man who is a candidate is a candidate from the date he puts in his nomination until the date of the election. But, under the definition of the minister, a man would be both a candidate 'and a member of this House. My election was protested; it was fought for three years, and I sat in this House during all that time, and during all that time I do not think I could have been reproached at the trial for anything that took place after the election was over.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: No, you could not.

Then, I am no longer a candidate because I am liable only as a candidate. Whether I am a member of the House or not, my condition up to the date I was declared to be a member does not change. The proceedings are taken against me as a candidate, and I was a candidate until the date I was declared elected. The moment I was declared elected, I ceased to be a candidate.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Technically and in accordance with ordinary English, as we would understand the English language, all that my hon. friend has said is correct. He is a candidate until he is elected; then, he is a member. But our law provides that during the time when a man is a candidate, if he does certain things, the consequences of his wrong-doing may be visited upon him, notwithstanding the fact that he has become a member; the mere fact of his having become a member does not relieve him from th consequences of his former acts. He is still, in the eye of the law, a candidate, answerable under the penal clauses of the Controverted Elections Act which has been in force for a long time. It has always been recognized that, under the Controverted Elections Act, the word "candidate" means any person elected to serve as a member and any person who has been nominated and who has not been elected. The object of this is to preserve the obligation and responsibility of that man for all acts done by him during his electoral contest when he was in fact a candidate. The mere fact that he has been elected a member dos not relieve him in any way and does not change his public or official capacity; he is still a candidate in the eye of the law, although, in fact, he is not.

I agree with the minister. The fact that my condition changes does not relieve me of responsibility for acts done by me when I bore another title. But what I think is not correct is that in the Controverted Elections Act it says that a member elected is a candidate. He is not and he cannot be. I cannot have a dual position. I was a member of the House of Commons, as I said just now, and I was not a candidate. I will not put up my knowledge of English against that of the Acting Solicitor General, but I will give an example. Suppose I am going to act as clerk for the Minister of Justice, and I am under bond, the hon. member for Brome (Mr. Mc-Master) being my bondsman, and the Minister of Justice says that my services are not worth the money, and he fires me.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I could not do that.

After I am fired, I cease to be a clerk of the Minister of Justice. I have committed something for which my bondsman would be called upon to answer; but does the fact that I am no longer clerk of the Minister of Justice relieve the bondsman? The question is very simple; the question is not whether I am called a candidate or a member; the point is that I was acting in a certain capacity at a certain time and that while I was acting in that capacity the law said that I should not do certain things. Therefore, it is an anomaly to say that an election will take place on such-and-such a date and when the election is over, the person who has the majority of votes will be elected, even though the election is contested, and at the same time to say that that man, although elected to the House of Commons, is still a candidate.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Our law so says.
If it is wrong, let us amend it.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: In that case we would have to amend a good many laws.
We are here for reconstruct dn.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The Controverted Elections Act and other Acts are worded in that way. I agree that technically a man after election day ceases to be a candidate, but in the eyes of the penal law, he is still a candidate.
Paragraph (1) agreed to.

On paragraph (v) " urban polling division ":
Would incorporated towns with a population of less than a thousand be urban, or rural?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I think the Bill requires a population of a thousand and incorporation. Anything under a thousand would be a rural division if I read the provision rightly. -
Even if it is incorporated?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The first requirement
is having a population of more than one
thousand. It would require to be an incorporated place also-they must be places which under the provincial law, are_ cities, towns or incorporated villages.	.
There are towns in Canada which are incorporated and have less than one thousand population.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: As this clause is drawn, they would be considered rural divisions unless they meet both of these qualifications:	first, that they have one thousand population, and secondly, that they are incorporated. If they lack in either respect, as the clause is drawn, they would be rural divisions. I do not know whether we might change the provision; I have an open mind on it, anyway.
We have a lot of incorporated villages that have not a thousand population.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Supposing we substitute the word " or " for the word " and."
Would the minister read the next paragraph?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
(w) " rural polling- division " means a polling division whereof no part is contained within a place having a population of more than one thousand persons, and which place under the provincial law is a city, town or incorporated village.
The first paragraph can be altered to in-elude ever'y place with a population of a thousand by substituting the word " or " for the word " and." That would mean that any place with a thousand population or which was in-coroorated under provincial law as a city, town or village, would be an urban division.

Any place which had a
thousand population irrespective of whether it was incorporated under provincial law. The question would be to define the limitation of the word " place."
And the population also.

For instance, we might
call a township a place, might we not? And if this township had one thousand of a population it would become an urban poll ing division under the suggestion of the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: That would be a difficulty.

We have in our province a lot of villages and small towns that should be more properly considered rural than urban. I should think that a popu-

lation of two thousand would not be too , schedule to the Act what towns and cities large a limit to make.	in the Dominion are urban.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: If we are going to have any limitation at all it should be one thousand. We have innumerable villages in Canada with a population running between one thousand and two thousand people that are all incorporated and have the whole working machinery of a municipality. It was to enable those to become urban divisions that a population of one thousand was fixed upon. But my hon. friend will see that it is not what this Act says with regard to incorporation, it is what the province of Quebec has declared, that would affect his riding. A " place" in my hon. friend's constituency in the province of Quebec would have to have in the first place a population of one thousand people. In the second place it would have to be, by the laws of Quebec, either a city, town or village. If it had both these qualifications then it would be an urban division. If it had the thousand population but no incorporation it would still be a rural division. If it had incorporation and less than one thousand people it would still be a rural division. That was the intention of the draftsman when he prepared the Act.
There are a number of small towns in my constituency. The town of Actonvale, for example, has a population of thirteen hundred or fourteen hundred, and it is an incorporated town.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Then you are all right.

We are all right to be considered as an urban division, but I would rather be under a Tural division.
Paragraph (v) agreed to.
On paragraph (w)-rural polling division:

I think the minister ought to put beyond doubt what is an urban and what is a rural polling division, because it is a matter of very great importance in connection with the voting. The hours of voting are different in the rural division from those in the urban division, and the method of making the lists is different, as I understand the Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
What does my hon.
friend suggest in order to place it beyond doubt?
I would suggest we should make it certain by stating in a

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: It would be out of date in six months at the rate that new towns are springing up.

The section does not seem clear to me, but if the minister thinks it is clear very good.
Mr. GUTHlRIE:	It is the Chief Electoral Officer who has the power to decide.
Why not give him the power to issue a proclamation at the time he is issuing other proclamations, dealing with this matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I think that would be a very good idea. When we come to that clause we will insert a provision to enable him to state in his proclamation whether it is a rural or urban division.
Has the word " or " been substituted for the word " and " in the other paragraph?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: No, I did not make the change.

Will the census
settle what the population is, and if so should not the census be mentioned?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I do not suppose it is the census, it is the Chief Electoral Officer who will decide this by his proclamation It would be unfair to decide by a census almost ten years old. The object of making the Chief Electoral Officer the final referee in such matters is to avoid any difficulty or uncertainty, and I think that the suggestion of the leader of the Opposition would meet the difficulty in every respect, because we shall have a clause which will state that the Chief Electoral Officer, when the writ is issued, shall make a statement as to whether the division is rural or urban.

There is one point in connection with this section to which I desire to direct the attention of the minister. Something has been said about incorporated villages being sometimes incorporated although they have less than a thousand persons. Suppose you have an incorporated village of only seven hundred persons, will it fall within the definition of an "urban polling division" or a "rural polling division"?
It is a common practice in the West for rural electors to vote in the town or village. Will such rural electors have to register?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: If they are qualified electors in a town or village, which is recognized as such under this Act, then they have to register. If, however, they are rural voters entitled to vote in a rural division they do not register.
I am speaking of rural electors who vote in the polling division in the town.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: If the returning officer or the deputy returning officer fixes the polling station in the town that will not afiect their rights; he might fix it there for convenience. He shall fix it in the polling division.

I think the minister misunderstands the question of my hon. friend. Take my own town of over a thousand inhabitants. It takes in polling places in the country three or four miles around. The point my hon. friend wants to have made clear is whether the farmers three or four miles from town will have to register personally the same as voters in the town.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The question then is whether they belong to a rural or to an urban polling division.
The hon. member wants to know whether they would have to register.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: An urban polling division is described as a polling division which is wholly or partly contained within places having a population of more than one thousand persons. If the voters to whom my hon. friend refers voted in such a division they would form part of an urban division and would have to register.

I think that would be a hardship on such voters. Why should they not be permitted to vote in the polling division in the town without registering? Their names would be on the list anyway. The fact that they are rural electors and for convenience sake poll their votes in the town should not make it necessary for farmers living four and five miles from the polling station in the town to come in and register. Their names will be on the list compiled by the enumerator, so why ask them to come in and register the same as electors living in the town or city?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Does the hon. member say that their names will be on the list compiled by the enumerators?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Then they cannot be urban voters if their names are on the enumerator's list. If the returning officer, in fixing the polling division includes any portion of the country, his polling division, whether it be in city or town or incorporated village, will embrace the whole territory and every one in it must register. The returning officer must fix the polling divisions for the convenience of the people, and if they are voters six miles out there will be a polling division there and those voters will be enumerated. But if voters are part of an urban polling division they w'ill have to register; rural voters do not register.

There is a matter in regard to which I should like to have the opinion of the minister. I am not a lawyer and therefore am not conversant with this particular section. In the Yukon territory we have what is known as an unincorporated, town, and I want to be sure that provision is made for the voters in such a place. I desire to quote a few words from the Consolidated Ordinances of the Yukon Territory, dated 1914. Under the interpretation clause of Ordinance 88 the expression "town" means "any town organized under the provisions of this Ordinance." The clause says:
Whenever the Commissioner is satisfied by such proof as he requires that any portion of the Yukon Territory (no part of which is within the limits of any incorporated city or town) contains not less than ten dwelling houses, he may cause notice to be posted in three conspicuous places within such area (one of which shall be the post office therein) that it is proposed to establish the same as a town after the expiration of thirty days from such posting.
The Ordinance goes on to provide for the election of an overseer. I am not sure whether there is such * an unincorporated town in any of the provinces, and I would ask the minister to express an opinion on that point.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
That corresponds very much with what is known in Ontario as the police village. Such villages have not the full powers of incorporated municipalities, but they have certain municipal powers conferred upon them. Such a place as my hon. friend has mentioned would constitute under this Bill, a rural polling place. Paragraph (w) agreed to.
On paragraph (x)-voter:

This paragraph contains some objectionable features. It reads:
" Voter " means any elector whose name appears on any list of voters prepared or added to

as directed by this Act, and includes any person who, whether or not a voter as defined, applies to vote or has voted at an election.
If a man who has no business to go into a polling booth, who is not on the list and who is not qualified, goes in and asks for a ballot, he immediately becomes a voter. He says: "I am a voter; I have asked for a ballot; I have asked to be permitted to vote; therefore I am a voter." Every voter should vote. What are you going to do? You have made him a voter by allowing him to ask for a ballot. Why give rise to a complication of that kind?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I do not see how any such complication could arise. The last sentence of the section is meant to cover persons who have not been included in the list. Some man has been improperly left off the list; he is certainly an elector, he has the right to vote, he goes in and applies for a ballot and in the eye of the law he is a voter. If he votes improperly he is liable to very severe penalties.
Why not make it "and" instead of "or"?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Suppose he applies to vote and you do not let him vote but arrest him before he gets his vote in? For the penal part of this Act he is still a "voter."
Mr. McEElNZIE: This says that he is a voter if he applies for a vote. A voter must have certain qualifications, but this says that any man who applies for a ballot is a voter. If it does not mean that it does not mean anything.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
It is only to protect the public from improper voting. Paragraph (x) agreed to. .
On new proposed paragraph "Hours oi the day":

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
In regard to that question as to the definition of standard time my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty) has pointed out to me that the de facto standard time in each province is standard time. Standard or de facto time is not fixed by Dominion law but by custom or by provincial legislation. When the Daylight Saving Bill was before this House that was recognized. Class 2 says:
During the prescribed period in each year in which this Act is in force, the time, for general purposes in Canada, in each province, shall be one hour in advance of the time which under the law of the province is the time prescribed for such province, and, if there is no time so prescribed, of the accepted standard time.

I	think my definition fixing the hours of the day as meaning standard time will be the de facto standard time in each province.
Mr. BUREAU-That was defined for a special purpose.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
It is the only definition we have. It is the standard time which must have been in force under all our election laws heretofore passed in this country.
(Mr. BUREAU: We might say that the provincial time shall be the standard time as defined by the provincial statute.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
When we passed that legislation we found that in every province, I think without exception, there was legislation fixing the standard time. What makes it clear that we were proceeding on that basis is what happened later on. We had subsequently to amend that Act because, following our good example of enacting daylight saving, several provinces modified their laws and made their fixed time an hour later, which produced the result that our legislation said that the time should be an hour later than
II	p.m. the provincial time. Then the
provinces came in and made their time another hour later and we got it two hours later. We had to amend the law to make it read that it should be an hour later than the time as fixed by provincial legislation at the date of the enactment of the first statute. That brought us back into line again. However we found that there must be another exception to cover the case where a province did not fix a settled time and we provided that it should he an hour later than the de facto accepted standard time, whatever it was. I do not think we ran any great risk. After all in a statute words mean what they mean in ordinary language. You do not need a special definition unless you wish to make them mean something different. When we read a time table in a newspaper stating that a train will leave at such an hour, standard time, do we not all know what it means? Why should you put a technical meaning upon the words of a statute?
They have eastern standard time, and central standard time.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: These are different standard times. In the east there is eastern standard time, in the centre central standard time, and so on across the continent. It is the accepted meaning.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: The only object in introducing it is to avoid any complication that might arise as a result of this so-called daylight saving.

Paragraph agreed to.
On clause 28-polling divisions:

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The question is on the amendment moved by the member for Brome (Mr. McMaster).

When this
clause first came up for consideration I think the minister mentioned that he was not aware of any cases where difficulty had arisen because of the returning officer being allowed discretion to state what particular localities he wished to designate as polling subdivisions. I would like to draw the attention of the minister to the recent byelection in Timiskaming, which was held under a clause precisely similar to the one we are now considering. While that byelection was in progress I received from Cochrane, Ontario, the following telegram from the secretary of one of the political associations there:
Intolerable conditions obtain in Temiskaming by-election. Through use of same polling divisions as in 1917 election hundreds of voters are practically disfranchised through inaccessibility of polls fixed. Fredericlchouse, Fauquier, Smooth Rock Falls, Glackmeyer Township where hundreds of votes were polled in the provincial elections are without polls; whereas Poller Post Office where eight votes were polled then and other small places have a federal poll. Cannot the provincial polling stations be used as subdivision 'of Federal polls by Order in Council?
IBefore replying to that telegram I spoke to one of the members of the Government about it and was informed that the Acting Prime Minister had received a similar telegram. I replied by saying:
I am informed that Acting Prime Ministet has received telegram similar to one sent by you to me, and that Clerk of the Crown in Chancery is at present looking into conditions re polling facilities. If matters not satisfactorily ' arranged within next few days, please wire me again, and I shall bring it up for public discussion in Parliament.
I understand that the 'Clerk of the Crown in Chancery did have the matter under review, and found that while it was obviously desirable that the polling divisions should be more in accordance with what would suit the convenience of the electors, yet he had not the power to make the necessary alterations, and in consequence in many of the districts the change was not made. I have since received the following letter in further explanation of the actual situation in the Timiskaming election:
As an example of the hardships which will practically disenfranchise hundreds of voters if polls are left as in 1917-
In 1917 they were fixed in accordance with a provision very similar to the one we are now discussing.

I will cite Smooth Rock Falls with its 385 employees of the Mattagami Pulp and Paper Company Limited, who have wives and daughters also entitled to vote. If the poll is fixed at Jaeksonboro as in 1917 it will be impossible for hundreds to go and vote. The only road between the two places is over the ice and there will be slush in April forbidding traffic. There is also a small switchback engine with box-car that could cover the 4 miles during the day but it is hardly practicable on a large scale, while the easy solution would be to have two polls in this division ; one at Jaeksonboro and one at Smooth Rock Falls.
Instead of only one poll for Moonbeam, Fauquier and Gregoire Mills, urhich are 4 and 6 miles apart (10 miles from Gregoire Mills to Moonbeam) over the track, there should be three polls as in the provincial elections.
Frederickhouse, where the Beaver Abitibi Company has a mill employing a few hundred hands has no poll because there is a poll at Clute in the same township. But the only way to get to Clute Post Office from Frederickhouse is to drive six miles in slush in April to Cochrane then about 8 miles out to Clute. For this difficulty there should be a poll at this industrial and agricultural centre of Frederickhouse also, and a poll at LaRocque Post Office which is in the geographical centre of Glackmeyer Township, whose inhabitants have to go to Clute Post Office out of the way to vote. Glackmeyer township has become an incorporated municipality recently and it has no poll in its limits.
Norembega in Fox Township has a large population which must, walk 6 miles and over a railway bridge to vote at Browser. Such Prussian methods force, needless to say, all our settlers' wives to stay at home and their husbands' votes are offset by the women's votes in the towns where polls are accessible.
The writer goes on to say that he is trying to have that corrected by adopting the provincial polling divisions.
I might also mention to my hon. friend that I think it was brought to the attention of the Government that during the last Dominion general election in the district of Edmonton, where the Hon. Frank Oliver was a candidate, the electors in what is known as Faulkner were obliged to cut their way for thirty miles through bush to reach the poll at a railway pump house, and many of them found it impossible to get there. That condition arose through leaving to the returning officer full discretion in the location of the polling divisions. I am sure my hon. friend does not want such an embarrassing situation to arise in the future, and I would suggest that he consider amending this section. In this connection let me say that I have consulted the member for Bro'me (Mr, McMaster) and he has given

me authority to withdraw his amendment, should the minister see fit to accept what I am about to suggest. I realize that the minister may desire ithat the returning officer should have some discretion, and he should not be obliged to rigidly follow the provincial divisions if there are good and substantial reasons for departing from them, and therefore I would ask the minister to consider striking out the words:
He may adopt, it convenient for the occasion, any or all of the polling divisions or subdivisions established under the laws of the province for provincial or municipal elections.
And substituting the following:
Unless there are good and substantial reasons to the contrary, of which he shall make a record in his return, the returning officer shall adopt any or all of the polling divisions or subdivisions established under the laws of the province for municipal or provincial elections.
That simply recognizes the established polling divisions and requires the returning officer to adopt them unless there are good and substantial reasons to the contrary, in which event he must put those reasons on record. I will not propose this amendment unless the minister desires me to do so, but I think if he peruses it he will see the reasonableness of my suggestion in view of the difficulties that were experienced in the last elections.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Of course, one outstanding difficulty is that the ridings are not coextensive, and consequently in a great many cases the polling subdivisions will not be co-extensive.
Quite so.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I understand in practice not only the municipal but also the provincial polling divisions are adopted. However, I would like to study the amendment.

What the minister has just said would be to my mind a good and substantial reason for not adopting all provincial polling divisions where
[Mr Mackenzie King.]
the ridings were not co-extensive and I think my suggestion meets what he has in mind.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
That would go in at
line 24, striking out the words " he may adopt, if convenient for the occasion"?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Well, I suppose the
returning officer should be the judge as to whether there are " good and substantial reasons."

That leaves it to him. I understood that my hon. friend was prepared to concede that point to the member for Brome. We discussed this matter together and we thought that by adding a provision requiring the returning officer to give substantial reasons why he did not adopt the provincial divisions would be providing greater security for tlje electors.

speechtext:
Well then, I will accept that suggestion.

On clause 33-when new lists of voters unnecessary:

Inasmuch as
this clause relates to the lists of voters, would it not be wise to let it stand along with the other one we are holding?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
If we change the other
clause, it would follow that we would change this clause also, but I would like to pass as many as we can.
Very good.
Clause agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I move that we reconsider clause 45 and allow it to stand. My reason for this is that it has been pointed out by the Assistant Clerk of the Crown in Chancery that the language in this clause and clause 44 is not very appropriate and that the clauses should be transposed to some extent. He will give me corrected drafts and I will propose the amendments when this Bill is again before the committee.
Motion agreed to.
As a matter of information might I ask if clause 62 has been disposed of?	.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Clause 62 has been carried.
Was any amendment made to it?	1

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: In line 23 the words were added "unable to read."
Would it be in order for me to make a suggestion with respect to clause 62?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It would not be in order without obtaining the unanimous consent of the committee to return to that clause. I will endeavour to secure the unanimous consent of the committee for the hon. member. Mr. Power moves, by unanimous consent, that the committee return to consideration of clause 62 which has been carried.
Motion agreed to.

Subsection 9 of section 62 reads as follows:
Whenever the deputy returning officer does not understand the language spoken hy any voter that officer shall swear an interpreter, who shall be the means of communication between him and the voter with reference to all matters required to enable such voter to vote, and in case no interpreter is found, such voter shall not he allowed to vote.
Take the case of a Frenchman in Toronto, who finds that he is unable to speak, English. The deputy returning officer does not understand him and cannot find an interpreter, and this man will be deprived of his vote. Or take the case of an English Canadian somewhere in Quebec, who cannot speak French. If an interpreter cannot be found 'this man will also be deprived of his vote.
They all understand English down there.
I am simply suggesting this to the minister. I make no comment on it whatever, but leave the matter to his good sense.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I do not think such a case as the hon. gentleman has mentioned could arise. This is identically the same provision as in the old law.
I do not care whether it is old law or not. If an injustice is done it should be remedied.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I never heard of an injustice being done under this provision, and I cannot imagine anything of the kind.

Section agreed to.
On section 100-advance polls for railway employees and others:

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Clause 100 was allowed to stand over last night in order that we might draft a section to meet certain objections that were then raised. I have drafted a section in which I have en-

deavoured to carry out the suggestions which were made. I move to amend section 100 by striking out all the words in subsection 14, and substituting therefor the following words:
(14) At the close ol the poll each day the deputy returning officer shall in the presence of such of the candidates or their agents or of the electors representing candidates as may he entitled to be present and are present :*-*
(a)	Unseal and open the ballot box.
(b)	Empty the ballots (in such manner as not to disclose for whom any elector has voted) into a special envelope supplied for the purpose.
(c)	Seal such envelope.
(d)	Count the unused ballots and the certificates in form TT which up to that time have
been presented.
(e)	Place the unused ballots and certificates in form TT in another envelope which shall be supplied for the purpose.
(f)	Endorse thereon the number of such unused ballots and certificates in form TT.
(g)	Seal up the said envelope.
The Deputy Returning Officer shall and such candidates and their agents or electors representing candidates as are present may affix their seals or signatures or both to both envelopes and the Deputy Returning Officer shall then place both envelopes in the ballot box and lock the same and the Deputy Returning Officer shall and every candidate or agent present who desires to do so may affix their respective seals and signatures to the ballot box in such a manner that the box cannot be opened or anything deposited therein or removed therefrom without breaking such seals.
At the re-opening of the poll each day the ballot box shall be opened and the envelope containing the unused ballots shall be taken out and opened, the ballot box being immediately thereafter locked and kept locked except as herein otherwise provided.
I also move to insert in subelause 15, line 33 after the word " box," the following words:
and the sealed envelopes containing ballots.
I also move to insert as a new subelause immediately after subclause 15:
Subject to the provisions of this section the provisions of this Act relating to polls shall, in so far as applicable, apply to advance polls.
The effect of that would be to give the agents and officials in advance polls all the authority and cast on them all the duties that are cast on other officials and agents under the general clauses of the Act. I think that carries out fully and precisely the suggestions that were made last evening.
This is too long an amendment to be grasped on the spur o.f the moment, but we will have it in Hansard to-morrow. I for one caniot follow it now.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I submitted it to the
leader of the Opposition earlier in the day.
[Mr. Guthrie.)
I did not know that.

The minister
was kind enough to let me have a copy of the amendment earlier in the day, and I think what he has said to-night as to drafting it along the lines that were discussed last evening is quite correct. But may I, in that connection, ask him if he would not he agreeable to adding one or two words to make the intention a little clearer?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Certainly.

Where it is
suggested in subsection (e) that there should be sealed envelopes, something was said last night about endorsing on the outside of the envelope the number of ballots enclosed.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: That appears in paragraph (i).

That is true.
I was going to ask, however, if it might not be advisable after sealing the envelope to place upon it the number of the last ballot. That would be a precaution.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
The ballots are not
numbered.
The stubs are numbered, and it is possible from the stub to ascertain what the number of the last ballot was.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: If the deputy returning officer puts on the envelope the number of unused ballots and the number of the certificates voted upon, I would think that would be sufficient.

It would be
an additional precaution, but in view of the minister's statement I will not press it. Another point I was more particular about was the reopening of the boxes the following morning. I presume it is the minister's intention that they shall be reopened in the- same manner in which they were closed in the evening, that is to say in the presence of the candidates or their agents. I would therefore suggest to the minister that he insert in the last section after the word "opened" the following words:
by the deputy returning officer in the presence of such of the candidates or their agents or of the electors representing candidates as may be entitled to be present and are present.
This is to make sure that the opening of the box on the following day is in the presence of the deputy returning officer and the agents of the candidates.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
We have made the provisions of section 54 specially apply They

go pretty fully into the counting o'f the ballots. However, I see no objection and move to add the words my hon. friend suggests.

The effect of this amendment will be that the ballots cast on the first two days will remain in the custody of the returning officer, enclosed in envelopes which will not be opened for the purpose of counting, until the close of the poll at the end of the election.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: That is right.
Amendments agreed to.

I have nothing to say about this section except that there is a schedule, which this amendment Tefers to. in which certain towns are named as advance polls. I see that the town in which I live, North Sydney, is mentioned in that schedule. I venture to say that no one in North Sydney ever asked to have that place included in this schedule, and there is no necessity for it to be there. I do not know of any travelling agents residing at North Sydney. It is a railway station, but it is not a terminus at which railway men reside; and I have never heard of any necessity for having an advance poll placed in that town. I do not see why we should go to the expense of holding a poll for three days in a place where hardly any number of the class of electors concerned will vote.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The committee cannot now enter into a discussion on the schedule to this Act. It would require a special motion to do so.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I may say in answer to my hon. friend that the schedule to this Act as drafted have been revised, a committee of railway men and the Commercial Travellers' Association having dealt with them. They have not made any change in regard to Nova Scotia, and I see that North Sydney still remains in the schedule. When we come to the schedule we shall be glad to have representations made, and if any place does not -want to be favoured with an advance poll no one will be anxious to impose anything unnecessary on it.

Subsection (1) says
"every railway employee, sailor, commercial traveller or other person" may vote at an advance poll. Does the minister not think that there ought to be something specific here? The words "or other person" are too broad.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Read on.

I have read the clause and I think that the classes contemplated in it ought to be stated specifically rather than comprehensively in the words "or other person," even though, as the minister implies, they may be more or less definitely enumerated further on in the clause. Any one might come along and say, "I shall be absent, because I have certain things to do in certain places and therefore I want to cast my vote at an advance poll."

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I am willing to strike out everything after the words "or other person."

I do mot see why you
should not enumerate the classes embraced in these words, such as fishermen, etc.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Well, for that matter, 1 do not see why we should not enumerate such persons as apple pickers. In my county some people g0' out for three or four weeks picking apples. After all, the important matter is the declaration which the voter has to make. He has to declare that his employment or calling is such as to necessitate from time to time his absence from his ordinary place of business, and his belief that because of the necessary absence from such place of residence in the pursuit of his calling or employment he will be unable to vote on polling day and therefore desires to vote in advance of polling day.

A lawyer may declar#
that.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, and so might a
doctor. Counsel in this country are engaged in assize courts and are away a great deal of their time..and if they can make that declaration conscientiously I do not see why they should not. I do not attach very much importance to the point, I must say.
According to the minister, he would give almost any one the privilege of voting. Under this clause almost any man in this House might make this declaration.
May I draw the attention of the minister to the fact that this is a declaration and not an oath?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
It is a declaration, but
if the voter makes a false statement he makes himself liable to a penalty.

Of course, the primary
object of the clause is to put the man upon his honour if not his oath. But any man

in this House might very easily make this declaration, and what would your advance poll mean? Hundreds of people might make this declaration, and although they might not have absolute knowledge that they were going to be absent on election day there might be a probability that they would be, and they would feel it no violation of conscience to make the statement here set out. To my mind, the words " or any other person " even plus the declaration which the minister has read and which I know is in the schedule of the Act, make this provision altogther too wide, and, I repeat, the person included in this very comprehensive expression ought to be specifically enumerated.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I presume the object of the draftsman was to make the clause wide.
Well, I do not see why it should be wide. The advance poll was made, in the first place, to meet the convenience of railway men.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: No.
Yes, and for sailors.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
No, first of all it was
intended for commercial travellers.

Commercial travellers
were afterwards added. Be that as it may, however, these three classes of people are away at all times and never forecast their movements, and consequently the advance election polls were instituted in Ontario, this being taken from their Act. If that is so, then I submit that the persons contemplated should be specifically stated.
This clause was drafted to allow certain classes of people to vote, whether railway employees, sailors or commercial travellers-

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Is ,the committee willing to stop there? Let us limit it at that.

-Let us enumerate the people we wish to take advantage of the advance polls and thus facilitate voting generally. Strike out "every railway employee, sailor, commercial traveller and say "every person, being an elector". It is either one of two things: You want to limit 'it to the people of certain callings or professions or you want to make it general. In the province of Queebc, speaking for the lawyers, we almost abandon the administration of justice so as to give every man a chance to vote. This is meant to apply to people of certain classes. We must either enumerate them or frame it in such a way as to facilitate voting generally, striking out any
[Mr Pardee.]
specification of classes and making it read "every person, being an elecor, whose name appears on the list."

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: That is too broad.
Then let us limit it to the classes of persons whom you want to prevent from losing their votes.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: When you start in mentioning classes of people you may be leaving out certain classes. I could tell you of a number of them. In my town there are bricklayers and stonecutters who are working away from the town and who leave on Monday morning and come back on Saturday night. In the season a large number of my people who are apple pickers are away for weeks; and there are other classes. The idea of giving this section breadth is to include any people who could make the declaration. I am not wedded to it. I am willing to limit it just as the Act was limited in the first instance or I am willing to take it as the section is drawn. We do not need to have a very long discussion about it. If bon. gentlemen have suggestions to make let us have them.

In Three Rivers and the St. Maurice valley there are men who go to the bush. If an election were held in September, November or February they would all be in the bush. I do not think it is intended to make 2,000 or 3,000 men vote in advance because they are out in the bush. They are away on account of their calling or profession and I do not think it should apply to these men.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I suppose that in my constituency there are 30 or 35 men who go out of town on Monday morning and come back Saturday night. They are bricklayers and stonecutters but I am not insisting on it. I am willing to leave the Act with the first limitation or take it as it is drawn. I think it is perfectly safe with the limitation.
Or other person?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: That is not a limitation. You should read the rest of it.
I think it should be limited to the three classes of persons named in the Act. '
I think it would be better to require a statement under oath. I do not think it should be strictly limited to any class because as the minister has said there are others.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Threshers.

Yes; they go
away just the same as the others do. Would it not be better to have them make a statement under oath?-

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: This declaration is punishable, if false, just the same as an oath would be.

Unless the law has been
changed the declaration is not a solemn declaration according to the Canada Evidence Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Whether it is a solemn declaration or whatever it is, it is punishable by subsection 15 of section 100. I think it is a pretty well guarded section, and I believe it will work out all right.

I am opposed to this section in its present form, and I would suggest that the simpler way would be to say "every person being an elector" and leave out the words "every railway employee, sailor, commercial traveller"? That is the simplest way.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
I think that is 'too
simple.

I move that the clause be made to read:
Every railway employee, sailor or commercial traveller, being an elector whose name appears on the list of voters.
I would' strike out the words "or other person" in line 2.
What about fishermen?
I would add "fisherman."

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
While I have no great
objection to the amendment I think that the clause is better as it is drawn particularly in view of what my hon. friend from Qu'-Appelle (Mr. Thomson) has said.
I realize there are a lot of other men whom I had not thought of. If the election came on in the fall of the year there are a great many men belonging to threshing outfits who would be away. When they came back on Saturday night they could vote at an advance poll. I prefer the section as it is drawn. I think the amendment should be voted down.
Amendment negatived; yeas 23, nays 35.

Since the committee is of the opinion that every person absent should under this clause have the right to vote at an advance poll, we might as well make it clear and strike out the enumeration which is not limitative.
Absolutely.

The hon. Minister of Justice has been a judge long enough to see the folly of such phraseology. We say, "John, Jack, and the rest," and we make "the rest include John and Jack."
The clause reads:
Every railway employee, sailor, commercial traveller or other personthat is, four classes. The clause should read:
Every person, being an elector-
That would be plain and clear.
The CHAIRA1AN: Do you propose it as an amendment?

Yes.
Mr. AlcKENZIE: 'If we were sure of having a staff of officers who were legal men those three words "or other person" would do no harm, for under the doctrine of ejusdem generis those words simply mean the classes that are mentioned before; but we are going to have laymen administering this Act, and they will determine that everybody who presents himself may vote. Aly hon. friend being a good lawyer knows the legal effect of these words, and I do not see why he leaves them in the clause.
Amendment negatived.
Clause as amended agreed to on division.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: I move that we go on to the forms.
I understand that a lot of corrections have to be made in those forms.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: They are clerical errors.
We need a rested mind and a clear brain to deal with those corrections. It is after twelve-we are getting old.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Aly hon. friend, the Alin-ister of Immigration (Mr. Calder) has made a very useful suggestion, namely, that a small committee might settle these forms, because the changes are such that any office clerk might make them.
We do not want to do that work here.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
On the understanding that I can get one or two of my friends opposite to meet me and go over these forms, I am satisfied, if that course is agree-

able to my hon. friend (Mr. Mackenzie King).

That is entirely
agreeable to us.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: We will get a committee of two or three. With that understanding I move that the committee rise and report progress.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: When the forms have been agreed upon they will have to be formally ratified by this committee,

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Yes.
Progress reported.
On motion of Rt. Hon. Mr. Doherty the House adjourned at 12.15 a.m. (Wednesday).
